text:
I declare open this hearing of the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee inquiry for the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the lands on which we meet today, and I pay our respects to their ancestors and elders past and present. I extend this respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who are joining us today.

Before we begin our estimates session, I'd like to speak on behalf of the committee in sending our thoughts to our colleague the member for Indi—Dr Helen Haines MP—her family, her team and her community as she continues to recover in hospital. The attack against Dr Haines on Monday was horrific. I know we have all come back to this place distressed and in shock at what has happened to our colleague and our friend. Dr Haines is much loved as a colleague here, as a strong advocate for her community back in Indi and indeed around the nation as a fierce participant in our democracy. Contributions will be made in the House of Representatives today from 10 am, and the committee will suspend to enable senators to attend the first of these statements as a mark of respect for Dr Haines. I note investigations are underway by Victoria Police, the AFP and ASIO, and I ask senators to please be mindful during these proceedings. Dr Haines is known to all of us as a person of integrity and someone who conducts public debate in a robust but respectful manner. As chair, I will especially be taking this spirit on board through our hearings, and I'm sure my fellow senators will join me in this.

Now, it feels odd to just go into my script after making that statement, but, into the Senate estimates proper: the Senate has referred to the committee the particulars of the proposed expenditure for 2026-27 for the portfolios of Home Affairs and the Attorney-General and other related documents. These are supplementary budget estimates proceedings, and the outcomes to be heard during today's proceedings are from the Attorney-General's portfolio. The committee has set Thursday 5 November 2026 as the date by which written questions on notice are to be provided to the secretariat. The committee has also decided that answers to written questions on notice should be returned to the secretariat by 5 pm on Thursday 17 December 2026. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice.

I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence to a committee. Officers and senators are familiar with the rules of the Senate governing estimates hearings. If you need assistance, the secretariat has copies of the rules.

The Senate by resolution in 1999 endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in the estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has the discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has also resolved that an officer of the department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution prohibits only questions asking for opinions on matters of policy and does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. I particularly draw the attention of witnesses to an order of the Senate of 13 May 2009, specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. The relevant extract will be incorporated into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

Witnesses are specifically reminded that a statement that information or a document is confidential or consists of advice to government is not a statement that meets the requirements of the 2009 order. Instead, witnesses are required to provide some specific indication of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of information or the document.

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. As chair, I'll be particularly vigilant in ensuring the cultural safety of First Nations people and culturally and racially marginalised groups during these proceedings. Officers called upon for the first time to answer a question should state their full name and their position for the Hansard record, and witnesses should speak clearly into the microphones, which, it seems, is not going to be an issue with these extra-large microphones that we've all got now!

The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Attorney-General's Department. I now welcome Senator the Hon. Don Farrell, representing the Attorney-General. I also call officers from the Attorney-General's Department in relation to cross-portfolio, corporate and general matters. Minister, would you like to make an opening statement?

Thank you for that opportunity. I probably should say something about Helen Haines. Helen and I got to know one another as she was very actively prosecuting the case on behalf of the prosecco makers in the King Valley. She was a very forceful advocate for her local community, and we had many meetings. My wife is very good friends with her husband, Phil. On behalf of us, personally, I want to wish Helen a safe and speedy recovery and let the family know that we're thinking of them and keeping them in our prayers.
Thank you, Minister. I understand Senator Cash has got a short comment.

I also, on behalf of the coalition, acknowledge Helen Haines. In particular, our thoughts and prayers are with her—we wish her a speedy recovery—and also with her staff, her family and her community at this time.
Thank you. Senator Shoebridge.

Thanks, Chair. On behalf of my party and my colleagues—Helen is considered a friend of many of us. It's been absolutely shattering, seeing what happened to Helen, to her family and to all of her team, who, somehow or other, are picking themselves up to continue to do the public service that they do in the face of the horrific attack on Helen. They have our fullest possible love and support and regard at this point, and we just hope that we will see Helen come back to be the community advocate, the voice of decency and principle and the bloody tough fighter for her community that she's proven herself always to be. Our thoughts are with her.
Thank you. Ms Jones, I understand you've got an opening statement.

I also want to acknowledge the horrific attack on the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines. It was an absolutely shocking event. This department has engaged extensively with Dr Haines in her capacity as Deputy Chair of the Parliamentary Joint Committee on the National Anti-Corruption Commission. On behalf of everyone in the department, I express our strongest support for Dr Haines, her family, her friends, her community and everyone who's worked with her here in this parliament.
Thank you. Are you okay for us to go to questions now?
Yes.
We'll begin with Senator Cash.
Minister, does the Albanese government believe that the use of the phrase 'globalise the intifada' is acceptable?

The issue of specific terms—I'm happy to raise the issue with the Attorney-General. From my own point of view, I have been a strong supporter of the state of Israel. I continue to be a strong supporter of the right of Israel to exist. To the extent that that term may imply the destruction of Israel, of course we do not support that suggestion. The government believes that the way forward in the Middle East—nothing is ever easy in the Middle East, but the way forward in the Middle East is to give recognition to both the right of Israel to exist within safe borders and to have the safety of its community but also that the Palestinians also have the right to have their own state and to live within safe borders. There are no easy solutions in the Middle East, I'm afraid.
That is not the question, with all due respect.

I understand it's not the question, but I'm trying to put the question into perspective. If things were as easy as banning one saying or another, that would be really good, but the Middle East is a really difficult issue to resolve. There's a very good book by Simon Sebag Montefiore on the history of Jerusalem, and it reflects all of the issues that have taken place over 5,000 years in that part of the world. To the extent that Australia can contribute and help to resolve issues, we want to do that. We want to do that in a careful way and in a way that reflects the rights of all of the people in the Middle East to safety and security.
Senator Cash, before you ask your next question, we've just had media join us in the room. I'm checking with the committee that it's okay for them to be here.
Subject to the normal rules.
Thank you. Senator Cash.
Senator, is the government committed to taking the strongest form of action here in Australia against antisemitism?
Yes.
Is the Albanese government aware that the Australian Human Rights Commission has nominated a Mr Ethan Floyd as a finalist for their Young People's Award?
I'm not particularly aware of that. Please understand that this is not my direct portfolio area.
I understand that. You're here representing the Attorney-General.
I understand that too.
Secretary, is your department aware that the Human Rights Commission has nominated Mr Ethan Floyd as a finalist for their Young People's Award?
Yes, I am aware of that.
When did you become aware of this?
I think it would have been in the course of late last week. I couldn't tell you with exact precision, but I think it was during the course of last week.
When you were made aware of this, who made you aware of this?
It was from within the department; an officer within the department—
Your department, not the AHRC?
My department, yes. I think it was in the context of a general discussion around the Human Rights Commission and preparing for estimates.
What was your reaction when you found out, on behalf of the government, that Mr Ethan Floyd had been nominated as a finalist for the Young People's Award?
I had not heard of him before that, so I had no visibility of his background. On the face of it, I didn't really have a strong view, because I wasn't really aware of him.
Are you now aware of his background?
I understand to the extent that I believe he was on the flotilla. I'm not quite sure of the exact language to describe it.
The Global Sumud Flotilla that the United States has condemned as a pro-Hamas initiative—that same flotilla?
I think that is correct, yes.
That is an outrageous slur on the Global Sumud Flotilla.
Thank you, Senator Shoebridge.
It's an outrageous slur.

And is this the same person that was listed as a speaker at a public forum in Darlington on 5 May this year to give a speech titled 'Why it's right to say: Globalise the Intifada', organised specifically to oppose the New South Wales government's proposal to prohibit that phrase? Was that brought to your attention?
No, it wasn't.
That's the first time—today, at this hearing—that you have heard of that?
Yes.
Did your department provide any advice to the AHRC, before Mr Floyd was nominated, about his nomination?
I would need to confirm this, but I don't believe we are normally consulted by the Australian Human Rights Commission in relation to who they nominate for their awards.

If you could confirm that for me. When you found out that Mr Floyd was part of the flotilla, did you raise any issues with the Human Rights Commission that this might contribute to fear within the Jewish community in Australia—that someone of this nature was being celebrated for his stance?
I have not engaged with the commission in relation to the nomination.
Did you raise this matter with the Attorney-General or her office?
Not with the Attorney-General and not with the office, no.

On becoming aware of Mr Floyd's participation in the flotilla that, as I said, has been described by the United States, one of our key allies, a Five Eyes partner, as a pro-Hamas initiative, you did not think to take it upon yourself—in fact, it was a one-word response to my question—that, given the minister's statement, given the government is committed to taking the strongest form of action against antisemitism in Australia, in particular given that, last December, 15 people of Jewish religion were slaughtered on Bondi Beach, you did not think, 'Perhaps I should raise this with the Attorney-General of Australia'?
No, I didn't raise it with the Attorney-General.
What action did you take post finding this out?
I have not taken any action. The Human Rights Commission is an independent entity, and the nomination of awards is a matter for the Human Rights Commission.

Yes, it is. You're also Secretary of the Attorney-General's Department. You have a minister sitting next to you that, sadly, is part of a government under which, in December last year, 15 Jewish people were slaughtered on Bondi Beach. You head the department which the minister has said is committed to taking the strongest form of action against antisemitism in this country. That is the appropriate response, obviously, from the minister. Yet, as the Secretary of the Attorney-General's Department, you did not think to take it upon yourself, if nothing else, to at least raise this with the Attorney-General herself.
No, I did not.
Senator Cash, I am going to need to share the call.
I will come back to this line of questioning.
Senator Shoebridge.
I assume, Secretary, you've received some information about the nomination about Ethan Floyd.
Yes—just from on their website.

I'll just read the nomination to put context to the questions and Senator Cash's point:

Ethan Floyd is a 23-year-old activist, community organiser and law student committed to advancing equality, dignity and justice. Since joining the School Strike 4 Climate movement as a teenager, he has advocated for human rights across a range of issues, including First Nations justice, housing, racial equality and LGBTIQA+ inclusion. Ethan supported the campaign for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice to Parliament and participated in the 2023 National First Nations' Water Roundtable at the Australian National University. He is a Director of the Tenants' Union of NSW and Democracy in Colour, a national racial justice organisation. At the University of Sydney, Ethan successfully advocated for free menstrual products across campus and, as an elected Fellow of the Senate, promoted investment practices aligned with human rights standards. In April 2026, Ethan joined the Global Sumud Flotilla to Gaza and has spoken publicly about his experiences. He continues to advocate for Palestinian freedom, dignity and self-determination.

They are the details in the award from the Australian Human Rights Commission.
You also forgot 'Greens candidate for New South Wales'.
Thank you, Senator Cash.
They are the details in the Human Rights Commission nomination. Had you had that in front of you?
No.

I think it's incredibly important for context for Senator Cash's fairly extraordinary start to this round of Senate estimates. Just also for the record, has Australia ever joined Donald Trump and his spokespeople in his declarations, his outrageous declarations, about the Sumud flotilla? Has the Australian government ever adopted Donald Trump and his administration's characterisation of the Sumud flotilla?
I really have to refer that to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. I don't have direct visibility of the position on that.

Minister, Donald Trump doesn't determine Australia's response to matters such as the Sumud flotilla. Senator Cash has put forward Donald Trump's characterisation. Your government doesn't simply follow, as Senator Cash suggests, Donald Trump's foreign policy, does it?
We disagree with Donald Trump on many things, for sure. I can go through, just in my trade portfolio, all of the areas where we disagree with—
Don't do that though, Minister.
I beg your pardon?
Don't do that, please.
Cutting me short like that, Senator Shoebridge, so early in proceedings is a little bit unfair!
I'm asking for an act of generosity.

I have to say that I'm not especially familiar with this area. I do say that there are many things where our government disagrees with President Trump. Of course, there's going to be an election in a couple of weeks time in the United States, and we'll see how many Americans themselves disagree with some of the policies of President Trump—
And perhaps Senator Cash.
I beg your pardon?
And some of the policies presented by Senator Cash as well. But could I just ask you—
I suspect Senator Cash is much closer to President Trump than—

I suspect that's right. Minister, are you aware that the Sumud flotilla's purpose was to bring food, medicine and critical supplies to the people of Gaza who are facing mass starvation and some of the most appalling material conditions possible as a result of the blockade by the State of Israel and the IDF? Are you aware that that was the purpose of the Sumud flotilla?

Look, I think I answered my response to that question in particular in general terms when I answered Senator Cash's issue. Our government believes in a practical outcome to resolve the dispute between Israel and the Palestinians. We believe in the right of Israel to exist within safe borders. I've just had the pleasure of re-reading Kershaw's book on Hitler and the shocking treatment of the Jews during World War II.
Minister, I'll just draw you back to my question, which is about the Sumud flotilla.

I'm trying to put it in perspective. This is not a one-event situation. There are multiple facets to the issues in the Middle East. Ensuring that people in Gaza receive adequate medical attention is an important issue, but the role that the federal government can play in this is not to exacerbate issues in the Middle East but to try and bring the parties together to the extent that a country like Australia can do that. We want to see peace in the Middle East. We want the Israelis to be able to live within safe borders and not have their people attacked the way they were on October 7 a couple of years ago. We also want the right of the Palestinians to also live within safe borders to be protected. That's the role I think Australia can play. That's the role that our government wants Australia to play. To the extent that we can influence world events, that is the role that we're going to play.

Moving to another issue, Secretary, have you sought any briefings from the Federal Court about the most recent evidence of serious data breaches involving the offshoring of transcripts that appear to have predated what I would describe as the VIQ data breaches by, it appears, a decade?
I can provide information on that. I note that that's in the justice and community group part of this hearing, not cross portfolio, but I do have information to provide.

Given that these matters may not only cut across one court or one agency but may cut across multiple agency data breaches, have you asked the agencies that are within your department's responsibility to review their data security as to whether or not they have also potentially breached people's data security or the government's data security by offshoring data given the experience that we now see from the Federal Court and, it appears, the Family Court, as well as what was the Federal Circuit Court?

We have certainly engaged on this issue specifically. We have engaged with agencies. I'll ask my chief operating officer to come to the table to talk to communications with portfolio agencies because I think there are a range of different agencies that have used transcription services over the time.

For context, Secretary, could I indicate that the evidence that appears to now be in the public domain was that in 2014 a former Auscript national manager made public interest disclosures in relation to the Family Court, the Federal Court and the AFP about the offshoring of sensitive data, and it appears nothing has been done. It's my understanding that all three of those agencies were within your department at the time.
I think that's correct.
Your question goes to the Auscript matters from 2012 to 2016. Is that what you're referring to?
Yes, although I had 2014, but you've obviously pushed it back to 2012. I think it's the same matter.

Broadly, they're the right dates. We have sought information from both the Federal Court of Australia entity and from the FCFCOA. I'm very conscious of the independence of the courts, but we're also very conscious of the importance of information security, so the department has sought some additional information from the courts. They have provided that very recently. We're considering that now and may have some further questions.
Alright.
I'm sure Senator Shoebridge looks forward to coming back to those questions. I'm now due to rotate the call.
I'm very much looking forward to coming back to that.
Senator Polley?

Good morning, everyone. Last estimates, the department provided an update on the work being undertaken to reform working-with-children checks. Following commitment to action through the Standing Council of Attorneys-General, the federal government invested some $37 million into IT. I was wondering if we could get an update on the progress in those areas.

Again, technically, that falls within the Justice and Communities Group area. But it does include engaging through SCAG, and the discussion around SCAG comes up in cross-portfolio. So I'll be guided by the chair. We can answer those questions now or under Justice and Communities Group.
It would be helpful if we could do it now.
Okay. Then I'll ask Mr Collett and his colleagues to answer that.
Senator, could I ask you to repeat the question?

Yes. At the last estimates, we got an update on the progress after the commitment and the agreement by the council of AGs. I just wanted to know where we're at now and what the progress is. There was some $37 million invested by the Commonwealth government into IT. I think it's very relevant, given what was on the news this morning. If you could, give us an update on that progress.

Thank you for your acknowledgement of the issues in the media today. Child safety remains an incredibly important priority for the government and for the department. We've continued to progress the working-with-children check reforms under the Standing Council of Attorneys-General agreement. At a high level, there were key policy decisions put to law officers at their meeting on 31 July. These go to the higher order policy and legislative changes that are needed across states and territories to achieve, ultimately, national recognition of working-with-children checks. I'll provide some high-level comments, and I'll ask my colleague Ms McMichael to unpack that in further detail.

It goes to the following: the policy frameworks around exclusion criteria—the sorts of criminal history offences and charges that are relevant; policy around risk assessments—how working-with-children check screening units standardise their practices around how they assess the risk of you or me or any other working-with-children check holder; and then policy decisions around information-sharing between and within jurisdictions. The standing council approved all of the matters put before them, and there's a range of further policy reform work we're doing now, as well as IT work with the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission. Ms McMichael, do you want to build on that?

In July, SCAG agreed to some of the milestones from when SCAG met at the July meeting. They agreed to a national baseline of serious criminal offences which automatically exclude or disqualify a person from holding a working-with-children check. They also agreed to a national baseline of standards for risk assessment processes. Those are the types of information that need to be checked for every applicant—as well as how that risk should be assessed and what information needs to be continually monitored throughout the working-with-children check. They also agreed to the different types of information that must be shared within and between jurisdictions to support those risk assessments. Those were the policy settings. Now, they're working on how that information will be shared, and then, early next year, they will focus on making the policy, operational and legislative changes within their jurisdictions to uplift to those baselines.

If I can add this, Senator, I'm conscious that you have a long interest in this very important area of policy reform. I'd like to put on the record the department's acknowledgement of and thanks to our state and territory colleagues across the justice departments and the community services departments. Responsibility for working-with-children checks sits under different ministers and different agencies across the states and territories. As both Ms McMichael and I noted, it is a very complex area of policy, legislative and IT reform, and it's a real example of the commitment across all levels of government to shift that and improve safety and protections for children in Australia. I'd like to record my thanks to our state and territory colleagues.
Yes, I agree with your comments there. In relation to IT, where is that process, and what's the timeframe for having that fully implemented?

Under the SCAG agreement, we have the National Continuous Checking Capability, which is being built by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission. They've built a pilot which became adoption-ready at the end of last year, and now the ACIC is working with jurisdictions to support them to onboard to the pilot. Under the SCAG agreement, jurisdictions are to make best endeavours to onboard to the pilot by the end of this year. There are a number of jurisdictions that we are expecting to onboard shortly. There's more information to come.

I'll add to that. The national continuous-checking capability provides, at the pilot level, additional access to Commonwealth information to state and territory screening units. When it's fully operational, it will provide that national service across all six million working-with-children-check holders. Importantly, it will then be available for governments to use in other forms of screening where you have workforces servicing vulnerable Australians, whether that's disability, aged care or so on. The applications are really quite broad.

I'm also conscious your question went to the funding that government provided through the MYEFO process last year. I also want to note for the committee's awareness the research that was funded by the Australian Institute of Criminology to better understand patterns of behaviour from perpetrators and the intersection with working-with-children-check screening. We know a lot, but the need for the evidence base to be built is critical, and the institute's upcoming research will be really important in informing ongoing reforms that states and territories can progress around best targeting risk assessments.

Have we got a timeline that you're working towards so that parents can have confidence that those working in areas where children are vulnerable won't be able to move from state to state and from jurisdiction to jurisdiction?

Absolutely. As Ms McMichael noted, the standing council's agreement that attorneys-general approved in November 2025 is publicly available on the department's website. The agreement is quite specific. It has very particular timeframes that attorneys-general have set for all governments to stage these reforms through, and some of those are already delivering. On the first priority, you would have heard the Attorney talk publicly around 'banned in one, banned in all'—that a decline in the ACT immediately causes a decline in Western Australia. All jurisdictions have now moved legislation. Since we last appeared before this committee, the Western Australian parliament has passed legislation in WA to provide for that. Those protections are already rolling out across this country.
Thank you, and thank you for the work. It's not an easy feat, bringing everyone together, so congratulations and thank you.
Senator Cash.

Can I turn to the nomination of Ethan Floyd for the Australian Human Rights Commission Young People's Award. I am going to table the nomination. Secretary, was it brought to your attention, when you were being informed of the nomination of Mr Floyd, that he is a Greens candidate for the next election for the seat of Cessnock in New South Wales?
No.
Sorry, Secretary. before you answer, I understand, Senator Cash, you want to table this document.
That is correct, yes—the nomination.
I'm putting that to the committee.
Yes please.
Thank you very much. That's tabled.
Thank you very much. Sorry, Secretary, what was your answer?
My answer is: no, I was not aware of that fact.
Is my question the first time that you've become aware that Mr Floyd is a Greens candidate for the next New South Wales election?
That's correct.
Minister, were you aware that Mr Floyd is a Greens candidate for the next New South Wales state election?
No, but I wouldn't expect a South Australian senator to know all of the candidates.
No, but we're talking about a federally funded government body that is putting forward people for awards.

You're asking me if I knew that this particular person was a candidate in a New South Wales state election, and my answer to that, Senator Cash, is no. I wouldn't have expected most people from Western Australia to know who the candidates were in New South Wales.

You'd be surprised that, when people in Western Australia that I spoke to found out that this person was nominated, they did their research to ensure that they properly understood what this person had done. Minister, are you aware of when this award will be given out?
No. I don't, Senator Cash, but I'm happy to find out for you and come back to you.
It's not a problem. I will provide that information to the committee.
Alright. Well, if you know the answer to the question, why are you asking me?

You'll understand shortly why I'm asking, and I can assure you it is no laughing matter, given the rise in antisemitism in this country under your government. Minister, the award is going to be handed out—

Antisemitism didn't begin in this government, Senator Cash. Antisemitism has been a curse right around the world for a very, very, very long time, Senator Cash, and you should know that. You should know that—
Fifteen people were slaughtered on Bondi Beach last year under your government.

You should know that. If you understand anything about the history of Israel, anything about the treatment of the Jews around the world, you will know that antisemitism did not begin and, unfortunately, won't end with this government.
No, but the rise of it in Australia to extraordinary—extraordinary—lengths has occurred under your government. Minister, this award—
There have been plenty of times in the history of Australia when antisemitism has been on the rise, Senator Cash. I wish it wasn't that way, but the fact of the matter is—
How many times have 15 people been slaughtered on Bondi Beach—
We are going to—
because of their religious beliefs, Minister?
Trying to take—

Minister, Senator Cash, we are just going to take a breath and resume the orderly way of estimates, which is the asking of questions and allowing possibly a slight pause and then a response to the questions without interruption. I would be grateful. Senator Cash, you've got the call for a question.
The question was: did the minister know when the Australian Human Rights Commission awards will be given out? He said he didn't. Secretary, are you aware of the date?
Please, Senator Cash. Please complete my answer, which was that I was going to find out for you.
No, and I said I will shortly advise the committee and it will become clear as to why. Secretary, are you aware of when the awards will be handed out?
Ms Chidgey has just pointed it out to me—10 December.
And what event occurs on 14 December?
Obviously, Senator, it's the one-year anniversary of the horrific events in Bondi.

That is correct. So, Minister, do you believe it is appropriate, given your answer to one of my initial questions—that being 'Is the government committed to taking the strongest form of action against antisemitism in this country?'—that a person nominated by the Australian Human Rights Commission, which is as you know a taxpayer funded body, for an Australian human rights award has, as part of his resume, the fact that 'on 5 May this year, he was a listed speaker at a public forum in Darlington titled "Why it's right to say globalised intifada"', organised to oppose the New South Wales government's proposal to prohibit that phrase; a person who participated in the global sumud flotilla in Gaza earlier this year that, as I have said, the United States condemned as a pro-Hamas—in other words, terrorist—initiative; a person who is a Greens candidate for the seat of Cessnock at the next election; and a person who, particularly given the government's statements this week about bringing down the tone, in February last year wrote that the climate movement must become dangerous again through stronger student and union strikes, blockades and disruption. Does the government believe that it is appropriate, given when these awards will be handed down—four days before the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre—that this person should be celebrated?

Senator Cash, I don't think it matters whether it's four days before the anniversary of the terrible shootings in Bondi or any other day. The job of the federal government, I think, in these circumstances, as you just said, is to bring down the heat, the tone, in all of the debate but also to fight antisemitism not just four days before the anniversary but every day. I can't repeat it often enough: antisemitism is a curse, and racism in this country is a curse. You trying to get a political advantage out of the terrible events in Bondi, I think, is inappropriate, Senator Cash. Certainly, in my discussions with the Jewish community, I don't think they want this to be a political issue. They want this to be the opportunity to continue to push back on antisemitism, and I don't think trying to exploit it politically is the way to reduce the temperature that Australian Jews now find themselves victim of. As a country, we need to push back and make it clear that antisemitism is unacceptable, as is any form of racism, in this country. I'm sure I speak for the Attorney-General. That's her objective as the chief law officer of this country. I know she does whatever she can to push back on antisemitism. This government will continue to do that. I mean, we engaged Jillian Segal. She had been on the IPEA board. She resigned from the IPEA board to take up the role to promote the issues of most concern to the Jewish community in this country.

We are doing everything we can in a democracy to push back on antisemitism and we will continue to do that. I just think your objective of trying to exploit those terrible events in Bondi and to blame the federal government for that is nothing short of unacceptable. I wish you'd reflect on what you're trying to do here. I don't think that by seeking to exploit this issue politically, you are in fact assisting the Jewish community in Australia. I'd ask you to reflect on what you're attempting to do here and perhaps review the nature of your questions.

So, Minister, in response to that, does the government believe it is appropriate then, given your commitment to tackling antisemitism in Australia for the federally funded body, the Australian Human Rights Commission, to nominate for celebration a person who believes it is alright to utilise the phrase in Australia 'globalise the intifada'?
Just before you respond to that, Minister, I'm going to indicate that once we've concluded this response, we will suspend, as I indicated at the beginning of proceedings today.
I think I've answered your question, Senator Cash.
We will now resume. I understand the committee still has further questions in cross-portfolio, so I'll return the call to Senator Cash.
Could I just get guidance in relation to questions on the prosecution of Ben Roberts-Smith insofar as it relates to departmental knowledge? Is that cross-portfolio or is it the next outcome?
I think it'll be in our Integrity and Security Group, which is not the next but the one after.
So, it's not Justice's?
No.
It's Integrity and Security.
Correct.
Thank you very much. Just very briefly then, Minister, to wrap up the previous line of questioning, does the government stand by the nomination of Ethan Floyd?

Nominations made by the Australian Human Rights Commission are a matter for the Australian Human Rights Commission. The AHRC is an independent entity, and the Attorney-General is not consulted on nominees.

I understand that, but independence actually means that the minister does not pick the finalists. It does not mean that the minister has no view, no questions and no responsibility for a commission within her own portfolio. Given it is a taxpayer funded body, I ask again: does the government stand by the nomination of Ethan Floyd?
I've answered your question.
We just have three more questions.
Senator Blyth.

I will be very, very brief. Just in following that up, obviously the minister or the Attorney-General can apply discretion here. Given this is taxpayer funded money, what is the government's position on whether the Human Rights Commission should vet those nominees? Is there a vetting process in place? It seems to be deficient if there is one. But where a nominee is selected and their statements conflict with Australian law or government position—I guess this is the question again—does the government stand by the Human Rights Commission and their nomination of Mr Floyd?
Who are you asking that question of?
That's for you, Minister.
For me? I have answered this on the previous occasion. If there's any more information that the Attorney-General can provide, I shall provide it to you in the course of today.
Thank you.
Senator Shoebridge.
Is the Australian Human Rights Commission an independent statutory authority? This question is to the secretary.
Yes. It's a statutory agency established under legislation with an independent accountable authority.

Thank you. Could I return to the questions I was asking about offshoring of data? I think we had some officials here. It's my understanding that this first became apparent in 2012. I now know it was 2012 to 2014. It involved the Family Court, the Federal Court and the Australian Federal Police, who were all agencies and/or entities inside the Attorney-General's Department. I asked previously if the department was advised about these data breaches—about data from Auscript being offshored from 2012 to 2014. Was the department advised?

We obviously became aware of the matters as they were raised in the media over the last week. We have done some searches to see if we can identify whether or not any notification was made to the department at that time. To date, we have not found any indication that we were advised.

The evidence seems to be that a former Auscript national manager made public interest disclosures to the family court, the Federal Court and the Australian Federal Police. Are you saying that there are no records that you've been able to find about any one of those three agencies raising those matters with the department?

So far, we have not found anything through our electronic searches in our file system to indicate that we were advised about it. I because it's from such a long time ago, there's no corporate knowledge of anyone recalling it, but we haven't identified anything in our systems.

Have you asked Ms Sia Lagos, who is, of course, the Principal Registrar of the Federal Court, for an explanation? I note that because an extract of an email from 2016 has been published which says, 'I have notified Ms Sia Lagos, who is acting chief executive officer and Principal Registrar of the Federal Court in Mr Soden's absence as I'm required to do so of the decisions and determinations I have made under the Public Interest Disclosure Act.' That was an email from the then deputy principal of the registrar, responding to the public interest disclosures. Have you sought advice from Ms Sia Lagos in her current position about what, if any, information she knew and provided to the department?

Yes, we have sought advice both from Ms Lagos, as the Principal Registrar of the Federal Court and the Federal Court entity, and from Mr Pringle, as the Principal Registrar of the FCFCOA. As you may be aware, given the timing of this particular historical event, there was the period where there was the Family Court, there was the period when the Family Court's corporate services were provided by the entity and then, of course, subsequently the Family Court and the Federal Circuit Court were brought together as the FCFCOA, so we have sought advice from both principal registrars and are continuing to work with them.
And what has the principal registrar, Ms Lagos, advised you about her knowledge of matters in at least 2016 and whether or not she informed the department of these very serious data breaches?

There are a couple of things I would say. One, I'm very conscious of the independence of the courts but also of the importance of the department having visibility. Two, I'm conscious that Ms Lagos will also be appearing this afternoon. But she has advised the department that she was advised of the PID in 2016 and it was referred, as was appropriate for the arrangements between the courts at the time, to the Family Court of Australia for consideration at that point. I would suggest that further details are really matter for Ms Lagos to explain to the committee.

So we now know that there are at least three agencies that were within the department and have been having data breaches offshore and data breaches through transcription services since, it appears, at least 2012. We have the then Family Court, the Federal Court and the Australian Federal Police. We've now had a raft of further data breaches, involving the privatised transcription service VIQ, that appears to cut across multiple courts, and we don't know the full extent of it. Will you undertake a full audit of agencies and entities inside your department to comprehend the extent of these data breaches and to ensure that Australians' data—and this is some of the most personal data you can imagine: transcripts in family courts, transcripts in federal courts, financial, personal—so we know the full extent of these data breaches?

I note that, in relation to the VIQ matter, we engaged with agencies across the portfolio that we were aware may have been using Vic. We've now had this more historical matter come to our attention. We will seek to understand which agencies within the portfolio may be affected, and we will work with them to identify whether or not there are any breaches relevant to them.
Well, which agencies within your portfolio responsibilities do you now know have used VIQ?

I'll ask Ms Inverarity to provide the specifics on that. I also note, as an addition to the secretary's comments, that there are a range of organisations within the government that have been involved in supporting the courts with this, including the Cyber Security Coordinator. The courts, as I believe they would have advised the committee last time, have engaged CyberCX as an expert firm to undertake analysis and provide advice to them.

I don't have the list of portfolio agencies who may have had contracts with VIQ, but what I can say is that we engaged with the Cyber Security Coordinator and the National Office of Cyber Security. When it became public that there were a range of Commonwealth entities who had contracts with VIQ, the National Office of Cyber Security then led engagement across the Commonwealth to undertake inquiries into the nature of the incidents. The department participated in the inquiries undertaken by the National Office of Cyber Security, and that was the context in which engagement with the portfolio occurred.

I've asked perhaps one of the most simple and straightforward questions that you could ask of the department in the face of what appear to be widespread damaging data breaches. Which agencies or entities inside the department have had contracts with VIQ and are therefore at risk? If you're not able or haven't come prepared to answer that most basic question at Senate estimates, I'm happy to continue this session until we get some answers about it.

The department itself had a contract with VIQ. That was because of the way that the Federal Court required transcripts to be obtained. For some courts, if the department as a party to litigation wished to obtain a transcript, it would be obtained through the relevant court. With the Federal Court, it was necessary for the department to go directly to VIQ, and that was the nature of the contractual arrangement that we had. It was to be able to procure transcripts in matters which we were a party to litigation in.

Have you undertaken an audit of those matters to determine whether or not any of those matters involving the Commonwealth had the data offshored in breach of our privacy laws, in breach of basic national security? Have you undertaken an audit of those matters?
I understand inquiries have been undertaken and we are not aware of any matters in which an order for a transcript that had been placed by the department was affected by the alleged breach.
I ask you to provide on notice full details of the contract between the department and VIQ. Do you know when that contract ran until?
I do not have that detail, but I'm happy to take it on notice.
Did it run until VIQ went into voluntary administration? Was it current as at that point?
I would need to take it on notice. I think it has been relatively contemporary, but the exact dates I'll have to take on notice.
So we have the department, we have the Federal Court and we have the Federal Circuit and Family Court. Do we have NCAT? Do they have a contract with VIQ?
Sorry—
Sorry. Did the AAT have a contract with VIQ?
We'd have to check that.
Did the ART?
I'm not sure off the top of my head. We can check that for you.

Well, I'm asking again. I could keep fishing for different agencies and/or entities. It is a straightforward question. Which agencies or entities inside the department had contracts with VIQ? You must be able to answer this.
I have asked our Chief Information Officer to ensure that I have a list as quickly as possible. I will have it available today.
Sorry, can I just make a correction? As I understand it, we did not have a contract with VIQ. We procured transcripts directly from them. I apologise.

We might press pause here because the answers are now more confusing, shedding more darkness than light on this matter. We will come back to this at a later point. What I don't want is to come back to it at a later point when there are agencies outside the courts, for example, and be told, 'We're not in a position to answer questions,' because their agency is outside the courts. So could I ask you to retain what officials are necessary to deal with this during the courts matters so we can move on to the next part of the session?
Yes.
Yes, we can do that.
I was going to ask you some questions about the use of generative AI in courts and tribunals more broadly, and I do have an aide-memoire to hand to you.
Are we now moving into the justice and communities section?

I just want to check whether or not it's best dealt with in cross-portfolio or if this might be better off dealt with in Justice and Communities. The questions will go to the fact that pretty much every court and tribunal in the country has a wildly different approaches to dealing with generative AI, causing significant confusion in the profession, particularly for unrepresented litigants. If you think that's best dealt with in the courts and tribunals session later today, I'm happy to take your guidance on that, Secretary.
I think that's correct. It is the officials from that group that have been engaged.
I'm also happy for you to have the aide-memoire in preparation for that.
Thank you.

My final question is on an FOI in relation to statements that were made by the minister and the government about the efficiencies that AI would produce to allow FOI backlogs and processing to be developed. Do you remember that exchange at the last estimates?
I do.

We've since progressed that FOI and found that the only information that's been released to us is two pages of what are described as 'talking points', and no evidence of any report or substantive body of work to justify the statements that both the Attorney and members of the department made about AI assisting in dealing with FOI. Was there ever a report obtained, was there ever credible advice obtained, before the Attorney-General made that statement?
The officers who can assist with those questions are in the Integrity and Security Group that's scheduled to appear later. They have come prepared to be able to talk to that issue.
Alright, we'll take that on then. Thank you, Chair.

With the caveat that Senator Shoebridge has asked for, we're now in a position to release other officers from the cross-portfolio outcome and now move to the Justice and Communities Group and Closing the Gap outcomes 10, 11 and 15. Senator Cash.

Secretary, I could probably pose this first question to you. It's in relation to what is now the final decision on the Tickle v Giggle case. Can you just explain, in plain English, what the decision means for biological-women-only spaces at law?
That's a matter in the human rights area, which is in the Integrity and Security Group.
So hold them over for integrity and security as well?
Yes.
We're going to have a lot in integrity and security. I will go to my next line of questioning, then: the Fair Work Court consultation.
Yes, you're in the right area.
On what date were you first informed that the government was considering establishing the new Fair Work Court?

Obviously, over the years, there has been ongoing discussion about the possibility of establishing a separate court with a fair work jurisdiction. It's been something that's come up multiple times over recent years. In terms of ahead of this iteration, I would have to take on notice the first time it was ever raised with me that the proposal was proceeding, but it was some period ahead of the announcement.
When were the chief justices of both the Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court advised of the final decision?
I'll ask Mr Collett to talk to that.
I'll be clear: the courts were both advised immediately prior to the government's announcement.
When you say 'immediately prior', what does that mean?
That day.
That day. Half an hour before? An hour before? Seven minutes before?
I don't know specifically when on that day. It was certainly before, but I couldn't tell you—
The courts were announced that day. Who advised them?
The Attorney-General's office advised the courts.
It was the A-G's office. Okay. And you—

Sorry; if I may—your question to Mr Collett specifically referred to the chief justices and when they were told. I just want to be precise, in that I myself don't have, and I don't think anyone here has, knowledge of whether the Attorney-General's office spoke directly to the chief justices or whether they spoke to somebody else involved in the administration of the courts.

That's fine. Perhaps on notice, then, you can take that. But the courts were advised that day. Could you take on notice when they were advised? Did either Chief Justice provide feedback on the Fair Work Court prior to the announcement on 23 July 2026?

The problem with that question is, as the secretary said, the concept of a fair work court or an industrial relations court is a longstanding one within the industrial relations policy space. I'm speculating, but I would imagine chief justices going back many years would've had different conversations about—
What about these particular chief justices, with all due respect, seeing as they are the current chief justices? In fact, Chief Justice Alstergren has been the Chief Justice for some time now.

As far as I'm aware, there was no formal correspondence that would amount to what you're describing. What we are unable to speak to is whether there were any personal engagements between the Attorney-General and the chief justices in other forums where views might have been expressed.
What role did the department have, then, in liaising with both courts?

Certainly, following the announcement from the Prime Minister, Minister Rishworth and the Attorney-General, we worked very closely with both courts. I'd note that the government has stood up a joint taskforce between our department and the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, given the crosscutting nature of this issue and the responsibility of both lead ministers. Right from the get-go of this work and noting the Prime Minister's comments around consultation, we've worked very closely with both courts and, through our colleagues in DEWR, the Fair Work Commission, and we've had a whole range of engagements, from the principal registrars down, with their corporate people and so on.

Can I just confirm that you said 'following the announcement' and that you meant 'following the announcement of the new court on 23 July 2026'? Does one not normally consult prior to an announcement, given that a new court is being established?

I can't speak to what 'normal' is, in that establishing a chapter III court is a very unusual thing for government to do. There are very few precedents here. As both the secretary and I have said earlier, there have been lots of conversations over the years around this sort of concept, and we've worked, since the government's announcement about the intention to establish the court, very closely with our colleagues in DEWR and with the courts and the commission.
Can I just confirm that no-one in the department advised either court in advance of the announcement? That was the role of the Attorney-General's office?
Yes.
That's correct.
OK. Is it possible to take on notice the consultation with both courts over the last 12 months in relation to what culminated in the announcement on 23 July 2026?
I'm not sure we'll have a specific answer to that, based on my comments already.

OK. Really, what I'm looking for is: given that we have announced a new court, which, as you've said, is a significant event, did you do any formal consultation with the courts on this particular announcement?
I can confirm that we did not.

You did not. Thank you. That was my understanding. Thank you for putting it on the Hansard record. Why did you not do any formal consultation with the two courts, given they are the leading courts in Australia that are affected, on this matter?

The announcement was a matter for government. Once it was announced, we established a task force between this department and the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations to oversee engagement with stakeholders. This department, in the context of the task force, took the lead on engaging—
'This department' is your department?
Yes. That followed the announcement and was the work of the task force. We can give you dates around those engagements.

Thank you. That would be greatly appreciated. Can I confirm—in relation to the announcement on 23 July, when was this department formally advised, given you are in charge of the courts, that the announcement was being made?
I think we might need to take that on notice. We should be able to provide that on notice.
Was it prior to the announcement, in terms of the courts, that day? Was it a week before? Surely someone here today has that knowledge within their possession.
We certainly had been doing policy work beforehand, and we were aware of the announcement beforehand, but we'd have to take on notice, as the secretary said, the question as to precisely when.
Since the announcement, have you received feedback at all, of any nature, from either of the courts?
Yes. We work very closely with the courts, since the announcement, through the joint task force, and have very much appreciated their support and technical expertise.
I might also mention that we did receive formal correspondence from Chief Justice Mortimer. I believe that was on 8 October.
And what was the nature of that correspondence from Chief Justice Mortimer?
It was providing information to assist in the development of the court. I don't have the correspondence with me.
That's not a problem. Has either the Chief Justice or the courts raised any concerns in relation to the announcement on 23 July 2026—the establishment of the new court?

I think they have sought to actively engage in the consultation to understand the impact that the establishment of a new court might have in terms of their pre-existing jurisdiction. They've sought to raise very constructive, practical issues that need to be taken into account to inform the model for the court, because there are a range of issues that go to jurisdiction, the model to support the court, the scope of its appellate jurisdiction—there's a range issues to be working through, and they've engaged in those discussions.
Senator Cash, I'm going to rotate the call. Senator Polley.
I want to go to the National Access to Justice Partnership and the $3.9 billion the government has invested with some questions.
Our relevant colleagues are coming up.
Thank you. My first question is: how is the Commonwealth evaluating the effectiveness of the investment in legal assistance services to improve access for justice for Australians?

How are we evaluating the effectiveness of the NAJP? We have a number of ways that we can do that. We have developed under the NAJP a data strategy which has been endorsed by the Standing Council of Attorneys-General, and we're now in the process of developing, in consultation with the sector and the states and territories, an outcomes framework which is also underpinned by a theory of change. We are developing that in a way so that we can have the data coming through the data strategy and then evaluate outcomes. The outcomes framework is not due to be finalised until 30 June 2027, so it's currently underway. In the meantime, we do receive six-monthly reporting, so we are able to see early information about service numbers increasing or otherwise, and have seen across the board in the first six months of reporting that there have been more clients assisted in the six months since the NAJP started than in the previous six months of the previous agreement. So we are looking at it in multiple different ways, but the full evaluation will come after we've finalised the outcomes framework.

I thought it was useful to get an update. With the upcoming summer and heightened risk of a natural disaster, how will the National Access to Justice Partnership actually help those that may be impacted by a disaster?

Under the NAJP we have rolled all funding in to allow legal assistance providers to determine how they address any client or service that they provide. But people affected by natural disasters are a priority client under the National Access to Justice Partnership. There's also a process through NEMA, which I'll ask Ms Mitchell to speak to, where we have developed off-the-shelf resources so that legal assistance providers can access funding where there are natural disasters.

In addition to what Ms Bogaart said about people affected by natural disasters being identified as national priority client groups under the NAJP, I would note that common post-disaster legal issues such as insurance and social security matters are also identified as Commonwealth service priorities under the NAJP. The National Emergency Management Agency has an off-the-shelf legal assistance package, and the department worked closely with NEMA in developing that package, which aims to streamline the activation process for post-disaster legal assistance resources, and that was a recommendation of the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements.

Great. We hear a lot about emerging technologies and, of course, AI. How do you see AI and other technologies assisting in the delivery of legal services to Australians? And how is the department supporting the legal assistance sector to build capacity in this area?

We see that AI offers significant opportunities in the legal system, including a potential to improve the efficiency of legal service delivery, improve access to justice, improve access to legal information and reduce administrative burden. In July 2026, the Standing Council of Attorneys-General agreed to establish an official level AI and access to justice working group. That working group is co-chaired by the Commonwealth and by the Victorian Department of Justice and Community Safety, and includes representation from all states and territories and New Zealand. The initial scope of that working group will be to share information on AI adoption, identify common issues, explore opportunities for collaboration and to look at specific opportunities for AI adoption to enhance access to justice. The working group has now met for the first time. We met on 15 October 2026 and considered a presentation on an AI scoping study that's been commissioned by the department, and had an opportunity to discuss opportunities and challenges of AI adoption in the legal system.
When's that due to meet again?
That will meet in approximately February next year. We will be looking to establish an expert reference group to inform the consideration of that group also in early 2027.

So we should be able to get an update at the next estimates. Thank you for that. I want to move on to some other questions, relating to the National Justice Reinvestment Program. How are the 26 active initiatives funded under the National Justice Reinvestment Program supporting the delivery of Closing the Gap targets? Can you give us an update, please.

The National Justice Reinvestment Program is aimed squarely at reducing incarceration rates, which are targets 10 and 11 under the National Agreement on Closing the Gap. The 26 initiatives have been in place for varying periods of time, but we are seeing some really promising early data and some strong progress from initiatives as they mature. Some of the early outcomes reported by individual initiatives to date—for example, one site reported estimated detention cost savings of at least $2.5 million over 12 months, one site reported crime rates had dropped by between 87 per cent and 95 per cent since their justice reinvestment activities had commenced and another site reported that 74 per cent of young people participating in its program had not offended since commencement and that 91 per cent of participants with an active court order were complying with those orders. Another initiative has had 242 referrals in 12 months. For example, one 14-year-old boy had had 77 police custody interactions since he was 10 years old and since engaging with the program has not been arrested or apprehended, since May 2025.

So we are seeing real impacts. These are community led, place based approaches where the local community determine what is needed to reduce those incarceration rates and contact with the justice system. Whilst we won't evaluate the program formally for another couple of years, to allow those programs to really take place and progress, we are seeing some really early signs of progress.
How's the department supporting the justice reinvestment initiative to build capability—for example, through access to place based data to support planning and decision-making?

We have been working really closely with those particular initiatives on access to data. A measurement and evaluation framework was co-designed with the initiatives over the course of most of last year and some of this year. That has now been finalised, which allows us to measure those outcomes but also to support communities to have and access their own local place based data. We have partnered, in the department, with the Australian Bureau of Statistics Life Course Data Initiative to provide initiatives with a range of locally tailored data products, including data on economic security, housing, education and health and data regarding investment from the Attorney-General's Department portfolio as a starting point. That team in the ABS has also delivered voluntary data literacy and capability building sessions for initiatives to provide guidance on how to interpret and visualise data and improve accessibility for users, and we're continuing to work to provide Commonwealth data but also to work with the states and territories to ensure that those initiatives can access state and territory data as well.
Thank you.
Senator Thorpe.

Thank you for appearing today. Since the 1991 Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, the recommendations of which this government has failed time and time again to implement, you did a Deloitte review in 2018. It was a desktop review that didn't talk to anyone. Someone just sat at the computer and said, 'Tick, tick, tick, tick.' What's the status? How many of the 339 recommendations to keep Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people alive and well have been implemented?

I do understand that the Deloitte review was a desktop exercise, and that it was self assessed, but what it did provide was an opportunity for government agencies to determine which recommendations they are responsible for and a framework for us to be able to assess ourselves against those. In the broader review, and in determining who is responsible for which, the Commonwealth has sole responsibility for 29 and joint responsibility with the states and territories for a further 194. AGD, this department, is responsible for 23 of those. We do monitor them and we do check the implementation of them regularly.

The Deloitte review, I understand, has had mixed responses as to its effectiveness, but it did find that 17 were complete, five were mostly complete and one was partially complete. Our main priority, as per the central finding of that royal commission, is to reduce incarceration rates of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. We do work, through a range of different mechanisms, towards those reductions.

Clearly, that's not working out for you. Clearly, we're the most incarcerated people on the planet. So again, I ask: how many have been implemented from your department, and why has it taken 35 years to implement the remainder?

We can provide more detail on notice but, in relation to the recommendations that were directed to us, we have actioned, to some degree, all of them. Some are complete, and some will never be complete because they require ongoing attention and work, but the vast majority are with the states and the territories. With the states and the territories, we continue to work through a range of mechanisms. I completely accept what you're saying in terms of—
I just heard that.

I accept what you're saying. In some jurisdictions, Closing the Gap 10 and 11 are going backwards. There's been some modest improvement in one jurisdiction in Victoria, but, otherwise, there have been ongoing challenges and a deterioration in some jurisdictions.
What recommendations is your department responsible for that have not been implemented?

I can provide on notice, and we have provided on notice in previous lines of questioning, the ones that we are responsible for and which ones are complete, mostly complete and partially complete. There are 23 of them. I could go through them if you want me to, but it might make more sense to provide them on notice.
There are 23 that haven't been—
There are 23 that AGD is responsible for, across all of the—
How many of the 23 have been implemented from your department?
Seventeen are complete, five are mostly complete and one is partially complete.
Which one's partially complete?

It is recommendation 99—to provide an interpreter without cost where there is doubt as to an Aboriginal defendant's ability to understand proceedings. While the government does that at the federal level and in federal courts, people do have access to interpreters and, also through our funding, to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Services. They can also access and use their funding for interpreters. We can't guarantee every single time that an interpreter can be found or in place, so that one is partially complete.

Yes, it's a big problem. I'll keep coming back to that until they carry me out in a box, because it's outrageous that we have a royal commission in this country with 339 recommendations and, 35 years later, we're still asking about them. There are still too many Aboriginal deaths in custody and there are still too many of our people incarcerated. Can I ask then how many recommendations have been implemented from the 1997 Bringing them home report.
The Department of Social Services is responsible for the implementation of that report.
So there are no responsibilities for your department?
No. The oversight of that particular royal commission sits with the Department of Social Services, so it's best to ask them for the implementation status.
Did you say they have oversight?
Yes.

Thank you. On 27 May 2025, the Senate agreed to my motion following the death of Kumanjayi White for all parliamentarians to address the overincarceration and deaths in custody of First Peoples. What action has the Attorney-General taken since then, and what support has she had?

We can talk to a range of measures working through the Standing Council of Attorneys-General, through the work on the Justice Policy Partnership, through the justice reinvestment program and ongoing engagement across the Commonwealth government. Ms Bogaart can take you through all those elements.

There are a range of things that the Attorney-General's Department is doing, as Ms Jones just mentioned. We have invested, or the government has invested, $115 million in the National Justice Reinvestment Program and an additional $10 million over four years in the Central Australian—
I'm happy to take that on notice, because you're going to eat up my last two minutes—my apologies. Could I have that on notice please.
What would you like on notice?
What you were about to read out in terms of the supports—the money.
Yes.
It does not equate to fewer deaths in custody, by the way, but I'm happy to take that on notice.
Thank you. Senator Thorpe is trying to assist the chair. I did indicate she's only got two minutes left, so thank you, Senator Thorpe, for that.

Since the Senate failed to pass my two bills to ban shackling during childbirth and strip searching of children who are being hurt by paedophiles in uniform, a number of cases have since been reported that continue to shackle Aboriginal women and girls in hospitals. What steps is the government taking to meet the committee's recommendations and address the issues raised by the bills?
Acknowledging the harm and distress that such practices cause—
Who cares? No-one cares here.
We do care.
We do care.
No you don't.

This particular issue of shackling was raised in a review that the department of health commissioned a couple of years ago now around healthcare in prisons. The minister for health is working with his state and territory counterparts—and, probably, detailed questions should go to the department of health—on a range of issues that arose in that report, including this particular matter, and working with those state and territory health ministers who are responsible, along with their corrections ministers, for preventing and stopping these practices. The Commonwealth is looking at this issue and working with the states and territories to ensure—
Sorry, how long have the conversations been going on—a couple of years?

The report by Nous into healthcare in prisons was the end of 2024, and the health minister has been working quite closely with health ministers in states and territories. You would need to ask more detailed questions of the department of health, but those conversations are—
Your department has not got anything to do with it? It's handballed to the department of health, is it?

It's not handballed. It's the department responsible for the policy issues. We are not the department of health and we do not have a corrections function either, so it is appropriate that the health minister is leading this body of work.
Thank you, Senator Thorpe. Senator O'Sullivan—sorry, no, I'm going to Senator Shoebridge and then Senator O'Sullivan. Senator Shoebridge is on my list next.

I do find that an extraordinary avoidance of responsibility. The shackles, the handcuffs, are not put on by health officials. In fact, it's my understanding that the shackling of women while they're giving birth is almost universally opposed by health officials, the nurses, the doctors—anyone in that room. The shackles and the handcuffs are put on by the carceral system, by police and prison officers, and it's your department that's responsible for coordinating this at a national level, not the health department. If you send it off to the health department, you will not answer it. Is your department leading a discussion amongst attorneys-general across this country to prevent women being shackled to their beds with handcuffs while they're giving birth to their children? If not, why not?

First and foremost, I do say it is a disturbing practice. Secondly, in terms of corrections and police, it's a matter to work with the states and the territories. They run the corrections systems, and it's their state police forces. It's not, as far as I'm aware, federal police that are associated with this. We have, as a standing item on the SCAG agenda, Closing the Gap. There is an opportunity there to engage with the states and the territories.

Minister, will you ensure as best you can that your government, through the Attorney-General, will have on the next SCAG agenda an item to lead this country away from a situation where women giving birth are being shackled to their beds by handcuffs and other restraints? Will your government undertake to lead that discussion at SCAG to prevent this happening?

What I will do in response to that is I shall raise it with the Attorney-General today. I will request that she favourably consider your proposal, and hopefully I'll be able to report back to you on that topic.
Thank you. Secretary, a recent Senate report into youth justice highlighted a series of disturbing trends. You're aware of that report that was delivered?
I am, yes.
When do we expect the government to provide a response to that?

Ultimately, the timing will be a matter for government, but the Attorney-General's Department is very much aware of the committee's report and the work that you and other senators did on that.
