Our department will take responsibility for the coordination of preparing the government's response, but the timing of that response is ultimately a matter for the government.
Secretary, I assume that at a minimum you'll be meeting the Senate timetable requiring a response within six months. Is that the goal, or is it intended to produce a response before then?
As Mr Collett said, ultimately the timing of the government response is a matter for government.

One of the key recommendations—unanimous recommendations—of that report was to progress national minimum standards for youth justice and youth detention. Minister, given there was clear legal advice provided to the committee that the Commonwealth can progress national minimum standards for youth justice and youth detention, is your government intending to progress that through SCAG?
As I said to one of your earlier questions, obviously this is not my portfolio. I shall raise it with the Attorney-General and come back to you.
Secretary, I assume your department is disturbed by the trends that are seen in relation to those two Closing the Gap targets, Nos 10 and 11. You must be disturbed by the data.

As I said to Senator Thorpe, it is disappointing that there has been a deterioration. It's not a universal picture around the country. There are some variations, and that goes to different approaches in state and territory justice systems and various laws that state and territory governments have implemented. But I agree that we are trending not in the right direction.

Well, I mean, let's not pretend. Closing the Gap No. 11 says First Nations young people should not be overrepresented in the criminal justice system. That's the goal, isn't it? The Justice Reform initiative, justice is failing, and others analysed the most recent data. They did that analysis as at May of this year, and they found that, over the five years to May of this year, the number of children in detention on an average day rose by 8.5 per cent, while the number under community based supervision fell by 13 per cent. The number of First Nations young people aged 10 and over in detention on an average day increased by 21 per cent. First Nations overrepresentation in detention grew sharply, with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children rising from 16 times more likely five years ago to be detained than a non-Indigenous child to around 23 times as likely, according to the latest data. That isn't just missing the target; that is matters are vastly worse over the course of this government, the Albanese Labor government. They've got vastly worse, haven't they?

Certainly, the numbers there are concerning. Over that period it reflects different positions that have been adopted in states and territories. There have been a range of changes, but I recognise that those figures represent a deterioration.

You say 'a range of changes'. What that actually means is, in the Northern Territory, radical steps backwards have been taken so that more and more First Nations children are being refused bail, placed into detention—children as young as 10. There are harsher laws against bail being applied to children in the NT and Queensland than applied against adults. Queensland watch houses, police cells, are filled to bursting normally with First Nations kids who have no access to any support, any health, in overcrowded conditions, sometimes for weeks or months. The New South Wales government has made harsher bail laws, which we have seen drive more and more First Nations children into jail, and yet the Commonwealth government has placed not a single legal restraint against them, has not withdrawn a dollar of funding, and, in the case of the Northern Territory, is paying 80c in the dollar for every one of these vicious attacks that the Northern Territory government has taken. Apart from handwringing, what have you done?

I don't believe it's just been handwringing. There is a recognition of the challenge. Consistent with the Commonwealth's responsibilities, we have implemented justice reinvestment initiatives in 28 locations.
Thirteen of which are youth-specific.

You're cutting the funding. It was $26 million. It's now gone down to $20 million. To have the Commonwealth government, which has a budget in the hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of billions of dollars, tell us this is a $20 million justice reinvestment program and to continually put that forward as a solution is insulting to the scale of the problem.

I should also add, there's very significant funding through the National Access to Justice Partnership for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander legal services that play a significant role in supporting young First Nations people who interact with the criminal justice system, and, as I said, there is the work that we're doing through the justice policy partnership with First Nations community groups and with the states and territories. We can talk to a range of issues that are being focused on in that forum. We continue to engage directly with the states and territories through the Standing Council of Attorneys-General.

To be clear, you engage with them, and they just defy you. They don't care what you say because they know you're never going to hold them to account. You're not going to pass a law. You're not going to take a dollar off them. You go to the meetings, and they just ignore you. They ignore the Commonwealth government. They just walk over you and keep putting more and more First Nations kids in jail. That's what's happened here for four years now. When are you going to have some serious response, pass a law or take a dollar off these state and territory governments that seem to be wilfully breaching the Closing the Gap target deliberately, intentionally?
Thank you, Senator Shoebridge. After the officials at the table respond to this question, I will share the call.
When are you going to take a dollar off them or pass a law?

Well, Senator, in our federation, the states and territories are responsible for their justice systems. They're responsible for their corrective services. We play a role through the National Access to Justice Partnership agreement and through the Justice Reinvestment program, consistent with the Commonwealth's constitutional responsibilities.
I'm conscious of the chair's comments about time, but also, just to clarify, I don't believe there's been a cut to the Justice Reinvestment funding, but we can provide further detail.

No, you haven't taken a single dollar off the Northern Territory government. Eighty cents on the dollar of every spit hood that's put on a First Nations child is paid for by the Commonwealth. Eighty cents on the dollar of every jail cell that is built to put a First Nations child in is paid for by the Commonwealth. You keep giving them money to abuse kids like this. You keep feeding them the money.
Thank you, Senator Shoebridge. I am going to share the call, and I'll go to Senator O'Sullivan.
Can I have people from the Children and Families Division? Is that you?
This is the right area.

I'd like to discuss with you NAP 21, a rather difficult subject of child sexual abuse and the prevention of that occurring online. I just want to understand what National Action Plan measure 21 is about. Could you, for the benefit of the committee, just explain the purpose of the website and helpline that you've created.

I'll pass to my colleagues to provide you a detailed answer, but, by way of context, it's one of numerous measures under the national strategy. This particular measure goes to providing an intervention for adults who may be experiencing thoughts and feelings that could lead to child sexual abuse. It's an attempt—a very important one—to interrupt and prevent practices. I must ask Ms Byng or Ms McMichael to provide you with some detail.

The Stop It Now! Australia service was launched in April 2026. The service provides advice and guidance on how people can manage unwanted feelings and stop harmful or offending behaviour. It also offers guidance for those concerned about another adult's behaviour towards children, and for professionals who may need advice on prevention, early intervention and referral pathways. International evidence shows that it's important that there is an anonymous element to the service. It's accessible through a national telephone helpline, a dedicated website chat function and online self-help modules. The service is supported by law enforcement, academics and clinicians and has been based on successful international models and built on the learnings and outcomes of the pilot program.

Thank you. Just to confirm, the website states that the goal of the new prevention service is to protect children from sexual abuse by intervening before an individual offends or reoffends. Can you confirm that?
That is part of the intention of the service.
How does the department and/or the service provider measure that outcome?

There is an evaluation that has been commissioned to evaluate the Stop It Now! Australia service. We have entered into a contract to evaluate this measure. The evaluation will examine the establishment, delivery and early operation of the service over its first two years and will consider the experience of service users and stakeholders, the effectiveness of the service in achieving its intended outcomes and efficiency of service delivery. That will inform.
When will that review commence, and when will it be available?
The service is being established in a phased approach at the moment and equally—
I'm talking about the review.

The evaluation is currently in its first stage, scoping and planning, and comprises five stages. There'll be interim reporting due November-December 2026. Then there'll be data collection, and the final report is due October 2027.
Can you tell me how much is spent on this website and service?

The Australian government has provided $9.6 million from 2021-22 through to 2024-25, and then approximately $4 million per annum will be available on an ongoing basis. The contract for the service is valued at $6.27 million, and that's for a two-year period.

I've taken a look at this material. I want to table, for the benefit of the committee, a screenshot of material that's available online as part of the learning modules that individuals can engage with. This is tabled source No. 2. If we could just distribute that everyone understands—
Is it the 'A Practical Strategy' one?
Yes, that's it. That's the one. What I've just tabled is a screenshot of a page from the website for individuals—
Senator O'Sullivan, I'm just going to put it to the committee. It is a screenshot from the website.
Have we got it at the table?
Not yet. You might want to wait.

What I've tabled is a screenshot of a page from the website for individuals concerned about their sexual thoughts, which has a section titled 'A Practical Strategy: Delay, Distract, Decide'. It instructs someone who is concerned about their urges to engage in sexual fantasies of or sexual behaviours towards children to 'call someone and focus on the conversation', 'leave the room or close the laptop', 'go for a brisk walk', 'do a puzzle, cook, exercise', 'to journal your thoughts' or 'use grounding techniques'. I don't see any advice there to seek professional help. The advice is to simply go for a walk. Is this seriously the response that the Commonwealth government has paid $9.6 million for, through a website service to assist people who have sexual fantasies towards children, act on them or want to act on them: they simply go for a walk?

I don't think that's the intention, and I'm conscious that this is one page from the website. Having visited the service, it's a multifaceted intervention in a very complex and difficult space. The clinicians available to Australians who access that service are trained and very well supported. You can appreciate that this is a very challenging area to operate in clinically, operationally and legally—I should say ethically as well. But it's a really important part of a whole-of-nation strategy. This is one aspect of a complex, multifaceted service.

The first time on this particular page that a referral to a health professional is mentioned is under the OCD subheading. The suggestion in this section is that if you're having sexual thoughts about abusing children but are not aroused by those thoughts, then it's possible that you just have a form of OCD.
Sorry, can you take me to where on the page you're referring to?

Senator O'Sullivan, to assist you: with the other documents tabled, we needed to find them on the webpage but couldn't. But, since then, I think we've had clarity that they're actually from the online modules.
Yes. They're on the modules; that's correct.

One is a screenshot from the webpage, which you've got in front of you. I've been provided with two other pages which I now put to the committee that we table. I just wanted to clarify where they were from; I couldn't find them directly on the website.
Thank you. It's a series of documents. If we could table them all together, that would be helpful.
I'm happy to table those, so the officials have them.
I'm happy to have a look at those.

The first time that a referral to a health professional is made is under this section and not any time earlier. Is a health professional really the last resort—following journalling, doing a puzzle or going for a walk—when someone is wanting to abuse a child?
Sorry, Senator; I don't have the document you're talking about. I've got the screenshot, 'A Practical Strategy', but I think, if I am following you, you've moved to a different page.
It's the actual module that the—I have tabled them all.
Apologies—they're coming.
No, that's okay, Chair.
They might even be hot off the printer right now.
You were referring to the page titled 'What do I do if my sexual preference is children?'
Yes.
I'm happy to read that.
And there's a page called 'Obsessive compulsive disorder'. I think that's the one you were referring to, actually.

Yes. The OCD subheading. This is the first time that actually seeking out health professional support is mentioned. My question is: is a health professional the last resort before journalling, doing a puzzle or going for a walk when someone is wanting to abuse a child?

Senator, the problem I've got in trying to respond to your question is I've got three pages taken from, if I understand it correctly, one part of a website and then one part of a module. I'm sure the intention—

Your website directs people to these online modules. What you've got there is a screenshot from the module that someone undertakes. So, when someone is seeking out support from this $9.6 million service, they're directed to undertake this module, and then—
It's one of many options available, in that there's a clinical service, there's a phone number—there's a range of supports.

Sure. But there's this module here that people are directed to, and it takes until you get to this OCD subheading before you get some advice to actually seek out professional help. So my question is: why? This is the sanctioned online module that the Commonwealth is directing people towards. The first time they see any advice to seek out the help of a professional is when they get to this subheading of OCD, and it says that, if you're not aroused by those thoughts, then possibly you just have a form of OCD, so, therefore, go and get help.
I'm not sure that that's the intention of what the clinicians are proposing—
It might not be the intention, but that's what it says.

The home page of Stop It Now has 'contact the helpline' on its front page. I take your point, Senator, but to get to this particular part of a specific module that's one aspect of a multifaceted intervention, you go through the home page that says 'a national helpline', 'contact the helpline' and there's a button to connect. I don't think you can get to this module without seeing it. That would be my understanding. I'm not a clinician, but that would be my understanding.

On another page, the website directs people who are concerned about their online behaviour to access the anonymous helpline that you're referring to. Can the department confirm for me what they would classify as 'concerning online behaviour'?

I suspect that's quite a multi—I keep saying 'multifaceted'. I don't think there's a single answer to that. This service is set up for Australians who are experiencing thoughts and feelings that may lead them to perpetrate sexual violence against children. It's designed to be as broad as possible to capture anybody who's in that circumstance and provide an intervention to move them away from it. As Ms Byng said earlier, it's based on a whole range of research, both domestically and internationally. It's informed by a UK model and a pilot that was run in Australia. There are so many different aspects to this. I don't have a single answer. We could take on notice whether there's a particular definition. I'm not a clinician myself, but I'm happy to do that.
Chair, how long have I got?
One minute.
Okay. Just to help me, is it for people who are actively viewing child sexual abuse material and child pornography or engaging in sexual communication with children online?

It is for anyone that is either looking at or thinking about looking at online child sexual abuse material. It is also for contact offending. That is if somebody is spending a lot of time with children and having inappropriate sexual thoughts about those children. So it's for both contact and online.
On this module, under the fantasies module, there is a page—
Which page are we on now?
I haven't got the page number in front of me; sorry. It would've been the third document.
The 'Exploring therapeutic options'?
In the fantasies module. Have you got that in front of you?
I don't have a fantasies module, I'm sorry.
Sorry, I gave them all away, which was a mistake on my part. What do I do if I have a sexual preference towards children?
I think the secretariat is about to provide that.
Under 'Don't beat yourself up'. Can we go to that? You haven't got this one?
I think the secretariat's about to provide that.
Under 'Don't beat yourself up'—can we go to that? You haven't got this one?
I think the secretariat's about to provide it to us.
Can we just distribute them all? It would be much more efficient if I—
Hang on. Is it under, 'What do I do if my sexual—
stopitnow.org.au.
It's the second one. It's the last dot point, 'Don't beat yourself up'.
Yes.
I found the section you're referring to, Senator.

Let me just quote it:

For many people, it simply does not feel realistic to never have sexual fantasies about children or to end masturbating to the thought of children. Mindfulness can help people come to terms with their feelings about this. Compassion and self-acceptance can also be very helpful. Having a sexual interest in children can feet lonely and you may feel society doesn't understand your situation. If you need to speak with someone about this please use the helpline for support and advise.

Does the government understand that there are some that believe that attraction to minors is maybe just a sexual orientation—
Yes, we're certainly aware that there are some people—
and that could be interpreted as some sort of acceptance of that behaviour rather than actually addressing it.
There's absolutely no sense from the government that that is the case, Senator, and the service that we're talking about here absolutely does not hold that view.
Thank you, Senator O'Sullivan. I'm going to now share the call and go to Senator David Pocock.

Thanks for your time this morning. I've got some questions about the department's consultation on copyright law. I'm interested in the status of consultations with AI companies, copyright holders, publishers and the creative industries on potential changes to our copyright laws.
Consultation is ongoing.
Why have these consultations been behind closed doors rather than an open public consultation on potential changes?

I'm sure my colleagues can go into a lot of detail about the copyright and AI group that has been in place for several years and has been the key mechanism for engagement with a very broad range of stakeholders from all parts of the creative sector, or stakeholders with an interest in copyright and AI, including tech companies, so I'll let Ms Inverarity talk to that.

I don't have a lot to add to what the secretary has said. We've been supporting the government with consultations over recent months, as you're aware, but it builds on many years of engagement with the Copyright and AI Reference Group, which, although not a public forum, has a very extensive membership. We would also note that the Office of AI in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet recently did undertake public consultation, although we accept copyright was not the focus of those consultations.
Whose decision was it to hold these discussions in private rather than having a public discussion around potential changes to copyright?

The reason I'm looking slightly puzzled—perhaps I haven't been clear. I wouldn't have couched them as 'in private' in that they're consultations through established mechanisms. The copyright system or sector, for want of a better term, has a whole raft of players, as you'd be aware, and we've had numerous—I've lost track of the number of consultations that Ms Priestly would have led—involving representative groups from artists all the way through to some of the biggest media companies in the country. So I wouldn't have described them as closed-door discussions.
Okay. That's very much the sense I've got from talking to people who've been involved.
I'm sorry, Senator; it wasn't our intention to describe it that way.
Sure. So where did the opt-out model come from? Who proposed that to the department?

I don't know that there's a single answer to that in that these are concepts that have been explored and discussed and debated for a number of years, and, as I'm conscious of your very real interest in this space, there are very different views across our society and globally. I don't know that we could pinpoint exactly who first raised that aspect. Ms Priestly?

Mr Collett is correct. I don't think we could pinpoint who raised it and I don't think any one stakeholder raised opt-out as a specific model. I would say that, as part of policy development and providing advice to government, we do look at models internationally. The European Union has an opt-out model as part of its copyright and AI laws, so there is precedent that we've been looking at internationally.
So opt-out didn't come from a stakeholder; it came from the department looking at the EU. It's got to have come from somewhere.
I don't think we have a particular moment in time where we could record that the first time somebody raised it with us was—
On notice, if you're happy to go back and look for which of the stakeholders has proposed opt-out, that would be very helpful. I understand you may have to go and look at what was said in what—

I want to be careful. I'm conscious that this is a really an important issue to you, to the committee and to all of us, but I don't know that we have a single answer to that. Our records won't show that on the 24th of a particular month an individual raised it. This is a well-understood concept within global copyright discussions, so I don't think we'll be able to source a moment in time where it started.

I also would like to clarify that the work that we've been doing has been to understand stakeholders' positions on the issue, their drivers and what they're interested in, not to have them pitch to us fully formed models. We've been engaging to understand their context and their operating environment to take that back into the policy development process, and through that engagement and policy development process we have, as Ms Priestly has already mentioned, evolved a model which would have opt-out elements to it. So there will not be one moment in time where before it we were not aware of the possibility of an opt-out model but then a stakeholder pitched it to us and it came onto the table. It's just been much more iterative than that.

Okay. I'm interested in why you're consulting on an opt-out model when it seems to me the near-universal view from creatives is that they don't want an opt-out model and I haven't heard anyone through the various committees that are ongoing say that it's a workable solution technically. So how does the department actually land on something that creatives don't want and seems unworkable in terms of the technicalities of opting out across the internet?
We're balancing that against positions put by the technology sector that opt-in cannot work.
So how can opt-in not work but opt-out work?
This is the policy development process that we're on—to hear all of that feedback about what is and isn't technically feasible.
Sure, but you've put forward opt-out—
We have consulted on a model that involves an opt-out approach.
So how is that more feasible than opt-in? You must have some sort of—

What we're trying to suggest is that there are so many different perspectives. We are open to engaging with stakeholders across the spectrum of views here to provide the most comprehensive advice we can to government, ultimately going to the Prime Minister's public statements around how best to position the country to deal with frontier AI in a manner that suits Australia.
Sure. On that: from the things I've seen, you're putting forward an opt-out model based on consultations.

We're not putting forward. We have tested a whole range of different issues. We are consolidating views and providing ongoing and regular advice to government, and, of course, our department is one of a number contributing to this whole-of-government exercise coordinated through the Office of AI in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. That transcends then to the ministerial level. The Attorney has her responsibilities, as part of cabinet with a range of her colleagues, to progress what is a very difficult novel and contemporary issue.
Is the model under consideration not an opt-out model though?
There are lots of things that are under consideration, and government has yet to take decisions.

Well, given that opt-out is clearly one of the models, why is that more feasible than opt-in? You said you said the tech companies said opt-in won't work. All the experts seem to say opt-out is totally unworkable. You're saying to every single person who has any photos or anything that they have to attach some sort of file to it and then just trust that OpenAI and Anthropic aren't going to hoover it up. How is that more feasible? There must have been a decision within the department where you said, 'Okay, the tech companies say opt in is not going to work, and so we're going to opt-out.'
We've tested opt-in with a whole range of stakeholders. We've tested opt-out with a whole range of stakeholders. We've tested a whole range of different aspects. There are myriad choices available.
So I'm asking then: how do you land on opt-out?
The department hasn't landed on any position.
We haven't landed on anything? We have consulted on an opt-out model.
And the department's not the decision-maker here. Our role is to provide advice, as part of one of a number of departments, for government to inform decision-making.

Maybe I'm asking the question in an unclear way. Why are you consulting on opt-out rather than opt-in or another model? You must have some sort of assurance or idea that opt-out works? But, given creatives don't want it and all the technical experts say that it's basically unworkable, how did the department land on a point where you're actually consulting on something that, from everything I've heard, is not wanted and doesn't work?

As Mr Collett and Ms Inverarity have said, I think we're consulting on a range of different options and different design elements to achieve a range of different policy objectives, one of those policy objectives being to facilitate AI training in Australia, the others being around protection, control and compensation for rights holders and other creatives. I think the reason that opt-out is one of the options that we have been consulting on goes to that first policy objective, around attracting AI training to Australia and responding to what we've heard from some stakeholders, particularly in the tech sector, that an opt-in model wouldn't be feasible to achieve that policy objective.

Finally, before we go to lunch, just so I understand the policy development: it is my understanding that AGD is in charge of copyright, but do you get told by government, 'Actually, we want options to facilitate investment' rather than, 'Well, what is the best way forward just on copyright?' Is that how it would work?

Obviously, something about grappling with the potential of investment in AI in Australia engages the equities of multiple departments and portfolios. It's not a zero-sum game that we focus only around copyright. We're responsible for the administration of the Copyright Act and we have the direct relationship with copyright stakeholders. But it's part of a broader whole-of-government consideration of national security issues, investment and economic issues, energy issues, and land acquisition and water issues, as well as copyright and other things. So we're part of a whole-of-government effort. Certainly, our role is to ensure that copyright interests are understood and that we test with copyright stakeholders possible options, but we do that connected with a broader government effort.
Thank you.
Senators have indicated to me that there are further questions remaining for the Justice and Communities Group, so we will return at 1230 with the Justice and Communities Group.
We will now resume with the Justice and Communities Group, and I'll hand the call to Senator Cash.

If I could just go back to a line of questioning from Senator Pocock in relation to copyright, I want to get a clear understanding of what the evidence was. Has the department put to the government a preferred or recommended model?
There's ongoing policy work that we're undertaking and providing advice on to government. There has been no settled position, yet, on a final model.
I just wanted to clear that up. So, no recommended model has been put to government. Is there a timeframe that you are working to?

Sorry, I should be clear in terms of 'model'. As I described to Senator Pocock at the end of the last session, there are connected lines of effort on this issue. Copyright is certainly one element of it, but there's a whole range of others. I think the more accurate characterisation would be that there's ongoing policy work that goes across all the different areas that I talked about: national security implications, engagement with the states and the territories, energy, water and land use as well as copyright. They're all factors that are being worked through. There is no one big model that we have advised on, but we have been doing ongoing policy work around options in the copyright space.
On timing, there's no particular date that we're working to, other than just working urgently to support government with its consideration of the issue.
Can I confirm: this department established the Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Reference Group in 2023. Is that consultation process still active?

It's an ongoing consultation mechanism and has been incredibly useful where we've been able to tease out a range of perspectives because, as you know, there is no single, coherent copyright community with an agreed set of views about copyright—

I would dispute that and say that in all of the discussions that I've had across the board with all rights holders—put aside the AI companies—the rights holders themselves who are directly affected, obviously, by copyright seem very firm that there should be no changes to copyright law in Australia.

I think it's a bit more nuanced than that. Different stakeholders are engaged on this issue and bring different perspectives. The reference group has proven to be a great mechanism where people can quite transparently talk through these issues. We have also had separate engagements associated with the discussion or the issues paper, but I think that mechanism remains available to be used to continue to engage with stakeholders.
When was its last meeting and what's its schedule of meetings going forward?
We'll have to check. We think the last time the Copyright and AI—oh, hang on, Ms Priestly does have the date.
Our last meeting of the Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Reference Group was on 28 October 2025.

I think it's just worth clarifying that the copyright and AI reference group has not been the group that we've used to consult on this proposal. Members of the copyright and AI reference group have absolutely been consulted, just not through that entity itself.

Understood. That's fine. Is there a need to change copyright laws in Australia, in particular given, as I said, it is really the majority of rights holders that do not want to see a change to the law and would argue that the current law is adequate in terms of the protections that provides to them?

There are a whole range of views across society and globally on this, and government has to grapple with what is the best way forward for Australia in dealing with frontier AI. There are a multitude of choices wrapped up in that and, as you say, very strongly held views by different players in that space.
Yes, exactly—in particular the AI companies. Is changing the copyright laws still part of the mix of consultation that is going on?

Yes. AI companies themselves have said that they cannot reduce their legal risk to a sufficient level to enable them to invest in AI training here under current legal settings established by the Copyright Act.
What are those arguments put by the big AI companies?

I can use their words to explain that to you, if you like, based on the evidence that they gave to a recent hearing of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. Anthropic said:

There are certain things that are just technically impossible to do. You can't license the entire internet. Billions and billions of information exists there which is available to be viewed and studied, and that's essentially what training is.

Microsoft said:

We see your copyright laws as providing a high level of uncertainty about the ability to engage in the training processes that are necessary to train a model.

And, finally, Google stated:

It's the sense of an obligation to go out and get prior authorisation and licensing agreements for all the content that we would want to train on. If that is really the obligation, just a conservative estimate on the back of a napkin would show that to train a medium-sized large language model would take us around 200 years to be able to get the necessary authorisation …
In relation to the overseas comparisons, what have the UK done?

I'll ask Ms Priestly to talk that through in that there are differences across every jurisdiction—but very happy to answer your question. I might just add, just for your visibility, Senator, you may be aware that the department, of course, has appeared before the joint select committee and some others.
Yes, I know that. I'm asking it in the context of Senate estimates, though.
Yes, fantastic. Ms Priestly.

The UK undertook consultation last year, I believe, on options to reform its copyright law. That then fed into, as I understand it, further policy development work being undertaken by the UK government. As far as I'm aware, they haven't reached a position.
Have the UK changed their copyright law?
Not that I'm aware of in relation to this issue.
Right.
Noting, of course, that there are some differences in the UK copyright act to the Australian Copyright Act.
Yes, but pretty much the UK, at this point in time, is firmly backing in their rights holders. That is my understanding.
Well, I think it's correct to say there's been no significant change to their copyright law.

Correct. Going back to the courts just in terms of the correspondence, written advice or submissions from either court concerning the establishment of the new court, have you received any correspondence raising concerns about the establishment—bearing in mind I'll obviously be asking this of the court, as well, and I'll be tabling it?

We said before, Senator, that we work very closely with the courts to develop advice to government. There are a whole range of complexities around the potential establishment of a court and a whole range of decisions that government has not taken, as Ms Inverarity said earlier. The implications in how the federal justice system works is, of course, of great interest to the chief justices, to their principal registrars and to the courts, as it would be to the Fair Work Commission and the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations.
Again, since the announcement on 23 July 2026, has the department received any correspondence, submissions et cetera from either court raising concerns?

As I mentioned earlier, we did receive a letter from Chief Justice Mortimer. My characterisation of it—again, I don't have it in front of me—is not that it raised concerns but that it did point out aspects where, depending on the policy choices the government might make, certain things would be more challenging and certain things would be less challenging. My reading of it was that that was to inform the policy development process so that issues that might be particularly challenging could be avoided or different options chosen, rather than expressing a concern with the establishment of a court in and of itself.
Can I ask one follow-up question on copyright before we share the call. What's the Productivity Commission's view on changes to the Copyright Act here in Australia?
I know the Productivity Commission did recently appear before the Joint Select Committee on AI. I myself wasn't able to watch that.
I'm assuming you're all over it, though, because you are the department that deals with copyright, so the views of the Productivity Commission, I'm assuming, would be taken into account.
I'm sure they will be and our team will be looking at it. I myself have not watched that evidence or read the transcript.
Ms Priestly, can you—
I did watch the evidence, but, sorry, I can't recall off the top of my head exactly what their position was, so I think we'd have to take that on notice.
Has anyone in this department spoken to the Productivity Commission about changes to the Copyright Act?
We engaged with them on several occasions towards the end of last year, I believe, but I haven't met with them in the last few months.
I will share the call. Thank you.
Senator Shoebridge.
We might continue on copyright/AI. You spoke in your answers to Senator Cash about a proposal in relation to AI, in relation to reform. Is there any current proposal before government?

I don't recall using the word proposal. The department has been working on a range of policy advice to support government in its decision-making. I don't know if we characterised that as a proposal or not.
Has this come from a request from the Prime Minister's office to provide advice? Are you generating it off your own bat? Where has it come from?

As I described earlier, there's work that I would characterise as whole-of-government, engaging multiple departments in terms of providing policy advice. That goes to a range of specific issues, but it's all subject to consideration by government.
Who's leading this whole-of-government approach?
The Office of AI in the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet is leading at the bureaucracy level.
That's the office that was announced a couple of months ago?
Yes.
So it's being coordinated through the Prime Minister's office.

It's through the Prime Minister's department for us, at the bureaucratic level, and, of course, the Prime Minister's office has an equivalent coordinating role across ministerial offices. But we're dealing—
Who does the Office of AI report to?
The Office of AI is a part of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, so it reports ultimately to the Secretary of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet.
Does it report through the secretary to the Prime Minister, or does it report directly to the Prime Minister?
It's a part of the department, and therefore it's accountable to the secretary, in the same way that I'm a part of a department and accountable to my secretary.
So the Office of AI in the Prime Minister's department is coordinating this whole-of-government approach.
Yes.
Have they asked for specific reforms in relation to copyright?
We've been engaging with them. We've been advising them on positions that have been expressed to us by copyright stakeholders, and there is ongoing policy work engaging with them.
Ms Inverarity detailed some of the evidence that was given by, I think, Anthropic, but if not Anthropic it was OpenAI—so one of those two entities—
It was Anthropic, Microsoft and Google.

that it would be an impossible task for these massive AI entities owned by US capital and US billionaires to train in Australia because of our copyright laws. Does the government accept that proposition put by those entities, obviously noting their self-interest?

Obviously, it's important to understand what their perspective is because it will influence their decision-making. I think we take into account a range of stakeholders. To have that overall perspective, the Office of AI is best placed to assist you in the overall conversations that have been happening.

Has your department reviewed the more than 250 pieces of strategic litigation being directed against those same entities in the United States that look to be collectively greatly reducing their capacity to simply hoover up protected works using fair-use provisions? Have you looked at the scale of the strategic litigation against those same entities to inform your view about whether or not their proposition is genuine?
We're certainly alive to the range of matters before the courts in the United States. We seek updates as required from our officials in the United States, so we are closely monitoring that.

What does that lead you to conclude in relation to their repeated wholesale industrial use of fair-use provisions in the United States and the risk they face going forward in the United States to continue training in the way they do, deliberately ignorant of copyright and other rights? What does that lead you to conclude in terms of their risk to help inform you of the bona fides of their approach to Australia?

I would say a lot of that litigation is on foot. As you said, there are multiple cases. I don't think at this stage we would say that there's a clear picture coming through the US jurisprudence as to how that issue is going to be dealt with.

Are you aware of any country in the world that has changed their copyright act to expressly allow or facilitate the training on otherwise copyright protected material in large language models? Are you aware of any country on the planet that has made those changes?
I'll ask colleagues to answer that, because we have been keeping a close watch on what's happening internationally.
I'm not aware of a specific change in a specific country, but of course—
Well, that's what I'm asking about.

The question is a really important one. Different countries have different regimes. There are issues with the Australian copyright regime that have different implications for this sort of work than, say, in the European Union or in the US. These are, it's absolutely fair to say, very contemporary challenges that all governments are facing.

But no other country in the world has passed laws, as you're aware, to reduce the rights of their own creatives, to limit copyright protections in order to feed these US multibillionaire tech bro owned entities. You're not aware of any other country in the world that's changed their laws and prejudiced their own creative industries' rights to feed the profits of these US billionaires, are you?

Well, I can't agree with the characterisation that you've placed at the end of the question. What I was going to say is we will take on notice to check the arrangements in Singapore, which we understand may have recently made some changes to its copyright laws. We'll come back to you on notice with that.
As I said before, a whole range of countries are grappling with these issues now. It's a very contemporary issue.

Minister, do you accept this argument from these US tech platforms—Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google—that their AI is so powerful that it could potentially cure cancer, but they're unable to distinguish copyright material? They've got this incredibly powerful tool that could take us to Mars, cure cancer, do these amazing things, but they're unable to distinguish, in the course of training, copyrighted material from non-copyrighted material. Do you accept that from them?

What I accept, Senator Shoebridge, is that we shouldn't be afraid of this new technology. All of my life I have come across changes in technology with people advocating, 'These are the consequences of this particular new technology.' Nine times out of 10, the fear that people have of that technology doesn't eventuate. By and large, in my experience, most of this technology has been good for society. It's an advancement of it. I'm still thinking about AI and what these companies are proposing, and I haven't come personally to a concluded view about it. I think I need more to do, more reading on it, to finally come to a position to make an assessment about whether, on balance, this new technology should be feared the way you appear to be fearing it or whether—

I just have a rational approach to technology that appears to already be escaping their sandboxes, attacking our websites, diving into our data, breaching our security. I just think I have a rational approach to it, which is shared, I think, by millions of Australians. They don't have a 'she'll be right' attitude; they have a 'government should be putting in laws to protect this' attitude.
Yes—sometimes what you consider rational, Senator Shoebridge, other people don't consider rational.
I think protecting Australians from aggressive, foreign tech is rational.

You may not think that's a rational response to your rationality, but, all I'm saying is, I'd like to know more about the opportunities that AI presents to benefit society before making a final judgement about the way forward. The government is obviously looking at this area of policy. We are obviously trying to get advantages for Australia in terms of a range of aspects of AI. We don't want to be left behind, if this is the way in which the rest of the world is going. If there are opportunities for jobs and investment in this field, we obviously want to look at that. But there are people in the government who are far more informed than me personally on this, and I will certainly be following their guidance on this. But, as I say, at a personal level, I'm sort of holding judgement on what I finally believe about the future of AI.

Thanks, Minister. I might move now to the document that I think I provided to you, Secretary. This is a document that's been produced by a number of barristers in New South Wales who are trying to come to terms with the incredibly complex and different rules in relation to the use of generative AI in courts and tribunals in New South Wales. They discovered from their review that every court and every tribunal has a different and differently complicated way in which generative AI can be used in submissions and in court proceedings. You'll see that this review included three federal jurisdictions. It included the Federal Court, the Federal Circuit and Family Court and the Fair Work Commission. I accept you don't have responsibility for the Fair Work Commission, but it also included the New South Wales NCAT and New South Wales supreme court. Some jurisdictions completely prohibit generative AI in submissions. Some are more permissive. Some allow it for submissions but require an express statement about its use. Some don't require an express statement. Some allow it to generate submissions. Some allow it to check submissions. Some allow it for experts' reports. Some don't allow it for experts' reports. Some allow it for experts' reports with prior permission. Some allow it for experts' reports with prior permission, subject to conditions. Some allow it for experts' reports subject to different conditions. What I'm articulating to you is: it's an unholy mess, with every different court in the country and every different tribunal having different rules for generative AI. Have you undertaken this kind of review?

We have placed AI on the agenda at standing committee of attorneys-general to engage with the states and the territories around use of AI in the justice sector from the perspective of opportunities, best practice and understanding the nature of the usage. I note we've got two layers of independence that come into play here. They are the independence of the courts, who very zealously guard their ability to make rules and policy within their own jurisdiction, and then the states themselves and their view about the way in which they will engage with the courts in their own jurisdictions.

I recognise this is a real issue in the way it has evolved. I do recognise that there have been different approaches adopted in different jurisdictions. I think we engage quite regularly with the Law Council of Australia, and we've got a meeting coming up in the near future. I think we've got this on the agenda to have a conversation with them about that.

I'll give you just one example in this which is on confidential materials—material that's subject to confidentiality. Or it may have been served. It's subpoenaed material or documents produced under a notice of produce. This can be a very large amount of confidential information provided during proceedings. The New South Wales Supreme Court has a three-stage test about that—whether or not it can be fed into an AI—which says that restricted material can only be uploaded on a closed platform, used only for the proceedings, and it can't be used to train.

The Fair Work Commission just says, 'You better take some caution.' The Federal Court says, 'You can load it up into AI, but you must not breach confidentiality, privilege or an implied undertaking.' How people engage in that, I don't know. The Federal Circuit and Family Court applies something similar to the New South Wales Supreme Court test. How are litigants who are providing material through Federal Court proceedings going to be ensured about the confidentiality of the material if some courts allow it to be fed into an AI model, some tribunals allow it to be fed into an AI model, and others don't? How are you going to take steps to ensure we have faith in the integrity of the judicial system, particularly the confidentiality?

Thank you for raising this. It is a very real and current challenge that we're grappling with. As the secretary said before, within the policy context, there are discussions under the Standing Council of Attorneys-General and a working group working with our justice department colleagues in the policy space. I'd also draw your attention to the courts working together. I think the Chief Justice of the FCFCOA last month convened a meeting of almost all of the intermediate and superior courts in the country to grapple with how the courts themselves are engaging with these sorts of issues.

There are both opportunities and real risks for citizens in this. There are real opportunities around increasing access to justice for vulnerable Australians and for Middle Australia. As I think you're rightly pointing out, there are real challenges with that as well. There are a multitude of streams of work between both the justice departments and the courts to deal with this.
When you say 'justice departments', do you mean state and territory?
Yes, those are our sister departments in the states and territories under the Standing Council of Attorneys-General and then between the courts themselves.

I think we should be really clear about the cost, the actual resource constraints that pretty much every state, every tribunal has—significant resource constraints. This is a substantial amount of work, hard work, which is going to require significant resourcing. Is there no intent for the Commonwealth to put in place a pool of funds and some cooperative model to allow the different tribunals around the country to get access to the scale of AI help, technical assistance, expert help to try and come up with some common rules? Otherwise, we're going to continue to have this dog's breakfast of every different tribunal with their tiny resources trying to solve this wickedly hard problem. This is surely where you need to show some leadership, put some funds down, bring people together and try and get some common rules, isn't it?

I certainly think that's why the Attorney-General put it on the SCAG agenda, to create that leadership at the national level and with the states and the territories. I'm alive to the level of the challenge in asking each of these courts to think about how they would amend their procedural directions and rules. I agree with you that opportunities to encourage consistency in approach would be positive, and we will continue to have that conversation under the auspices of the Standing Committee of Attorneys-General.

The key thing you haven't answered is funding. Overstretched, underresourced tribunals, trying to come up with answers, each of them potentially engaging their own experts and none of them having the capacity to get the scale and depth of support is not the way forward. The Commonwealth providing some funding, providing that deep pool of expertise, and helping these tribunals come to a common position is so obviously necessary. But that's not on the table?
I've described the work that we're doing at the moment, which is through the Standing Committee of Attorneys-General and the working group that sits under that.
Along with the courts' work.

I will quickly run through a couple of matters because we're running a bit behind time. Community Legal Centres Australia is running this Justice Where We Live program for regional and remote legal services. Are you aware of that?
Yes, we are aware of that project.
They've asked for an additional $20.8 million per annum to fund that access in remote and regional areas. What's the government's response to that?
In terms of Community Legal Centres Australia's funding ask, I think they were seeking a loading for centres in regional and remote areas. Is that right?

Yes, indeed, and it's because of the extreme costs of travel, the costs of ensuring that basic services are provided to the officers and also the costs of recruiting. You lose endless hours of your legal team doing the travel to provide the same service. And yes, they've got a series of loadings. Is that being considered?

During the NAJP funding negotiations, those factors, including the additional costs associated with delivering services in regional and remote areas, were contemplated in coming up with the allocations under the existing agreement.
But they weren't implemented.

They were. The funding distribution model, which has been in place for many years now, in the most recent negotiations, we did ensure there was a loading both for RRR areas and for delivery to First Nations people in recognition of the additional costs that are related to that. So those loadings were applied in the distribution of funding to states and territories. It's then a matter for states and territories to determine the funding that then goes to each centre.
So there is no guarantee that any of these community centres are getting the loading because it's mediated through states and territories?
Each state and territory was distributed funding with a range of factors taken into account, including the RRR service delivery and First Nations delivery.
Have you followed through with the states and territories about whether these remote community legal services have actually had the funding contemplated in what was given to states and territories?

We do have some numbers around the impact that the funding is having for clients in regional and remote areas. There's been an increase of almost 3,000 clients under the first six months of the National Access to Justice Partnership, compared to the last six months of the National Legal Assistance Partnership. Their clients reside in outer regional and remote areas, so that accounts for approximately one in four clients assisted nationally being from those regional and remote areas.

Because we're running short on time, could you provide on notice what, if any, checks have been taken with states and territories to see if the amount that was negotiated for remote and regional communities has actually been passed through to the services on the ground?

I'll save taking it on notice. No checks and balances are done. The funding is provided to the states and territories. The distribution of funding takes that into account. The states and territories tell us the funding amount for each centre. We do receive that information, but they're not required to report to us on anything in terms of how the funding is used or the particular ways the funding is distributed. We do get reporting on the types of clients and the priority clients, but it isn't something that we could check, so I would rather not take it on notice; I'd rather just tell you.
I appreciate the answer. Can you then provide on notice the funding for these remote and regional community legal services. If you have before and after NJAP, if you could provide that.
There are no loading arrangements. But what we can provide you—
I'm not asking for loading amounts.
is the funding amounts provided to each CLC in the country based on state and territory reporting.
We're on common ground here, Ms Bogaart, because I heard your answer. So if you could provide the amount that's provided pre to those centres and the amount that has been provided post—pre the NAJP.
And NLAP-funded services?
Yes, NLAP against NJAP.
We can do that nationally.
Yes, for these remote and regional, to the extent you have the data. I accept that—
Yes, we'll do what we can.
You'll be pleased to know this is the last matter before we move on. The rest I'll put on notice. On a different matter, where is stage 2 of the public interest disclosure reforms up to?
That is in the next group, so you haven't missed the chance to ask that question. I'll make sure they're ready.
That is incredibly heartening, but I don't want to move off this courts matter and allow the matter we discussed earlier about VIQ to fall off the list.
I have the information that you requested here. I can give it to you now or obviously provide it on notice.
Now, please.

In relation to VIQ, I can confirm the department obviously doesn't have an active contract with VIQ because they have wound up. We have used VIQ in the past to purchase specific transcripts when provided, as they were the sole provider of those transcripts. If I can give you an example of that, we from time to time order transcripts of extradition proceedings for the purpose of ensuring accuracy when dealing with matters being reviewed or appealed in a higher court. At the date we were notified that VIQ operations would be winding down, which was 3 June 2026, the department had no active contracts with VIQ Solutions. We, the department, engaged with the National Office of Cyber Security in June 2026 when it became apparent that multiple government entities held contracts with VIQ, and the cybersecurity coordinator liaised with government departments, the VIQ administrators and CyberCX, the entity that the federal courts had engaged to do an independent cybersecurity assessment of the incident. The cybersecurity coordinator identified that there was no malicious cyberactivity relevant to the incident.

I have the list of our portfolio agencies that used either VIQ or Auscript which I can read out or, again, I can table.
If you could read them out.

This is just VIQ: the ART/AAT, the CDPP, the OAIC, the High Court, the Federal Court, as you know, and, as I've already indicated, the department. I understand the Office of the Special Investigator had a contract but never actually procured any transcripts under that contract. In relation to Auscript—this is a bit more historical, as you would appreciate—we understand the ART/AAT used Auscript, as well as the High Court, the Federal Court entities and the department.

Given that, including the department, there are six other agencies that have had contracts and engagement with VIQ, have you undertaken a department-wide audit, including of these agencies, to work out the extent of the data breaches by VIQ?

No, we haven't, and the reason for that is that CyberCX is still working with the courts. For us, the transcripts that we obtain are transcripts from the court. So I think it's important to hear the final conclusion of the CyberCX report, and then we will assess what further steps, if any—
Is CyberCX working with the High Court?
Not to my knowledge.
Not that I'm aware of.
Is CyberCX working with the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions?

I think it's important to clarify that CyberCX is working with the courts who were using VIQ to generate the transcripts, if you will. The other agencies were purchasing transcripts through that mechanism. I understand, further to the secretary's comments—
Well, I—
Sorry, if I could just add—CyberCX, I believe, last month provided a further report to the courts. They are working through that, and we will continue to seek advice from them.
No, sorry. So the High Court procures transcripts?

I do want to check that, because traditionally their transcription has been in house. I think they may have used VIQ or Auscript in some matters, but I think, generally, they do transcription in house.
For the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, what were they using VIQ for?
I'd need to check on that. I'll take that on notice for you.
For CDPP, were they using VIQ to record transcripts of interviews, or is it solely to obtain transcripts in other courts?
I think it's the latter, but I'd like to take that on notice to make sure that I can give you an accurate answer.
The ART and the AAT?
Again, I'll take that on notice.

Well, this is why an audit would make sense: to know what the risk is. We know there have been data breaches in the Federal Court and we think there have been data breaches in the family court, but you haven't even asked the question about the AAT and the ART.
No, I can confirm that the AAT and AAT didn't use VIQ for their own transcripts. As I understand it, it was to purchase transcripts for relevant matters, in the same way the department has purchased.
Alright. Why are you resisting an independent audit?

I'm not resisting an independent audit, but there is a process underway through the courts with CyberCX. I would like to see the outcomes of that. If required, we will definitely engage with these other agencies.
Did you say some report from CyberCX had been delivered a month ago?
I understand that CyberCX provided a further report to the courts in September, and they're working through that now.
Did the courts provide the report to you?
I'd have to take that on notice. I haven't personally seen it, but the courts are working through that with CyberCX.
Have you requested a copy of the report?
We've requested advice on the outcomes of that work.
Have they provided the advice?
The courts have provided a range of advice and will continue to do so. This is still contemporary work and we are continuing to follow—
What advice have they provided?
I don't have a single answer, in that we've had lots of contact with the courts over the past several months. They've provided a whole range of advice to us around the circumstances.
Sorry, Mr Collett. All of these questions have been about the CyberCX report that you've just told us was delivered to the courts a month ago.
Yes.
I'm asking you about what advice you've got from—and when we say 'courts', I assume we're talking the Federal Court entity and the—
The FCFCOA?
FC—
The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia.
I wish there was a better name for the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia; can you work on that too? I'm asking you about that.

Sorry; I misunderstood your question. The courts, both of the two entities you just referred to, have confirmed that they have received the CyberCX report, they're working through it and they'll provide further advice to us.
You haven't requested and you haven't been given a copy of it?
I'd have to take on notice whether we've been given a copy. We have not requested it, to my knowledge. We are waiting for the courts to work it through. We're conscious of their independence.
You said they've given you certain advice in relation to it. I was asking what that advice is, and then you just simply said 'advice'.
They've advised us that they've received the report and that they're working through the content and detail of that and will provide further updates to us.
Did they advise you about the extent of the data breaches that was apparent from this most recent report?
I don't have any specifics at hand on this recent report.

Could I ask you to provide, on notice, a full detailing of what you've been told by the two courts in relation to this September report. Can you provide, in full detail, when they told you and what they told you.
Yes, we can take that on notice.
I would have thought we could have got some actual detail in this exchange, so it's quite frustrating that you give none of that detail, apart from simply telling us that they've got it.
We can certainly take that on notice.
Thank you. Senator Shoebridge, you asked for officials from the first session to be held over. Are they okay to be released now?
That was to address this. Yes, thanks.

That's what I thought. I'm just checking that the commitment we gave earlier to hold officials over from the first group has now been fulfilled. I can say that we can release those officials. We're also now done with Justice and Communities Group. We will now move into Integrity and Security Group. I will hand the call to Senator Cash.

This is where I was directed to ask questions in relation to Giggle v Tickle. Following the High Court not accepting the application for leave to appeal, the Federal Court's decision now stands. Can you explain, in plain English, what the ruling means for biological women's spaces. What is the status of Commonwealth law?
I will ask Ms Mills to assist with that response.

The Sex Discrimination Act makes it unlawful to discriminate on the basis of a protected attribute in certain areas of public life. Those protected attributes include sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and others. The act also provides specific exemptions and exceptions that might apply where discrimination is not unlawful, and then courts—

For example, the Lesbian Action Group have now been in court for three years trying to get an exemption so that they can have biological-only lesbian events. Is that one of the exemptions that you are referring to?
There's a range where there are certain exemptions for things like competitive sporting activities, where the strength, stamina or physique of competitors is relevant.
I don't think that applies to the Lesbian Action Group.
No, not in that one. But, yes, there are others where services which by their nature can only be provided to members of one sex—

Biological lesbians, I would put to you, is possibly that. Probably, in fact, I'd say it is that. I'm just a bit confused. The biological lesbians have now been in court for three years trying to seek an exemption to have biological-only lesbian events. Is that one of the exceptions? Biological lesbians cannot meet lawfully as biological lesbians without getting an exemption. Is that the current status of the federal law?
It would be up to a court to determine that on the—
Sorry; I'm going to remind senators to allow witnesses to finish answering the question before they are then asked another question.

It would be up to the court to interpret the legislation in the context of the individual facts and circumstances of the matter. In the one that you've mentioned, I understand that's been referred to the ART, so it wouldn't be—

Yes, it's gone through the system, and the court has referred it back to the ART. But, at law, as it stands, given the result in Tickle v Giggle and the current law—we are talking about federal law that this department administers—a lesbian dating app cannot exclude biological males who identify as women participating in biological-only lesbian events. Is that the correct status of the law?
It wouldn't be appropriate for me to give legal advice.
Well, you would be able to say what the status of the law is. You are the department that administers the law. Secretary, are you able to answer my question?
I think, as Ms Mills has indicated, obviously, it's subject to interpretation by the courts. That has been going through, and it's now with the ART.

I'm asking the more general question about the current status of the law. I know that they're going through the ART; we established that. In the current status of the law, are biological lesbians able to meet as biological lesbians under federal government law, as it stands today, without the exemption, and exclude biological males who identify as females?

The law is in the Sex Discrimination Act as it has been for some time. What the full Federal Court found in that particular case was that Giggle and Ms Grover had engaged in unlawful direct discrimination against Ms Tickle by treating her, as a transgender woman, less favourably than a person assigned female at birth. That case was very much on its facts—

Basically, for Sall Grover, her app only wanted biological females and said no to a biological man who identifies as a woman, and that is currently unlawful in Australia? It is actually a very easy answer. Can you confirm that is the current status of the law? If it's not, can you tell me, please, on behalf of all the biological women in Australia, what the current status of the law is, as it stands federally?
I have described the court's finding. These are individual cases that turn on their facts. The court found unlawful direct discrimination in that particular matter.
Minus an exemption, does the current law guarantee that biological women can establish biological-women-only spaces without fear of legal action?
I can only say that the court's finding was about the particular facts of that case.

The answer is clearly no, because biological rights in the Sex Discrimination Act are actually second to those who identify. Are there any protections for, for example, a lesbian association that wishes to hold a public event and advertise it only for biological lesbians to ensure that it does not face legal action in terms of turning away a biological man who identifies as a woman?
As Ms Mills said, there are some exemptions under the act, and the commission itself also has a power to grant temporary exemptions in certain circumstances as well.

Can you just confirm the Lesbian Action Group have now been trying for three years to go through the court process to actually get an exemption so that they can have a public event that actually excludes men who identify as women? Is that the current status of the case, as you understand it?
Yes.

Minister, do you think it is acceptable that the Lesbian Action Group in Australia has now been in the court system for three years, trying to get an exemption for what I thought most Australians would think is nothing more and nothing less than common sense? In other words, they actually just want to meet as biological lesbians and not allow men who identify as women to be part of certain functions. Do you think it is acceptable that they have been in the court system now for three years and still have no legal certainty?
I think I've indicated earlier today that this is not my personal—
You are a minister in the government.

I am a minister in the government, but we do have an attorney-general. I shall forward your question to the Attorney-General because she's the appropriate person to answer that question on behalf of the government, and we'll try and come back to you as soon as possible with a response.
Minister, has the government had any discussions about changing the law to recognise biological sex?

Not that I'm aware of, but I wouldn't expect to be involved if there were discussions going on because this is not my portfolio area, but, again, I shall seek a response to that question for you from the Attorney-General.

Secretary, following the decision of the High Court, which said that the full Federal Court's decision was final, did the department brief the Attorney-General or her office about the implications of the decision for biological women in Australia?
I'd need to check that with colleagues.
We provided a summary of the judgement.
Were any questions asked of you, like can you explain the judgement and what it means for biological women?
No.
Can I ask you: what was the nature of the briefing? What was the summary of the law?
It was as previously stated in terms of asserting the summary of the facts of the case and the outcome and then the description of the exemptions that apply for protected attributes.
Senator Payman.

My line of questioning is around the modern slavery risk assessment. KPMG conducted a review of modern slavery risk assessment services for the department, which was completed earlier this year. KPMG offers this type of service and was being asked to audit its competitors. What conflict-of-interest assessment was undertaken?

For the particular conflict of interest or perceived conflict of interest you mentioned, in July 2025, as a part of the panel procurement process, the department approached five suppliers. In that process, we identified perceived potential conflicts of interest where a supplier could have a tool themselves and were undertaking modern slavery supply chain mapping tools. We asked all the candidate suppliers who wished to request for a quote to address that particular perceived conflict of interest. KPMG was engaged in September 2025 and given the contract to provide the services. We put in extra controls and treatment in addition to the standard confidentiality clause in the contract. We asked that material collected and created be confidential indefinitely and that the information from market scans and assessments could not be shared beyond the relevant project teams. We also ensured all the KPMG officers working on that audit signed conflict-of-interest declarations and confidentiality undertakings. We also ensured separation of KPMG teams who worked on two aspects of the audit so they don't share information and have a full separation of personnel. We also asked them to use publicly available information where possible. During the contract, in November, you're probably aware that another supplier—Fair Supply—raised this particular concern with the department. The department took two extra steps. One is that we updated the statement of work and the contract with KPMG to further clarify and ensure their report did not identify any particular supply or tool. We also offered KPMG to sign a non-disclosure agreement with Fair Supply. In the end, Fair Supply provided publicly available information about their product to the department, who passed on that information to KPMG. They did not require KPMG to sign a non-disclosure agreement.

The department also facilitates 15 other providers participating in this particular market scan. They can take steps they consider necessary to manage the risks for their business. Some providers request certain information—including specific data, inputs and algorithms—not be shared beyond KPMG. Other providers chose not to share certain information—including specific data, inputs and algorithms. In June, we received verbal assurance followed by written assurance from KPMG. They have complied with all the contracts and the conditions, including those additional ones I've just mentioned.

It's like you were anticipating this question. Just so that I've got extra clarity, when it comes to the department being aware of KPMG's conflict of interest, can you reiterate what the specific undertakings were that the department took to ensure how they would be using commercially sensitive information from its competitors when it comes to KPMG looking into their own competitors? How was that handled? Was it through the NDA? Is that what you mentioned?

No. First of all, the department proactively managed that conflict of interest and potential risk because we were aware that other suppliers, not just KPMG, were approached and that that risk could also arise. As I said, we signed a procurement contract with any successful suppliers. In that contract, we didn't just use the standard contract clause; we included additions.
Around the other suppliers, did any of them decline to participate or provide any particular demonstrations or limit information they supplied?

As I said, there are 16 participating providers in total. Some required KPMG to take additional steps to ensure the information provided to the particular personnel are kept confidential and not shared more broadly. It's a part of their conditions to provide that information. Some providers, such as Fair Supply, did a demonstration, I believe, of their product. But all the information contained in their demonstration was already publicly available.

On that, in the Mandarin, a representative of Fair Supply asked who would handle presale engagement with agencies after the report. Who is responsible for that now? What role, if any, does KPMG have in referring agencies to vendors?

The KPMG has no role in that, and in fact that is not the intention or the purpose of the project, the audit. It is not to advance anyone's interest. It's more to look at the tool as an aggregate in the market and how that can play a role in modern slavery risk assessment.
Has KPMG or any of its related entities received any commercial benefit, such as work from Commonwealth agencies, arising from the knowledge that they've gained through this audit?
No, not that I'm aware of.
Did the department conduct any review of how the conflict of interest was managed after the contract concluded on 26 June?
Do you mean a specific review into how the contract is managed?
Yes, into how their conflict of interest was managed.

As I mentioned, we sought assurance from KPMG verbally and in written form, and they provided those verbal undertakings and written undertakings in July, and they complied with all the contract terms.
Wonderful. Are you able to provide the committee a copy of the written—obviously you can't provide anything of the verbal commitment.
Can I take that on notice? I think we can, but can I take it on notice.
Yes. Thank you.
Senator Cash.
