To continue with my line of questioning in terms of the outcome of the Tickle v Giggle case, can I just confirm that, at the conclusion of one of the most contentious cases considering social issues in recent memory, which has, as we've discussed, confirmed the ability in law to basically sideline biological women from meeting safely and privately, the department provided what was a noting brief with a mere summary of the judgement to the Attorney-General.
We provided a summary of the judgement and some questions in response to that.
Questions in response to that?
In terms of summarising, like I said, how the court determined the case, a summary of the facts of the case as well as the issues I raised previously in terms of the how the legislation is set out.
Senator Farrell, can I confirm your evidence that the government hasn't considered putting through legislation to recognise the biological rights of women?
No. Well, what I said was I wasn't aware of it but that I would inquire of the Attorney-General, who would be able to answer that question, and come back to you with a response.

Senator Farrell, the government voted against the bill that I introduced, which was a change to the Sex Discrimination Act to bring back common sense and recognise the biological rights of women. Why did the government do that?
Because we took a decision as a government that we weren't going to support that particular legislation.
Confirming you would not support recognising at law the rights of biological women in the Sex Discrimination Act.
Confirming that we didn't support that particular piece of legislation that you brought forward.
Which was to protect the rights of biological women. The government didn't support the legislation.
I mean, it's a fact.

Did the department, following the outcome in the Giggle v Tickle case, put out any advisory notes or guidance, in particular for small businesses, as to what the legal status of the Sex Discrimination Act is now when it comes to biological rights?
No, Senator.
Can I ask why.
It's not the department's role to provide advice on the acts. The Australian Human Rights Commission has a role in engaging with business on the application of discrimination acts.

Given, as I've stated, it was one of the most contentious cases considering social issues in recent memory, did you have discussions with the Australian Human Rights Commission and, in particular, Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody about providing small businesses with guidance so that they understand their legal obligations?
We regularly engage with the Human Rights Commission and discussed the case as it arose and the guidance that they were providing on their website. I believe they have a summary on their website.
A summary—
but we did not engage with them in terms of providing advice to businesses, noting that the legal position has not changed.

Thank you very much. I have now, following the decision, been contacted by small businesses across Australia who do not understand what their legal obligations now are. They understand that you can advertise for a biological-only women's event. The issue now is this—and this is what I'd like to seek clarification on, and I do have a number of questions from a constituent, but they go to clarifying the law: they have sold out an event of 250 people. It has been advertised as a women's-only event. They have been unable to get any form of guidance as to what their staff will now do at the door if a biological man who identifies as a woman turns up. They do not have an exemption under the act. They didn't know that they could not do this. So what is the legal status for them, for an advertised women's-only event? What do they do if a biological man turns up who identifies as a woman?
I appreciate that you've received that query. We can't provide legal advice—

I'm not asking you to reply to that; I'm asking you to interpret the law for me on behalf of small businesses across Australia who genuinely now have no idea what the law states, and they just want to know. You administer this act. It is your department. What does the law state?
That is legal advice.
Stating what the law is is not legal advice; it is stating what the law is.
Specific to the circumstances that you've described, it is.

Okay, I'll put it then as a general question in relation to the law. What does the law say an organisation must do if a man turns up who identifies as a woman to a women's-only public event? What does the law state?
Each case will turn on its facts, and a court will apply the criteria in the act to determine whether a particular instance constitutes—

That's the good news! For every small business across Australia: I would like you to know that the advice from the department on behalf of the government that administers this legislation is that you have no legal certainty. And the bad news is you better find a good lawyer, budget—I don't know—thousands of dollars, and try and seek advice as to what your current status is at law. Is that the advice from the department—'Get a lawyer'? It is a very reasonable question. What is the status of the law? A biological-only event—is it allowed at law currently, following the outcome of Tickle v Giggle, or is it not? To go back to Ms Mills's evidence, do transgender rights trump biological rights under the Sex Discrimination Act, and, on that basis, do small businesses need to say yes to men who identify as women?
There are a range of factors in the act that would need to be considered in a given case.
How does a small business do that? Please tell me.
Any business can seek advice should they—

They have sought advice. I will not go through the list. From a commission, from a commissioner, from a professor of human rights, from a lawyer and from several other small businesses, they have not been told what their legal status actually is. I quote: 'I still have not been able to get a clear answer about what we should actually do at the door.' Minister, is it acceptable that a small business who wants to run a biological-only female event is unable to get clarification as to whether or not—and the event is being held shortly, on 7 November. It's sold out. There are more events locked in for 2027. Is it acceptable that they cannot get (a) from this department, which administers the act, or (b), it would appear, from anybody else clarification on the law? Do they say no to biological men who identify as women, or do they have to accept them because otherwise they'll be in breach of the law and end up like Sall Grover, up for a million bucks in costs?
Nobody would like to see anybody, particularly a small business, up for a million dollars in costs, Senator Cash.
Well, that's Sall Grover's case.

I'm simply saying nobody wants to see a small business in those circumstances. You've been asking the questions of the officials here, they've indicated to you that they're not in a position to give legal advice and I think that is the—
I'm not asking for legal advice, with all due respect, Minister.
Well, I think you were. Some of your questions were directly—
I'm merely asking for an interpretation of the law.
It's been a long time since I did a law degree, Senator Cash, but I think asking that question would be deemed to be legal advice.
An interpretation of the law as it stands.
If you're asking a lawyer, 'What is the interpretation of the law?' I think that is legal advice. That aside—
I've got one more question.
I again make the point this is not my area of responsibility. I shall refer your question to the Attorney-General and get back to you.
I'm going to ask you then, Minister, one final question before I hand over the call. What's the status of murder in Australia? Can you interpret the law for me, or is that legal advice?
What is the status of murder?
Is it a criminal offence or not—or is that providing me legal advice on the Criminal Code? Yes, exactly. That's the answer I need.
You know the answer to that question.
Seriously.
Well, you should be serious, Senator. I don't—

I am. I'm asking about the rights of biological women in this country, and you are making a mockery of the questions by failing to answer what small businesses across Australia are now asking for clarity on.
Thank you, Senator Cash.
I reject that outright, Senator Cash. I have taken your question, and I'm referring it to the Attorney-General, which is, I think, entirely appropriate in the circumstances.
Thank you, Minister. I'll now rotate the call and go to Senator Darmanin.
I've got some questions about fraud prevention and anticorruption.
I'll just get the right officers to the table.

Thank you. I understand one of the Attorney-General's Department key activities is around building counterfraud capability across government, so I wondered if you could talk to us a bit about the emerging priorities that the department has in supporting entities across the Commonwealth in improving their counterfraud and anticorruption activities.

Certainly. The Commonwealth Fraud Prevention Centre within the department has been around since 2019 and received ongoing funding in the 2026-27 budget. Our immediate priorities are to continue our existing work supporting the capability of Commonwealth entities to prevent and address fraud and corruption risks in their entities, and we do that in a number of ways. We have a fraud practitioner training program, which is actually underway in Canberra as we speak. We lead cross-system collaboration between entities involved in countering fraud, in particular to improve maturity in respect of fraud measurement, data collection, prevention of fraud, fraud risk management and response. We administer the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework, which sets key requirements for entities in respect of fraud risk management within their entities—and corruption risk management, I should say—and we provide support, guidance and advice to entities in meeting the requirements of that framework.

Our focus at the moment is improving measurement capability, both in terms of measuring fraud losses and in terms of savings that can be gained from prevention; improving our understanding of the level and nature of fraud across the system; progressing policy and legislative reform, where appropriate, to support better fraud prevention and response; and improving awareness and understanding of fraud risks across the full Commonwealth spectrum in terms of various functions. We have Fraud Awareness Week coming up in November, and the theme is 'Understanding the hidden impacts of fraud'.

Can you talk about the successes that you're seeing across government from the work that you're doing and, I guess, maybe make some comment on the level of maturity that arises out of the work that you're undertaking and how that might vary across departments.

Maturity does vary across departments, and the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework does recognise that. It talks about entities putting in place reasonable and appropriate measures for their entity. Obviously there are a wide range of Commonwealth entities. They vary greatly in size and role and operating environment, so the framework is designed to be responsive to that but so is our service offer within the department. We support large, mature entities to continue improving their existing capability. We support smaller entities to have consistent fraud risk assessments in place and control frameworks that are appropriate to their entity. Over time, with the guidance and products and support that the centre has offered and also the training program which I mentioned, we're seeing more consistent application of those concepts across the board. And, I think, with the update to the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework in 2024, there has been a really significant increase in awareness across the Commonwealth public sector of the requirements of that framework and how they can be met.

Do you have a specific example that you could point to of a success where you've worked with a department and then you've seen outcomes from that in a quite tangible way? I think that would be useful to understand.

Yes. We are working with entities across the Commonwealth in an ongoing way and we see many examples. One that I would particularly highlight is that the Department of Education have significantly improved their payment accuracy in the context of childcare subsidy, which has led to significant savings to government as a result of fewer inaccurate payments and a better targeting of those payments towards where they're more appropriate under the program guidelines.

I might add that we work very closely with the Fraud Fusion Taskforce in both understanding what they see at an operational level and looking for those opportunities for whole-of-Commonwealth legislative settings or other arrangements that we can assist with to support protective measures across a range of agencies.

Thank you. AI is the theme of the moment. What sorts of risks are you seeing emerging as a result of the increasing use of AI in the community and how are you monitoring that in terms of the response in your support to agencies that you work with?

We're looking at AI through a number of different lenses. One is to consider how AI tools could assist in mitigating fraud risks. Another is thinking about how entities' adoption of AI as part of their activities may then change their risk profile in relation to fraud and corruption or, indeed, create opportunities to do it better. The framework requires that, if there's a significant change to the activities of the entity, they should refresh their fraud risk assessments and control frameworks. So we're providing advice now to think about whether the use of AI might give rise to that. Then, of course, the third angle is the changing threat environment from the potential the use of AI by bad actors. We are working with counterparts in government to consider how overall frameworks for responsible use of AI in government and technical upgrades can be used to consider fraud and corruption risk mitigation as well.

The fraudsters are always acting much more quickly than you can respond and detect and then improve. How do you deal with that challenge? I know that's a big question. How are different departments thinking about being thorough, fast and responsive?

You're absolutely right. What we say is that there is always going to be fraud and it is a hidden crime. So it is a continuing challenge to stay ahead of fraudsters and to understand the nature of the battle that we're fighting. We work really closely with international counterparts as well to understand how they're looking at the problem, and we facilitate conversations between entities, as I think I mentioned, and communities of practice to consider the emerging risks and some shared insights and lessons in terms of combating those. I think what that looks like will differ from each entity's perspective. But, again, the requirements of the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework are intended to be principle based and technology agnostic, so they apply in changing threat landscapes as well. It's a responsibility of entities to consider how their risks may be evolving and changing all the time.
Thanks very much.
Senator Blyth.

I'm going to pick up along the same lines of Senator Cash's questioning. I want to speak a little bit more about the Tickle v Giggle decision. You mentioned that you provided some advice to the Attorney-General in terms of a summary of the case. Are you able to table that for the committee?
We'll need to take that on notice just to consider whether it contains legal advice or other content.

That's fine. Could you take that on notice and then provide what you can from that that doesn't breach any of the requirements of that. Following on from what Senator Cash was asking, without asking for legal advice, and it seems like the Attorney-General hasn't necessarily asked for information from you, have you provided any advice to anyone in terms of what the implications are for businesses in Australia following that Federal Court decision?
No, we haven't.
And no-one's asked you to?
No.

Would that be something you normally would be asked to do? This is quite a landmark decision. It changes how businesses run. It changes how schools operate. If you had something of that size and a case of that magnitude, would that be something you would normally in the course of your work be asked to consider?

I've been around way too long, over the course of many years and different issues that have arisen. Sometimes we get campaigns of letters on issues. Sometimes it's just a few letters that come in. Sometimes it's quite significant. I'm not aware at this point that we've received any significant numbers or any correspondence. I'd need to check that. It's possible there's some, but we've not received a significant volume.
I mean in terms of advice where, say, the Attorney-General of the day would normally ask for the implications of a landmark decision.
No. I don't think we would say that—
So you wouldn't normally do that in the course of your—
I think it's—
department operations?
quite variable, but I wouldn't say we would normally, in a case of this type, be asked for further advice beyond what we've provided.
What would you say this case type is? Would you say it's a landmark decision in the Australian context?
That's an opinion.
It would be giving an opinion to characterise the case. We provided a summary.

I'm trying to figure out what you would normally do. You're saying you wouldn't normally, in a case like this, so obviously you classify them in particular terms. You've never had within your department—and you've mentioned you've been there a long time—a significant case where the Attorney-General has asked for or you've been asked to provide information in terms of what implications this will have in the Australian context and in broader society on businesses, on schools or on whatever it might be that the case impacts?
I'm sorry; I misunderstood your previous question.
That's okay.

I was answering the wrong question—or not answering the right question, I should say. Depending on the matter, if it's a High Court matter that raises novel issues or different issues, we would, either at the request of an attorney-general or of our own volition, provide advice. That is certainly something that does happen from time to time. It's not every case. It really does depend on the matter.
And it didn't happen in this case. So can I confirm that you haven't provided it of your own volition and the Attorney-General hasn't provided—
We provided a summary, as Ms Mills articulated—
But that sounds like that's routine. That happens on everything?
No, it doesn't.
Not every court case.
Important cases.
Okay, so it was important enough to do that, but not necessarily to go further.

Cases vary a lot. Obviously, if the Attorney-General is intervening in a matter him- or herself or it's a constitutional matter—there would be cases on which the department and Australian Government Solicitor would be closely involved and on which we would provide a lot of briefing. In this matter, we provided a summary of the outcome and, as I think Ms Mills has said, it is an articulation of the law as it has stood for some time.
Do you think that the erosion of biological rights for women, who are 50 per cent of the population here in Australia, is significant?
Again, you're asking for an opinion from the officials.

It could be framed in another way. You've got to use your abilities. That's an implication of the case—that the biological rights of women have basically been eroded and no longer exist in Australia. That's a direct result of this case, so I'm not asking for your opinion. That's legal fact now.
We wouldn't necessarily accept that characterisation.
What would you say the result of the case is then? Let me just understand. We can't get legal advice from you, but you seem to have a view on this.
That's not the case.

I indicated earlier that the finding of the full Federal Court was that Giggle and Ms Grover had engaged in unlawful direct discrimination against Ms Tickle by treating her, a transgender woman, less favourably than a person assigned female at birth. That was what the court found.
Is it fair to say, though, that the court has found that a biological female—a person assigned female at birth—and a biological man who identifies as female are essentially the same thing now by law?
The court was considering—
That's what the court's found?
Ms Tickle's status as a transgender woman in that judgement.
But it's a biological man who identifies as a woman. That's what the courts found. I'm trying to understand where women's biological rights exist in that.
I think I've described what the court's decision was. I can't go further into giving legal opinion.
No, and I'm not asking you to. It's just that you said that women's biological rights still exist in Australia. You said to me—
I don't think we did.
that's not your understanding—
I don't think we did say that. What I said was that the court found that Giggle and Ms Grover engaged in unlawful direct discrimination against Ms Tickle by treating her—
We're going to go around in circles here. I guess this is what I was saying—that the biological rights of women no longer exist in Australia. Is that a significant finding of the court?
That is not an accurate description.
But I'm trying to understand how that's not accurate, because biological women's rights are now inferior to a biological man's. That's what the court has found.
That is the interpretation that you're putting to it, but I think that would be contested by others.
How is—
Can I ask one clarification question?
Yes, Senator Cash.
I'm also now confused again.
I'm really confused!

The nuns clearly haven't taught me this either! Can I confirm, then, in relation to the status of law, under the Sex Discrimination Act and men who identify as women, would it be possible, therefore, if every man in this room identified as a woman—at law, we need to accept that—that we therefore have one hundred per cent gender equality in this room when it comes to female representation?
That is a hypothetical. We can't—
How is it a hypothetical? Again, we're asking what the law says.
No. You framed it as, 'If every man in this room,' and—
Well, what does the law say in relation to that?
Ms Chidgey has—
Are men able to identify as women?
The Sex Discrimination Act itself doesn't define woman or man or sex—
No. Well, that would be a small problem, I would put to you.
and that's consistent with the Convention on the Elimination on All Forms of Discrimination Against Women.
Senator Farrell, do you know a very easy way to clean up this mess?
Tell me, Senator.

Yes, exactly. Support my bill to bring common sense back to Australia, recognising the biological rights of both women and men in this country. You don't need to discriminate against transgender people, but by God you do need to recognise biological reality. That is not ideological; it is merely common sense. Senator Farrell, why won't your government recognise the biological rights of women in this country?
We don't support your bill. I concede—
It merely recognises, Senator Farrell, the biological rights of women.
Senator Cash—
And men—ironically, as well, for the men in the room.
Senator Cash, I feel like I've reminded senators a few times.
As one of the men in the room, I'm not asking you to defend my rights, with all—
But I will, as a biological man.

With all due respect, I'm not asking you to do that. The Sex Discrimination Act has, by and large, been supported by both the ALP and the coalition over a long period of time. You're talking about a particular case which has made some determinations, and you're proposing a way forward. The government doesn't support your way forward. Nor does it—I think there is more than one bill in this area—
I'm talking about my bill.

I know, but I'm indicating to you that there's more than just one bill in this area. I think Senator McKim also has a piece of legislation. The short answer is we don't accept that your solution is the way forward here, Senator Cash. I'm happy to refer the issue to the Attorney-General to get a formal response for you. Have we voted on your bill?
Yes, you have. You voted against the protection of biological rights—
Well, there we go.
because you didn't even allow the bill to be introduced into the Australian—
Yes, that's right. That's what I thought.

Well, you allowed it to be introduced, and you denied its first reading. So, effectively, yes, you voted against allowing the parliament to even debate whether or not, for example, biological lesbians are at law allowed to meet as biological lesbians.
I do need to rotate the call. I'm seeking an indication of how much longer we're going to go.
I have a few more questions. I'm happy for you to rotate and come back if that's easiest.
I will do that. Senator Polley.

I have some questions in relation to identity and information division and privacy, particularly around the exposure draft on the second tranche of privacy reforms. Can the department elaborate on how the proposed fair and reasonable test for handling personal information will strengthen protections for Australians.
The officers take will you through that.
Sorry to ask, but would you mind repeating the question for us.

I just wanted to get an update in relation to the exposure of the draft bill on the second tranche of privacy reforms. Can you elaborate on how the proposed fair and reasonable test for handling personal information will strengthen protections for Australians?

A general update would be that we have recently conducted some public consultation on an exposure draft bill and accompanying consultation paper at the end of August to the middle of September. That was a successful consultation. We had around 460 written submissions and we're working through the results of that process.

In terms of your question specifically about the fair and reasonable test, essentially there's some dissatisfaction with the current privacy framework insofar as it's particularly complex and not well understood, and difficult to administer. There are three Australian Privacy Principles that provide requirements for how personal information should be collected, used and disclosed, and these are difficult for many entities to understand and apply. They include technical distinctions such as between primary and secondary uses of information, and between solicited and unsolicited information. The proposed new fair and reasonable test, which was generally supported in the recent consultation, would provide a new clear baseline standard for all personal information handling. It would require entities to ensure that all information handling is fair and reasonable in the circumstances, unless it's required or authorised by another law, and a small number of exceptions apply.

To reduce duplication and simplify compliance obligations, it would replace some of these existing technical privacy principles, so the test would need to be considered by entities and they would need to consider a non-exhaustive list of legislated factors to help them determine whether particular information handling was fair and reasonable. These were set out in the exposure draft we consulted on: what a reasonable person would expect in the circumstances; whether the purpose for the personal information handling could be achieved with less or no personal information; whether the handling is related to the entity's functions or activities; whether the purpose for which the information was sought was transparent to the individual; and whether any privacy impact is proportionate to the benefit. No one single factor would determine the outcome but all relevant factors would be considered. In particular, this uplifted protection would reduce reliance on consent, which is being used as the primary privacy safeguard currently, but many individuals are telling us that that's not always meaningful because of long, detailed privacy policies that sometimes aren't clear in terms of what an individual is agreeing to.
Given concerns about smart glasses capturing images and recording video covertly, and AI processing data, how do the measures in this exposure draft address evolving privacy risks?

The attorney has spoken about this. The government's aware of community concerns around smart glasses and other wearable information-processing devices. It's largely because these devices can record and share images and other personal information in a range of situations, sometimes without people actually being aware that they're being recorded. The government has also spoken about the fact that these technologies can have beneficial uses, including as accessibility aids. And we understand the Attorney has met with Vision Australia on this issue.

In terms of the measures in the bill that would go to addressing some of the concerns with these technologies, the first point is that the Privacy Act does not apply to individuals wearing the devices, but it does apply to entities when they're collecting, using and disclosing personal information collected via the devices. Some of the things that would apply in the updated exposure draft are updated definitions as to what personal information is and about the collection of information and what constitutes collection. The fair and reasonable test is, I think, important in terms of when the information can be collected and how it would be able to be used and disclosed. Then, in particular, a new right to erasure would apply to large digital platforms and their collection of personal information. That would allow individuals in certain circumstances to seek deletion and destruction of their information once it's held by a platform.

There has been debate, which you actually touched on in your response. I was wondering if you could talk a little bit further about smart glasses being available for people with vision impairment and having access to more affordable glasses of this nature. There's a big cost disparity between what people with a sight impairment would currently pay for visual aids—some of those glasses—and what people pay for most of those that are on the market. Can you talk us through the meeting that happened further? Also, how useful can these devices be for people with disability?

One thing I would say is that not all smart glasses operate in the same way. They are generally collection devices for information, but they can be combined with a range of AI or facial recognition technology and other types of information processing. I think it's really a question not of the device but of how it's used. My understanding is that information can be collected for a range of uses. These can be beneficial and can be legitimately used by persons with disabilities to assist them to use information—for example, to describe their surroundings et cetera. Alternatively, they can be used by nefarious actors. I think the research shows that this has been a particular problem in terms of harassment of women in certain situations. They can be used just to target particular individuals and upload their information for less useful and less legitimate purposes.

Ms Fitch said in relation to an earlier question that the Attorney-General herself had met with Vision Australia in relation to these issues. We also received a submission from Vision Australia and other disability organisations in relation to the consultation paper that we put out. The thing that I've struck and have been told is that they can be quite life-changing for people with a disability, and that's something that we've heard loud and clear through this consultation process. I just thought it's worth adding that as well.
The consultation took place and you've got the submissions. When are you going to be able to provide information as to the outcome of that consultation period?

We received about 460 written submissions through that process. We also held, I think, seven targeted consultation roundtables. We are working our way through that volume of feedback that we received on the consultation process. So that's what we're doing currently.
This is my last question, Chair. How do the measures provide for stronger, more meaningful standards for consent?

Currently the Privacy Act doesn't define or include standards for consent. It just says consent can be express or implied. Currently the practice seems to be in some instances that individuals are being asked to read lengthy privacy policies and consent or otherwise based on quite vague terms and information. The exposure draft bill suggests a new definition of consent which makes clear that it should be voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous. That is intended to make it more meaningful so that individuals know what they're actually consenting to when they indicate that.
Thank you.
Senator Shoebridge.
You were giving that answer in relation to questions from Senator Polley about smart glasses, is that right?
That's correct.

If somebody just heard your answer, they might have the mistaken belief that that's the kind of consent that would need to be given before people are recorded by somebody using smart glasses as they walk around the street, but that's not your proposal at all, is it? What you're proposing doesn't apply to consent in those circumstances when individuals are wearing the glasses and recording people as they walk about the street.
It's correct insofar as the current proposal, the exposure draft that we consulted on, does not propose to extend the Privacy Act to individuals in Australia.
Can you read to me the elements of consent that you are proposing in relation to corporations when they're taking data. I think you read them just before, Ms Moran. Could you read those elements.
You're asking the definition of consent?
Yes.

What Ms Fitch outlined is that the exposure draft bill and the proposed amendments in relation to the definition of consent provide that it must be voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous. The purpose of the amendment to the definition of consent is to ensure individuals have genuine choice and control over handling of their personal information in the context of the Privacy Act.
And you're intending, if the bill goes to the next stage, to say, if corporations are gathering data or material, they need to get that consent before they handle material. Is that right?

That's not quite right. The exposure draft bill doesn't suggest that consent should be required for all personal information handling, only for sensitive information, for trading and in certain other circumstances.

But the intent is that the corporations should get that for that sensitive information. Corporations should be getting that if they're acquiring sensitive information. Sensitive information would be vision of somebody at the gym or vision of someone's family at the beach. That would meet 'sensitive information', wouldn't it?
If it's biometric information it would be. Not all images would necessarily meet that standard, but generally speaking—

But, to be clear, the concern that Australians have about smart glasses isn't some corporate doing it, although maybe you could see circumstances in which corporates put smart glasses on employees and send them out into the society. The concern that most Australians have is that people can just buy these things at Kmart for 30 bucks, whack them on and go out into places where people have some expectation that they won't be recorded—
Senator—

Let me finish, Ms Chidgey. And simply record people—record women at gyms, record families going about their business in the supermarket and record people at beaches, and none of your proposals are even going to touch on that. They're not even going to touch on it.
There is the statutory tort in the Privacy Act as well that does apply to serious invasions of privacy by individuals—
But you won't know.
Senator Shoebridge, you just pulled Ms Chidgey up for interrupting you.
Fair point.
You are now doing the same thing to her. Ms Chidgey?
I would just add, as you would have seen, that there are a range of local governments who are also banning the use of smart glasses in particularly sensitive settings, which is appropriate.

The idea that, in the face of a nationwide privacy issue like this, the Commonwealth government's answer is, 'We're going to let Glen Innes shire work it out,' or, 'We're going to let the Murray-Darling council work it out,' or, 'We're going to let the Penrith council sort it out, on an ad hoc basis'—it's remarkable if that's the answer. You're going to let North Sydney Council sort it out?

I think that goes to some of what we were talking about in terms of smart glasses having some significant beneficial uses as well as inappropriate uses. These measures work to distinguish those issues.

Have you had a look at what those councils have done? Those councils have banned the use of smart glasses in a whole variety of public facilities, and they've done it because of deep and real concern about privacy, but, because they haven't got the resources and because they haven't got heaven knows how many bureaucrats able to go and actually churn their way through this stuff, they haven't had the opportunity to have the discussion with the disability community, including the vision impaired. You do, but you're not doing it to help the councils make the decisions. You're not doing it to have some kind of coherent national policy. You're letting Glen Innes council do this, North Sydney Council do that and Brisbane council do this, and you're showing no leadership. It's this department all over. You're always looking for someone else to actually do the hard yards and find responsibility—always at someone else.
I don't accept that, Senator.
Senator Shoebridge, I struggled to hear a question in that.
Are you serious that the way forward is letting local councils sort it out? Are you serious about that?

We have described the way in which the enhancements that would be made by the tranche 2 privacy reforms would deal with any businesses or corporations captured by the Privacy Act dealing with that information. The other measure that exists in the Privacy Act is the statutory tort for individuals.

But, to go back to the statutory tort, Ms Chidgey, in order for you to take action on the statutory tort you need to first of all know your privacy has been breached. If you're recorded without your knowledge with covert devices and then it's just shared off in a part of the internet you never have access to, how would you ever know that your privacy was breached? How could you ever exercise a right under a statutory tort? People are asking to be protected in the first place, not to be given a potentially unusable remedy once the breach has happened. Do you understand that? People want protection, not a technical right that they probably can't use. Do you understand that? Have people told you this in their submissions?
I think that goes to the range of measures that local governments are implementing as well as the improvements through the Privacy Act that will have an effect on misuse.

Have you pulled any of these councils together and taken them through the issues that have been raised when you've engaged with the disability community? Have you begun that leadership to bring the mayors and councillors together to help them navigate this? Have you done that?
We have not met with local government.

So you're working away over here in a silo. You're saying councils need to sort it out with their very minimal resources. I think they get less than two per cent of government revenues. Your answer is councils, and you're not even talking to them. How are you not talking to councils?
Councils, as you're aware, have been taking action.
I ask you how it is you're not talking to councils, and your answer is that councils have been taking action. Is that really the answer?
I'm saying we haven't met with them. They've obviously been making their own decisions about action they need to take in the context of their responsibilities.

Ms Chidgey, this is the point. They are making a series of important decisions with a fraction of the resources you have and none of the bureaucrats that this department has. They haven't got the resources to engage with the disability community like you have. I'm sure they're doing their best, but you're letting them go out there and make decisions to respond to the very real concerns that residents are putting forward. You're not helping them. You're not giving them resources. You're not connecting them with the disability community. You're not driving any kind of coherent national reform. You're just letting them go. I ask you why you haven't met with them, and your answer is, 'Because they're doing stuff.' That is not an answer.
We've been made aware that the Attorney-General has met with the local council association. The department has not, but the Attorney-General has.
When did the Attorney-General meet with the local—
We don't have the exact date, but we could take that on notice.
Which local council association?
The Australian Local Government Association, ALGA.
Could I ask you to provide full details of what, if any, the discussions were and what proposal was put forward by the Attorney, and can you provide minutes, please.
We weren't part of the meeting. We can take that on notice and see if there's anything that the department is able to provide.
Minister, could I ask you to provide that material in relation to the Attorney—
In the next five minutes? Did you say in the next five minutes?
No, I didn't.
I'm sorry, I must have misheard you—
If you can, I'm very happy for it to be in the next five minutes, don't get me wrong; by all means, do.
I was just looking at the clock there and I think the Attorney might be in question time. It might be difficult for her to come out and—
If you can in the next five minutes, that would be wonderful, but I'd just ask you to take it on notice.
Yes, certainly, I will do that.
Thank you, Minister. I'll now hand the call to Senator Blyth.

I am going to go back to the officials that we had earlier, because I'll just keep going on the Giggle v Tickle decision. I'll follow on with some clarifying questions. Has the department undertaken a review of the relevant sections of the Sex Discrimination Act following the judgement?
No, Senator.
No, you haven't. Is it my understanding, then, that you didn't feel that such a review was necessary?
The department wouldn't generally just do a review of its own volition. We would engage with ministers.
So nothing was requested from the minister or from the government?
No.
No.
No.
Sorry, that was 'no'?
No, Senator.
Has the department prepared options to clarify the legal meaning of 'woman', 'man' and 'sex' in the Sex Discrimination Act?
No.
No. Have you prepared any options to explicitly protect biological female-only spaces?
No.
No. Has the department been asked to draft any legislation to address the implications of the judgement?
No.

No. Was the department asked to provide any advice to the Attorney-General in relation to Senator Cash's Sex Discrimination Amendment (Restoring Common Sense and Recognising Biological Sex) Bill 2026?
We provided a summary of the proposed legislation, yes.
To the Attorney-General?
To her office.
Are you able to table that for the committee?
We would have to take that on notice.
We would have to take that on notice.
Do you recall, in general, what was in that summary, Ms Mills?
I'll just take that on notice, thank you.
You have to take that on notice? Okay. If we can then have on notice either that summary you provided or what is possible where the legal advice is taken out—

Senator, sorry to intervene, but I don't think it's common practice to release advice that the department gives to the government in these circumstances. I'll check on that, but I don't think that is standard practice.

Thank you. I appreciate that and I appreciate that the legal advice is not something that the committee would normally see, but I think, in this instance, it's helpful for the committee to see the department's advice that they gave in relation to that bill, particularly given that it didn't get past its first reading stage. Can I ask whether any women's organisations were consulted by the department since the full Federal Court's decision, and have any of them requested legislative change?
No, we haven't.
Has the department ever spoken to or consulted with the Lesbian Action Group?
Sorry, I missed that last question.
Whether the department has consulted with the Lesbian Action Group?
I'd need to check that with colleagues.
Not that we're aware of.
That's the group that's been in court for the last—no, okay.
No.

Can I ask, given the judgement and the concerns that have been raised about female only spaces, what further work is the department undertaking to give women and women's organisations certainty about their rights in Australia?
We're not undertaking any work at this time.

Can you confirm that as of today that—and this is probably better for the minister, given that the department isn't working on anything. Minister, can you confirm that the Albanese government is not planning to do anything to protect the rights of biological women in Australia?

I don't think that's a fair assessment of the government's position. I think we do protect the rights of both men and women in this country. We have legislation which we enforce in this area. I don't think that's an accurate description. But in terms of something specifically in the area that you're asking about, I shall inquire of the Attorney-General and come back to you.

Thank you. That would be most helpful because I think it's fair to say, yes, there is a lot of legislation, but where the biological rights of women collide with those of men, it seems that the men's rights are still coming first. It would be very interesting to see what the Attorney-General has to say. I've been contacted, like Senator Cash, by constituents and one particular instance is that schools are able to apply for exemptions where they can be single sex. You can have girls schools and boys schools, and that's something where an exemption is allowed to apply. I've been contacted by constituents where there are, at a girls school, girls enrolled who identify as boys. Would that be a breach of the Sex Discrimination Act?
That's asking us for legal advice again.

It's not. It's asking how the legislation would apply in that instance. It's not legal advice. It's like saying if someone goes out and shoots someone—as Senator Cash was saying—is that murder? But in terms of that, that exemption applies. And because we now don't have biological definitions within the Sex Discrimination Act, what are the implications of that in that case? Is it as clear cut?

I think we've been clear that these judgements about discrimination are made on a case-by-case basis, and that there are things like exemptions in the act that apply in certain circumstances. We can't provide just a broad piece of advice in response to your question.
Can you understand now how this piece of legislation is very difficult for people to understand what is right and wrong under the act. Is that something you can appreciate?
I acknowledge you and Senator Cash have received queries.

Are you aware of the backlog of cases that may now—because even yourselves in evidence today make this seem like only the courts are going to be able to decide this and that everything seems to be 'get a lawyer' or 'go through a court process'. Are you aware of or has your department put anything in place to allow for an influx in cases that will be in relation to this?
It's the Australian Human Rights Commission that deals with complaints in the first instance.
Not complaints, cases.
Well that—
And the Human Rights Commission falls under—
But the cases usually come through. I think that question would be best directed to the commission, but it would be speculating as to whether this case will have the effect that you're indicating.
Am I right to assume that the Attorney-General's Department is ultimately responsible for the funding that goes to the Human Rights Commission—that they sit under it?
They have an appropriation made through the budget process.
It comes through the department, but it's allocated through the budget process and through budget decisions.
But it's coming through the department. So, ultimately, if they run over budget—
No, they have a specific budget that is allocated to them through budget processes. There's just an administrative mechanism that goes through the department.
That's fine; they can have that. But the money still has to sit somewhere. So it's not sitting with the department?
No.
It sits with the commission.
It sits with the commission. So, if the commission run over budget on something, what mechanism do they use to seek more funds?

They work through the budget process. They're an independent entity. They have an accountable authority, in the same way that I'm the accountable authority for the Attorney-General's Department. If there are funding pressures, you apply through a budget process.
Do you ever provide legal advice or support to the Human Rights Commission?
Not legal advice. But we do provide support. They are a part of the portfolio.
This is what I'm trying to establish—how independent they are from the portfolio. So they're a part of the portfolio.
Yes, in the same way that the courts are.
What kind of support do you offer to the Australian Human Rights Commission?
I might just indicate I'm going to share the call after this response.

It takes a range of things. Obviously, as the department at the head of the portfolio, we coordinate budget processes. We engage with them on financial, IT, human resources—but in a support capacity, because they are independent entities.
In terms of that budget process, how do you support them in that? Are you helping them to decide how much they will need?

No, they're independent. For every entity in the portfolio, it's up to them to manage their budget. If they're under budget pressure, they have to make a case to government through the budget process, but that is for them to determine.
I'm just trying to figure out where that support then comes in from your department.
We would coordinate, but ultimately it's a matter for them to make the case to government.
What does that mean—'coordinate'?
It happens for every department that has a portfolio. You coordinate the budget process with all the entities in your portfolio, and that's what goes through the broader budget process.
I'm going to share the call, Senator Blyth, with Senator Shoebridge. I can come back to you if you have further questions. Senator Shoebridge.

I was going to ask about ad tech regulation in the context of privacy law reform. Last week, the ABC reported that a foreign company—I think this company was an Israeli tech company—used online ads to track and target devices, including at ANSTO and a series of other Australian government and critical infrastructure sites. Have you reviewed how privacy laws operate to permit and to facilitate this kind of access through online ads? Have you reviewed this privacy attack that happened very recently and was reported by the ABC last week?
We've been conducting work on privacy reform for some time, as you know, and are always interested in developments but have not specifically done any very close analysis of that particular incident.

These are reports that have come through a citizens group who have been tracking these attacks. There were a series of attacks on Australia's infrastructure, ANSTO, the ABC and a number of other agencies. It happened when an ad was loaded on a website, and then, without clicking, simply scrolling past the ad provided the avenue for an attack onto that device, and through that device, in one case, onto ANSTO; in another case, onto the ABC. Are you saying that that series of attacks has not been reviewed by the department?

There are a range of reforms that we're looking at that were in the exposure draft that go to direct marketing and looking at how different forms of marketing like ad tech would operate. Again, the existing rules in the Privacy Act, which are outdated and unclear in how they operate in the digital age, would be replaced by organisations needing to take reasonable steps to action opt-out requests. There would be greater transparency measures that would be required. Australians would be able to be clearer about what they're entitled to expect in terms of these websites using their personal information in a range of circumstances, including the sort of instance that you're referring to.
I think the example you gave would be subject to criminal laws for cybercrime.

Well, of course the intrusions would be subject to criminal laws. But the difficulty is that these entities are using the information they're getting from the providers of the ads—information about where the person's device is, what the nature of the person's device is, what they look at online, how long they're online. They assess their age. They may find out who their employer is. They're picking up all of that data from the ad provider and sometimes from other platforms because there are no privacy laws prohibiting that harvesting of data against people. When they start developing a full picture of a person, they're saying: 'Hang on, Ms Fitch works at the Attorney-General's Department. I'd like to know what's going on at the Attorney-General's Department. I'll whack an ad on her device and use that to get in and breach the Attorney-General's Department.' That's what's happening because there are no privacy laws protecting this.

One thing I would say is that one of the reasons we are working to update the Privacy Act is to make it much clearer that this sort of behavioural information is covered within the definition of 'personal information', so the Privacy Act would clearly apply.
Is it the intent to prevent these platforms from harvesting that data—is that the intent—unless there is prior, express consent given?
I think Ms Fitch said at the beginning we don't know the specifics of this matter, so I suppose we just want to be a bit cautious about giving you particular examples about that matter.
To assist the way going forward, why don't we just talk about online ads and data tracking?

I think Ms Fitch has given you just an overview of the particular measures in the bill that would go to these types of issues around direct marketing and trading in personal information. Ms Fitch has mentioned the definition of 'personal information'. You know that we're amending the definitions in the act to bring them much more into line with how information is actually collected and used in modern-day standards. We've talked to you already about consent and what that would look like, and the new definition of 'consent'. Obviously, we've also got the fair and reasonable test, which is a new baseline standard. So there are a range of measures in the tranche 2 bill that would, in broad terms, address the issues that you have raised in relation to this matter.

Why don't I ask a simple question, then. Under the proposed reforms, the drafts, would websites need people's active consent before sending that kind of information out to a third party? I'll repeat it again—what the person's device is, what their location is, what their browsing history is. Would the proposed reforms require active, prior consent before that information can be gathered and then transmitted?
If those organisations are trading in personal data, the answer to your question is yes.
What if they're just an advertising company?
I think the definition of trading would probably cover the sort of instance you talk about, if they're exchanging personal information for money or other considerations.

They may have other arrangements. They may have other reasons why they want to provide that information. They may want to provide that information simply because they want to target the Attorney-General's Department. They may want to gather it not for a financial reason but because they don't like the Attorney-General's Department, or they may want to gather it because they want to target another entity. It may not be a financial reason. Unless it's being gathered for a financial reason, there's no prohibition?

No. What Ms Fitch has said is, if they're trading in it, you have to seek consent of the individual under the new definition of consent. Otherwise, the fair-and-reasonable test will apply across the board.
But trading requires a financial exchange or some kind of financial benefit, does it?
I've got the bill somewhere here, but there is a benefit that needs to be—
If they're doing it for reasons unrelated to some kind of benefit—if they're just doing it because they maybe don't like this particular organisations or they—
The fair-and-reasonable test would then apply.
Would that prohibit the gathering of the data and the transmission of the data?

If it were a disclosure and not a trade, then, as Ms Moran has said, the fair-and-reasonable test would apply. The range of legislative factors that I referred to earlier would be part of the assessment as to whether that was fair and reasonable. Under the circumstances that you're describing, without wanting to go into hypotheticals and with the qualifier that we've already given—that I don't know all of the circumstances of the incident—I would think it would be unlikely to be fair and reasonable in that instance.

Which government agency do you understand is responsible for dealing with this most recent attack that I've described? That's the click-free-ad attack that has targeted the ABC and ANSTO and a number of other entities. You clearly aren't responsible for it—that's my reading because of what we've heard. Which agency do you understand is responsible for it?
I understand the Australian Signals Directorate has had involvement with the matter.
Yes, but I asked who's responsible for coordinating the response.
You'd need to ask the Australian Signals Directorate, who would have the lead on a cyberattack.
The only thing I would add to Ms Chidgey's response is there's obviously the National Office of Cyber Security, which generally is the coordinating agency in relation to cyber incidents.
I understand from the reporting that inquiries are being directed to ASD.
While we're on privacy reform and we have you at the table, so you don't bounce back and forth, how many submissions were received on the tranche 2 privacy proposals?
About 460.
What is the current proposal in relation to the small-business exemption?
From the exposure draft bill and the consultation paper that were released in August, at the moment there's no change to the small-business exemption.
My understanding is a number of submissions said that was a problem because it creates a significant potential privacy breach. Are you in a position to respond to those submissions now?

I think in broad terms—I mean, we've obviously said there were 460-odd, so there was a significant volume that we received, and we are working our way through them. I don't think it's incorrect to say that a portion of those dealt with issues relating to the small-business exemption.
There have been pushes for a children's privacy code—a tougher, firmer children's privacy code. What's the stage of that?

I think the tranche 1 bill, which passed the parliament in late 2024, had a requirement for the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner to establish a children's online privacy code. The OAIC and the Privacy Commissioner are undertaking that work currently, including a consultation they've done on a draft code, and they're working towards having that registered by 10 December, which was what was outlined in that legislation.
It's required, isn't it, by 10 December?
Yes, correct.
Do you understand that they're on track?
They are.

Coles and Woolworths are trialling facial recognition. There was a legal case involving Bunnings brought by the Privacy Commissioner which had—I think this would be the politest description—mixed results. Is it intended to place specific provisions to protect people's biometric data, particularly facial recognition, in these tranche 2 rules?

It's not proposed to change the general technology-neutral nature of the act. There are facilities in the Privacy Act which allow for more specific regulations to be made or to clarify how the rules in the act apply to particular technologies. We are aware of a range of organisations considering trialling facial recognition technology in a range of instances. I think that one instance that the Privacy Commissioner has made a determination on, relating to Kmart, is still before the ART. I know that the OAIC has released some guidance on how they intend to treat facial recognition technology under the current law, and that's the current status of things.
So, just to be clear, no intent for specific reforms dealing with facial recognition?
Other than that biometric information is considered sensitive information and there are general uplifts to the standard on how that should be treated within the tranche 2 proposals.
I note the time, Chair.
Thank you for your assistance, Senator Shoebridge. Senator Cash.
