I was made aware by the Director-General of OSI that the investigation was progressing, but in terms of the nature of the arrest—I don't believe I had any detail on that.

That was your evidence at the time. You then provided me with a written answer on notice, BE26/046. It states the secretary was notified on 1 April. It also states that OSI gave the department a copy of the media release on the morning of 7 April, which was the morning of the arrest.

The CDPP have provided me with an answer to a question on notice. I asked: in obtaining the consent to prosecute Ben Roberts-Smith, was the jurisdiction of the arrest discussed wit the AGD? Its answer: yes. Can I ask when was the jurisdiction of the arrest discussed with the Attorney-General's Department?
I'd need to check, because I don't think I was involved in that specific conversation.
The first I was aware was on that morning, through the media materials from the OSI.
Is there anyone else here that would be able to answer: when was the jurisdiction of the arrest discussed wit the Attorney-General's Department?
I'm not sure if there'd be anyone else other than Ms Chidgey, but we'll check just to make sure.
Can I confirm, Secretary, when was the first time you became aware of the jurisdiction of the arrest of Ben Roberts-Smith?
I refer back to my answers.

How about I put it simply to you. Given your evidence, I just want to re-confirm. Did you have any knowledge of the jurisdiction of the arrest of Ben Roberts-Smith before he was arrested on a plane in front of his family at Sydney Airport? This is a question to you, Secretary, on your own personal knowledge.
I think it was just the day.
Yes, I think we found out on the day. The team that was dealing with the procedural documents might have more to add.
The instruments for consent do sometimes differ by jurisdiction, so we were aware of the jurisdiction by virtue of the way in which the instrument was presented.
On what date did you become aware of the jurisdiction—in other words, that it would not be Queensland, his home state, but it would be in Sydney, New South Wales?
I would need to check at what time we became aware of that.
When was the Attorney-General first made aware of the jurisdiction of the arrest of Ben Roberts-Smith?
We would need to check with her. But I think it would have been clear on the instrument that was put to her.
And when you say the instrument was put to her, remind me on what date that was.
Sorry. I think we're just checking. There are variations to the way the instrument is presented by jurisdiction.

Okay, but it's a very simple question that I have. The arrest took place in the jurisdiction of New South Wales on 1 April, is my understanding. Prior to that, the Attorney-General was presented with a brief in relation to the consent to prosecute. On what date did the Attorney-General of Australia find out about the jurisdiction in which Mr Roberts-Smith was to be arrested?
The submission that was provided to the attorney in relation to her consent and authorisation did not identify the location of the arrest.
I'm not asking about the location. I'm asking about the jurisdiction.

Sorry, location or jurisdiction were not identified as part of that package where consent or authorisation was sought. I'm not aware of when the attorney would have learnt of the plans for the arrest, including the jurisdiction in which they were occurring.

Given that the answer from the CDPP on notice—as I've said, BE26/187—in obtaining the consent to prosecute Ben Roberts-Smith was the jurisdiction of the arrest discussed with the AGD, their answer is yes. Would you be kind enough to take on notice when the department was first advised of the jurisdiction, by whom and in what manner, et cetera.
I'm happy to take that on notice.

Thank you very much. Could I just now go to Ms Sharp? Obviously, it was an appointment by the government to the role of CDPP. Her previous role was Counsel Assisting the Office of the Special Investigator that was investigating alleged crimes in Afghanistan. Given that Ms Sharp's previous OSO role was disclosed in the Attorney-General's appointment press release, or should I say the CDPP's appointment press release, was the potential for a conflict of interest between her former responsibilities and her subsequent role as CDPP specifically assessed in relation to the prosecution of Mr Roberts-Smith?
That is a matter for the director and her office. Our understanding is that she did consider that issue.
She did.
Yes.
Why is that your understanding?
Because that is what the Director of Public Prosecutions has advised.
So, the Director of Public Prosecutions has advised—when you say has advised the Department, the Attorney-General or both?
The department.

When did the Director of Public Prosecutions advise—and I just want to be clear here—was the advice that there was no actual conflict of interest, or was the advice there was also no perceived conflict of interest.

We would need to take on notice when we first engaged with the CDPP about that. The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions will be appearing later, so they can confirm. But the assessment, as I understand it, was that there was no conflict of interest.

I'm interested in the Attorney-General and the department's perception of this because, obviously, this is a very serious set of charges, and a perceived conflict of interest must also be taken seriously. As you would be aware, public confidence in prosecutorial independence depends not only on the absence of actual bias, but also on the proper management of circumstances that could reasonably give rise to concern. Did the department request that the CDPP provide this advice to you?
We discussed this issue when it arose with the Director of Public Prosecutions and—
When you say, 'When it arose—
I was aware that it arose in the context of debate on a bill, for example.
I think you're referring to the bill—
My colleagues might want to add to that, and I have discussed it with Ms Sharp more recently as well.

Prior to that bill being debated in the parliament—and you are correct—I was the one asking the questions in relation to whether or not the government believed there was an actual conflict of interest or even a perceived conflict of interest between Ms Sharp's former role as counsel assisting the Office of the Special Investigator and her role now as the person prosecuting Mr Roberts-Smith. How did the department satisfy itself that there was not a direct conflict of interest or even an indirect or a perceived conflict of interest?

The director will be able to take you through in further detail, but it is common practice for directors of public prosecutions and their officers to provide advice to investigating agencies in the course of performing their responsibilities. This instance is in the substantive aspects not different to that. As I understand it, Ms Sharp gave some advice to the Office of the Special Investigator, and that often occurs in the engagement between the Office of the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions and the enforcement agencies they're working with in informing the brief of evidence that needs to meet the standards in the prosecution policy of the Commonwealth.

I'd put it to you, Ms Chidgey, that this is different because the Attorney-General of Australia and the government have made a decision to have a Victoria Cross recipient charged with war crimes. I would have thought that one might ensure that, given the nature of the CDPP and her previous role, a rigorous conflict of interest assessment would have gone through, in particular by the Attorney-General, when the brief of evidence was presented to her to sign off on the prosecution. Did the Attorney-General of Australia undertake a rigorous conflict of interest assessment?
I'm not aware that there was a particular conflict of interest assessment. What I can say is that there is not a conflict of interest in these circumstances for the Department of Public Prosecutions.
Why do you say that?

I say that because it is not a conflict for the director or officers of the CDPP to have provided advice and engagement to investigating agencies. That is a common part of the way all directors of public prosecution and their officers operate, and the decision that is ultimately then made on meeting the standards in the prosecution policy of the Commonwealth is nevertheless made independently by the director and by that office.

What about, though, the fact that again these are some of the most serious charges that can actually be brought against a person in Australia—war crimes along with the ISIS brides and crimes against humanity. Again, I go to a perceived conflict of interest, particularly when it comes to the independence or the perception of the independence of the trial and also the confidence of the Australian people in relation to the proper management of the circumstances that could reasonably have given rise to the concern. When you say that a conflict of interest assessment was undertaken, what does that mean?

That would be a matter for the director to take you through, but she and her office considered this issue. For the reasons that I've given, the CDPP prosecutes a lot of very significant matters with significant impacts on individuals. The engagement between the office, the director and the investigating agencies and the provision of advice is part of the way they operate, and it does not prevent the CDPP from making independent prosecutorial decisions that meet the standards.

I understand that, but this is not an independent prosecutorial decision. This is a decision of the Attorney-General of Australia. The only person in Australia who can consent to a charge of war crimes being brought is the Attorney-General of Australia. Again, just for the Hansard record, did the Attorney-General of Australia satisfy herself that a rigorous conflict-of-interest assessment had been undertaken in relation to Ms Sharp as the CDPP and the person who is now in charge of the prosecution and Ms Sharp's previous role as special counsel assisting the Office of the Special Investigator, who investigated alleged war crimes in Afghanistan?

I think what I would say is that the Attorney-General made her own decision about whether to consent based on the information that was provided to the Attorney-General. The Attorney-General made that decision independently based on the advice she had. The decision of the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions to put a case forward for consent was not affected by conflict of interest.

I'm sorry; we seem to be going around in circles, then. Did the Attorney-General receive independent advice from the Solicitor-General or the Australian Government Solicitor about a conflict of interest in whatever way, shape or form it took, from an actual conflict of interest all the way through to a perceived conflict of interest?
I can say that we did not obtain advice on a conflict of interest.

Did you as the department provide any advice to the Attorney-General of Australia independent of the CDPP, her own advice about herself, that there was no conflict of interest? Did you as the Attorney-General's Department obtain any independent advice, given the nature of the charges?

The department provided advice to the Attorney-General to support the Attorney-General to make her own decisions on consent in these matters. We did not provide specific advice on a conflict of interest. As I've said, the circumstances that arise in this matter are consistent with Director of Public Prosecutions practice and do not present a conflict of interest.

I just put it to you that, given this is a Victoria Cross recipient that served our country and we were the ones that actually awarded him for that service, one might have thought that perhaps a little bit of extra rigour might be appropriate when determining whether or not there was a conflict of interest. But you have basically accepted the CDPP's advice to you that she believes there is no conflict of interest, whether that be an actual conflict of interest, a potential conflict of interest or a perceived conflict of interest.
That's correct.
Thank you. Is there—
Senator Cash, I just want to know if you're going to move onto a different—

No, I will have more questions here, but this is on the conflict of interest. Was any conflict management plan put in place when Ms Sharp became the CDPP in relation to her previous work as the special counsel assisting the Office of the Special Investigator and the person who would potentially bring and has in fact brought a brief of evidence to the Attorney-General requesting to prosecute Mr Roberts-Smith for war crimes?
There was no conflict to be managed.
Because the CDPP advised you of that pursuant to their procedures?
Yes.
Okay. I'm happy to rotate the call.
Senator Darmanin.

I've got some questions for the Pacific Branch. I understand from previous hearings that the Commonwealth is a key supporter of the Pacific Islands Law Officers' Network. Could you just update the committee on the work that the department has been doing on the network since the last estimates, please.

Again, just like the February estimates, it's a great time to receive these questions because we're just recently back from the annual meeting of the Pacific Islands Law Officers' Network, which Australia had the privilege of co-hosting with Tuvalu in mid-October. At that annual meeting, the network agreed to an update to its strategic plan to really include a focus on illicit drugs and other transnational crime. The design behind this is for lawyers across the Pacific, including from our team at the Attorney-General's Department, to really swing in behind Pacific leaders and Pacific police efforts to combat illicit drugs and other transnational crime, which we know has been an increasing problem and an increasing concern across the Pacific.

It was a real privilege and a real pleasure to be at the PILON annual meeting where members decided to make that change to their strategic plan. What that means is we'll have a dedicated working group and dedicated funding to support that working group to mean that lawyers across the Pacific can help make sure that the legislative frameworks that allow transnational crime to be combated are made fit for purpose and that lawyers such as prosecutors across the region have what they need to be able to effectively support law enforcement in dealing with these really important regional issues for our Pacific partners and for ourselves as part of the Pacific region.

The PILON has continued throughout the year. Its work is not only limited to the annual meeting there, so it's also continued important work on the other strategic priorities of combating cybercrime and sexual and gender based violence. By way of example, in August the PILON Sexual & Gender Based Violence Working Group held an understanding trauma workshop in Fiji attended by 46 participants from across the Pacific, which was really about helping lawyers, prosecutors, witness support officers and others involved in the criminal justice process to understand the risks and possible methods of dealing with trauma both for themselves in dealing with sexual and gender based violence matters—which is very difficult, I think, for all involved, including the lawyers—but also for that working group in continuing the work on how to support vulnerable witnesses, which can include children and others, in those SGBV matters.

So I would say, in summary, it's been a really big and important year for the Pacific Islands Law Officers' Network, and it remains a real privilege for the Attorney-General's Department to be a member of that network and to contribute funding and technical assistance.

Thank you. It sounds like it was a successful meeting and update to the plan. Can you share some of the feedback that the department received from PILON members about Australia's contribution, in particular.

While we were at the annual meeting, during the formal parts of the meeting itself, the formal sessions, there was thanks passed on to the Attorney-General's Department for the funding and for the technical support we provide, just as there was for New Zealand as well. Australia and New Zealand are long-term co-funders of the Pacific Islands Law Officers' Network.

In addition to that, I guess, more formal recognition during the sessions, what really comes home to me every time I attend the PILON annual meeting and engage with fellow members—for example, of the executive committee—is their comments on how meaningful it is for their lawyers on the ground and back in their offices to have access to a network like PILON to support them in their work. At the annual meeting, for example, this year, we launched—I think it was a record—five publications produced by PILON, which included things like a cybercrime legislation implementation handbook with really practical checklists, case studies and ideas for jurisdictions thinking about developing and implementing cybercrime legislation. There was a revised effective asset management guide, which comes into play when you're looking at assets that are seized through proceeds-of-crime frameworks, for example.

The feedback we get from members, both senior officers and the more junior officers who make up their supporting delegations, is that that kind of publication and that kind of work is a really practical resource that each jurisdiction can take back and adjust so that they can use it on a day-to-day basis back home, across the 19 Pacific jurisdictions that we're working with. In short, again, I'd say there's formal recognition of Australia's role and support in the meeting sessions, but possibly even more important for me is that feedback from members about how practical and useful these resources are for their work.
Is the Pacific branch the only team that engages with Pacific law and justice issues, or are there other resources that are deployed in this area? And what's the FTE of the Pacific branch?

To take the last question first, I think the FTE for the Pacific branch in this 2026-27 financial year is approximately 21, which includes me. But it is also correct that there are many other areas across the department and the portfolio that are engaged with Pacific law and justice work. The last time I gave evidence, in February, I spoke about the work of the Australian Government Solicitor in providing pro bono training for lawyers from across Papua New Guinea in particular. They've done a lot of work with the Office of the State Solicitor and the Office of the Solicitor General in Papua New Guinea. That training has continued this year. We also have areas like the Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking Branch—I certainly don't want to speak in detail about the work that they can speak to themselves—who are engaged with Pacific law and justice partners and Indo-Pacific partners in the work that they carry out across the region. I might leave it there; otherwise, I could probably talk your ear off all day on it.
Thank you. I'm sure the Chair would not appreciate that!
Thank you very much. We'll now return to Senator Cash.

If I could just continue with my line of questioning, a prosecution in relation to alleged war crimes obviously carries significant public importance, and that importance makes it essential that the process is demonstrably impartial and fair. I would believe any potential conflicts should be properly examined rather than accepted without further explanation. So, since the issue of the conflict of interest was raised in the Senate in relation to the bill, when did the department seek extra information from Ms Sharp as to the extent of her previous involvement in matters concerning Mr Roberts-Smith?
During the line of questioning in the Senate around that conflict, I sought further information from the CDPP around the director's assessment of whether a conflict existed or not.
You went back to the CDPP herself?
I went back to her office.
So not to the CDPP herself?
I did not go directly to Ms Sharp. I went to members of her team.
How long did it take for them to respond to you?
It would have been in the course of the—
Senate debate?
Senate debate.
Understood. Does the department know whether Ms Sharp had access, while working for the OSI, to evidence, legal advice, witness material or investigative material concerning Mr Roberts-Smith?
You'd have to ask Ms Sharp, sorry.
Okay. So you didn't satisfy yourselves in accepting her word that there was no conflict of that?

I think it goes to the same issue I've discussed before that engagement between the CDPP and investigating agencies is a feature of the way that the CDPP performs its functions. So there wouldn't necessarily be anything inappropriate or a conflict in having engagement, including CDPPs sometimes getting draft briefs of evidence and providing some advice on any further work that's needed. Those briefs obviously contain evidence and material, so there would be nothing unusual about that.

Just to understand your evidence—does the department have actual knowledge as to whether Ms Sharp, as the CDPP, had access, whilst working for the OSI, to evidence, legal advice, witness material or investigative material concerning Mr Roberts-Smith? Do you have actual knowledge of that?
We don't have the details of what she would have seen.
You don't, but you would say—I just want to get this evidence very clear—it would not be unusual for that to have occurred and for there still not to be a conflict of interest.
That's correct.

Can I just go very briefly to the consent. Ms Chidgey, your answer to BE26-055 says:

The Attorney-General may vary or withdraw an authorisation provided under subsection 268.121(2) of the Criminal Code (Cth) for proceedings to be brought in the Attorney-General's name.

And we discussed at the last estimates that the prosecution of Mr Roberts-Smith is brought in her name, as we established, under that subsection. Can I confirm the Attorney-General can then withdraw her authorisation for the prosecution of Mr Roberts-Smith?
I think there's a slight nuance, in that the Attorney-General gives both consent and an authorisation, and I think it's the authorisation that can be withdrawn. One of them is just a moment in time—
That was the consent.
Yes.
So the authorisation is an ongoing authorisation until the authorisation is withdrawn.
That's right, because it allows the proceedings to continue—
Understood.
in the Attorney-General's name.
So an authorisation to withdraw the proceedings could, therefore, be issued at any time right up until the judgement is actually issued.
There has to be an authorisation for the commencement of proceedings.
Yes.
But then, yes, it could be withdrawn at any time subsequently, while the proceedings—
The proceedings are ongoing. So, at any time, the Attorney-General of Australia, in the same way as with the ISIS brides—
Yes.
could withdraw the authorisation. If the authorisation is withdrawn, what is the effect on the proceedings?
The proceedings would need to be withdrawn.
Yes. So they come to an end.
That's correct.
Understood. Are you able to recommence proceedings? Are you able to again give consent, or does double jeopardy apply?
If there hasn't been a final judgement in the matter, I think you could re-enliven proceedings.
Okay.
A court would consider whether there was still fairness to the accused in all the circumstances, but—

Yes. It's a very serious matter, obviously, to withdraw proceedings. Can I also confirm section 71 of the Judiciary Act—a separate section. We can withdraw authorisation, and the proceedings against Mr Roberts-Smith—and Mr Schulz, for that matter—could come to an end today. Section 71 of the Judiciary Act lets the Attorney-General decline to proceed further with any indictable Commonwealth prosecution once the accused has been committed for trial. Is that correct?
Yes.
My understanding is that Mr Dreyfus, the former attorney-general, used section 71 of the Judiciary Act to end the Collaery prosecution in July 2022.
Yes.

Understood. Nothing in section 268 displaces that. Is it also then the legal position that the current attorney-general could also end the prosecutions against Mr Roberts-Smith and Mr Schulz under section 71 in the same way that the former attorney-general Mr Dreyfus determined that he would end the Collaery prosecution in July 2022?
I think that would be legally possible. I think, in this circumstance, because there's an authorisation, that would be the more obvious—

Yes, I'm just trying to work out—there are several legal paths available to the Attorney-General of Australia. One has been exercised by Mr Dreyfus in relation to a prosecution brought by the CDPP. He brought that to an end. Is that decision reviewable?
I need to take that on notice. I think, generally, these kinds of decisions are not reviewable decisions, but, yes—
They're final because it's the Attorney-General of Australia making the decision—
other than, potentially, the constitutional provisions.
Can you also tell me this: section 8 of the DPP Act allows the Attorney-General of Australia to direct the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions?
Yes.

So the first way to end the prosecutions is to withdraw the authorisation. The second way, if you chose not to do that, is to go down the path of section 71 of the Judiciary Act, which former attorney-general Mark Dreyfus did in relation to proceedings authorised, I think, by Christian Porter when he was the Attorney-General. Would section 8 of the DPP Act mean that the Attorney-General could direct the director to stop the proceedings, effectively withdrawing the authorisation?

Yes. That would be a withdrawal of authorisation, because the authorisation says the director can carry this on in the Attorney-General's name. If the Attorney-General directed the director not to continue, that would be taken as a withdrawal of the authorisation.

Okay. The point is that the Attorney-General here is the sole arbiter in terms of whether or not the proceedings actually continue, because the Attorney-General, by their position, is the only person in Australia who is able to bring the proceedings to an end prior to a final judgement being given.
Yes, that is the Attorney-General's decision.
Thank you. I might move on to another topic—
Senator Cash, before you do that, I've got Senator Hodgins-May in the room.
Hello.
Sorry to disturb your flow.
That's alright. I looked over, and there was another person!
You were in the flow of things over there. I'll now hand the call to Senator Hodgins-May.

I've got some questions in relation to lobbying. Earlier this year, Four Corners reported 12 substantiated Lobbying Code of Conduct breaches since mid-2023. Can you tell me what consequences were imposed in those cases?
I think I'll ask my colleague Ms McKeag to answer those questions.

In relation to those 12 breaches, my understanding is that action was taken through engagement with the lobbyists and the breach was rectified by way of information that was missing on the register or other circumstances corrected.
So there was no penalty; it was just a discussion?
There was no further action taken. That is my understanding.
And have there been any more substantiated breaches since this article aired?
Sorry; what was the date of the article?
It was for Four Corners, earlier this year. I'll get the date.
We may need to take it on notice and just check the records.
I think I have to take it on notice.
Sure. That would be good—and, similarly, about any alleged breaches or investigations that are going on in relation to the Lobbying Code of Conduct.
I think I would need to take that on notice.
Sure. Has the Attorney-General's Department considered publishing anonymised investigation outcomes and compliance statistics regularly?
The department doesn't usually disclose information in relation to investigations for privacy reasons.
Are anonymised investigation outcomes something you've considered that might be in the public interest and worth publishing?
The department provides statistics in relation to breach information in the course of estimates. It's something that we could take under consideration.

I suppose the nub of it is why the public should have to wait for the media to report on these sorts of investigations to understand whether the rules are or aren't being enforced. So any further information provided by yourselves would be, I suppose, preferable to having to wait for those media stories and articles. How many AGD staff are dedicated to administering and enforcing the code and register?
I think currently it is about five FTE.
If that needs to be clarified on notice, feel free. Are you confident?
Yes. I will take it on notice.
What circumstances would lead the AGD to sanction or remove a lobbyist from the register rather than issue a warning?

It depends on the nature of the breach. There are a range of sanctions under the lobbying code. We also have mandatory reporting periods. Twice a year, lobbyists are required to update information on the register. Lobbyists that don't comply with those registration requirements may be removed from the register. That's a regular process that the department undertakes. In relation to ad hoc reports of suspected breaches of the lobbying code, we investigate them on a case-by-case basis and take into consideration the nature of the breach, whether it was inadvertent or intentional and consequences in assessing its seriousness. It's those serious breaches that may be referred to the secretary for consideration of whether a person should be removed from the register, or not registered.
In answer to my previous question about the five FTAs, is it possible to also outline what their roles are when you provide that on notice—the different functions.
We can, yes.

The code restricts lobbying on matters with which former officials had official dealings. AGD has described this as having its ordinary meeting. Is there a documented interpretation underpinning this interpretation? Sorry, that's a strange question. And have you ever sought legal advice on it?

There is a prohibition period, as you've identified, that prohibits ministers or senior officials from engaging in lobbying in relation to matters that they had official dealings for specified periods of time after they retire from that office. 'Official dealings' aren't defined in the code, so it takes its ordinary meaning.
Have you sought legal advice on it?
No.

How can AGD verify compliance when a former official works for a lobbying firm representing numerous clients and the register doesn't necessarily reveal which clients they work for or what lobbying they undertake?

Perhaps I can speak broadly to the process for investigation. I can't comment on particular matters or hypotheticals. We may receive information in relation to a suspected breach of the code that may contain information that a person has identified raises concerns. We put that information to the lobbyist and seek a response. We would consider both sets of information together. Where appropriate, we would seek additional information and then we would finalise our assessment.
Is it completely reliant on someone raising a concern? There's no proactive monitoring per se?
To be clear, somebody has to register a client.

Senator, I think your example was of someone representing multiple clients but not making that clear on the register. It is a requirement that they register in respect of each client, so not having done that would then be noncompliance, which we might have brought to our attention or become aware of in some other way, and then we'd take the steps that Ms McKeag has been talking about.
Okay. So every single client is documented on that register.
They should be, yes.

They should be; okay. The ANAO's 2020 audit found deficiencies in governance, risk management and evaluation. Perhaps you could briefly give us an outline of what AGD has implemented since then to address those findings and how it measures whether the regime is working. If there's additional detail, please put that on notice.

Yes, we can. Following the 2020 ANAO audit of the code, the code was updated on 28 February 2022. Those updates enhanced the code's transparency objective and improved its practical operation by allowing the secretary to decide not to register or reregister a lobbyist who committed a serious breach of the code on or after that date for a period of up to three months. A serious breach would include unregistered lobbying and breaching the principles of engagement with government representatives. The changes also strengthened disclosure requirements for former government representatives by requiring them to provide the title of their most recent government position for inclusion on the register, and where they're subject to a temporary prohibition on conducting lobbying activities related to their former role, they're required to provide information about that previous role and confirm they meet their prohibition period obligations at initial contact with government representatives. Furthermore, the changes required lobbyists to declare that they've not breached key parts of the code in their annual statutory declaration, which is part of that July—

Thank you. I'm about to be wrapped up, so I have just one final question on this. Have you done any work to advise on extending the code to cover in-house corporate lobbyists. I'll probably have to pass the call after that.
The code only applies to third-party lobbyists. In reform of the code—
And there's no work being done to extend that to in-house corporate lobbyists? There's no consideration being given to that?
Reform of the code would be a matter for government.
Okay.
Senator Cash.

I just want to go back to the withdrawal of authorisation in relation to a consent to prosecute where it's been given the consent by the Attorney-General. If the Attorney-General was to determine that she or he, depending on who it is, would withdraw proceedings, do they have to provide reasons, or is it solely for the Attorney-General to make that decision?
It's for the Attorney-General. There's no legal requirement for reasons.

Thank you very much. Could I now turn to the el Matari case? Mr el Matari of Greenacre declared himself ISIS's commander in Australia. He was jailed in Lebanon in 2017 for trying to join Islamic State. He was deported in 2018 and was arrested in Sydney in July 2019 for planning an insurgency and preparing to travel to Afghanistan. He did plead guilty to those crimes in October 2021, was sentenced to seven years and four months, with a non-parole period of 5½ years. He was not paroled. His full sentence expires on 1 November 2026. Is the department aware of whether or not a continuing detention order has been applied for?
The Department of Home Affairs administers that scheme and will be best placed to answer your questions.

I understand that, but you are the Attorney-General's Department and I would have thought that the Attorney-General would want to know whether the department that administers the legal side of things is all over whether or not a terrorist who admitted to his crimes and was jailed in Australia is walking out free on 1 November and whether the government is actually attempting to keep him behind bars. Do you have any knowledge as to whether a continuing detention order has been lodged or is being sought to keep this man—the terrorist; let's call him the terrorist because he's a convicted terrorist; he admitted to it—behind bars, or will he walk free on 1 November?
I think that does need to be put to Home Affairs. We wouldn't be in a position to judge the appropriateness of disclosure of any sensitive legal or operational information, so it—
How is that operational information? I would have thought the Australian public would actually want the government to say, 'You're damn right; we're going to try and keep this terrorist behind bars.'
The issue of where consideration of any such order is up to is a matter for the Department of Home Affairs.
In relation to the process, then—which this department did administer; is that correct?
Yes.

In relation to the process, if no application is on foot and the terrorist walks free on 1 November, what happens? How long does it take to actually get the continuing detention order in place or to put in the application and get it turned around?
Again, that would need to be put to the Department of Home Affairs. The range of measures that might be available is in the Home Affairs portfolio.
In your experience, as the department that did administer this, what is the normal turnaround time from application to keep a terrorist behind bars, given that in but a few days he's walking free?
I'm not able to answer that. Obviously, there are a range of measures that sit within the Home Affairs portfolio. That would be for them and for the AFP to answer.
In an article in the Sunday Telegraph of 18 October 2026, the Attorney-General's office declined to comment on the grounds that governments do not comment on parole matters. Is this a parole matter?
I think when it is a parole matter the government doesn't comment. Continuing—
Okay, but this is the Attorney-General's.
I think that continuing detention orders, as we've said, are a matter for the Department of Home Affairs.

Has this department—being the department that, obviously, is in charge of the laws in the country—had any discussions with Home Affairs or offered to brief Home Affairs or provide them with advice as to how to keep the terrorist behind bars?

Following machinery of government changes, the entirety of that responsibility, including the expertise that we had, transferred to the Department of Home Affairs. So they have the expertise, they manage the provisions of the legislation, and it's their minister who is the decision-maker.
Secretary, you haven't had any secretary-to-secretary discussions in relation to keeping the terrorist behind bars?
On this particular matter, I have not had a discussion with the Secretary of the Department of Home Affairs.

The alleged Bondi gunman has been listed as an associate of Mr el Matari, the terrorist who pleaded guilty to those charges. After Bondi, did the department review Mr el Matari's case or advise Home Affairs or the AFP to do so?
It would not be our responsibility to review the case. It's a matter for Home Affairs and the AFP.

Given 15 people were slaughtered on Bondi Beach and the connections have arisen, do you not think that perhaps, even just morally, the department might say to Home Affairs or the AFP, 'You might want to have a look at this guy'?
We operate consistently with our responsibilities. I think you would need to put that to the Department of Home Affairs, the AFP, and ASIO and relevant agencies.
In relation to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, does that sit within this department?
Obviously, the royal commission is independent, but it sits within the portfolio, so to speak.
Of the Attorney-General's Department?
Yes.

A March 2026 submission to the royal commission named Mr el Matari, the terrorist, as the most dangerous member of a 28-person network and alleged he was directing members from inside our country's highest security prison, including offering access to weapons and explosive supplies. Given that the royal commission sits within the department, as you've just stated, is the department aware of that submission?
I'm not personally aware. You would expect if there was information of that order, that it would be brought to the attention of ASIO, the AFP and the joint counterterrorism team.
Who would bring the information of that order to the attention of ASIO, the AFP et cetera?
Sorry, did you describe it as an order?
No, it's a submission to the royal commission.

We would need to take that on notice. We work closely with ASIO, AFP and other National Intelligence Community agencies in relation to the royal commission and any evidence there. But I would say that that would be a matter for ASIO and AFP.
Can I just confirm then that in relation to the terrorist Mr el Matari's sentence expiring on 1 November that the Attorney-General's Department can't assist me in relation to any of my questions?
I think it's appropriate to put those questions to the Department of Home Affairs which has responsibility in relation to the questions that you're asking.
Okay. Did the Attorney-General ask for a briefing in relation to this matter?
What matter are you referring to?
The release of the terrorist in but a few days time onto the streets of Australia if we don't get a continuing detention order.

The Attorney-General I think would be aware because we've provided advice over time, when parole decision-making comes up, that it's the end of the sentence. But it would be Home Affairs providing advice to the Minister for Home Affairs on the high-risk terrorist offender orders and also the AFP can consider measures it has at its disposal as well.
Okay. I finished with that topic because I know that we are—
We are running a quite over time at this point in the day. I understand Senator Hodgins-May has a very short block of questions.

And it's just finishing on lobbying as well. And just perhaps before I move on, just to finish up on that last question I asked, the official said it was best to ask the minister. I wonder, Minister, if you could comment as to whether the government is considering extending the code to cover in-house corporate lobbyists, considering they do much the same work as third-party lobbyists? Is this something your government's contemplating?

Thank you for the question. That's not something I've got information about in front of me. I can certainly take that on notice for you. We expect everyone to comply with the rules of the code, and I think the officials have taken you through how that works. Of course there's been work undertaken most recently around aligning the code with the parliamentary pass procedures. And, of course, it sits within a framework of a number of other pieces of rules and regulations. It can't be taken without context of the work that's been done there.

Yes, sure. If there's anything on notice, please, from your counterpart, that would be useful. Changing track but still on lobbying, has your department issued any transparency notices or undertaken any compliance assessments under the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Act concerning lobbying by entities in which the Japanese government holds a significant share, such as INPEX or by Japanese state agencies?
Sorry, is the question in relation to the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme?
Yes. And whether the department's issued any transparency notices or undertaken any compliance assessments under that act?

The department has issued five transparency notices under the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme, and they're published on the department's website. I think your question relates to a Japanese entity.
Yes, INPEX or Japanese state agencies.
No.
So, no transparency notices or compliance assessments?
For compliance assessments, we don't disclose any investigations or activities.
So, the only thing disclosed are transparency notices?
That's right. Obviously, the register itself is public as well.

INPEX Operations Australia is registered for parliamentary lobbying and is described as providing political analysis and engaging with ministers, shadow ministers, parliamentarians and their staff. What activities and entities does that cover, do you know?
I don't know. I'd have to take the question on notice. The register is publicly searchable.

If these entities are approaching ministers in relation to Australian energy policy—for example, gas tax, design of the gas reservation scheme, funding or CCS projects—and related trade relationships, would that constitute lobbying under the act?
I think I'd have to take the question on notice as to any activities information we can provide.
We can't really provide specific advice that relates to a particular entity. That would be us providing legal advice about the operation of the act.

I'm not asking for specific advice about a particular organisation or company. I'm just wondering if entities are approaching ministers in relation to energy policy during a significant policy development period. You don't need to mention specifics of those corporations. In relation to trade agreements, would that constitute lobbying in that scenario?

The lobbyist code of conduct and register applies to third-party lobbyists having to be registered and to disclose their clients. So if a third-party lobbyist approached a minister, they would need to be a registered lobbyist in order to comply with the requirements of the code and the register.
Are entities lobbying on behalf of foreign governments under any additional restrictions to Australians in the lobbyist register?

There's the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme on the one hand, which has certain requirements. Separately, there's the lobbyist code of conduct and register. We can go separately through the criteria for registration on the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme, but that Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme applies if you're undertaking registrable activities on behalf of a foreign principal, which is a foreign government or foreign political organisation.
I suppose what I'm trying to understand is if, in practice, they are under any restrictions, whether as part of the FITS or the lobbyist register.
It's a little bit hard with the information you've given. We can either go through now or we can take our notice to set out the criteria each under of those frameworks that would apply.

I understand the committee is short on time, so if you could provide those on notice. Final question, I hope. Does the commercial exemption under the FITS Act apply to activities undertaken for a foreign government related entity where the purpose is to influence government policy such as gas regulation?
If I could take the question on notice—the exemptions are quite technical, so I think I'd have to give consideration to the legislation and set out what the legislation requires.
Okay. That's all from me, Chair.
I think there were some other senators who had some questions, but they aren't in the room, so that means we are in a position to release you from the program today.

text: We'll now resume from our afternoon tea break with officers of the Australian Information Commissioner. Ms Tydd, would you like to make an opening statement?

agency: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
text:
I appreciate the opportunity to provide a brief opening statement to the committee on behalf of my highly valued colleagues the Freedom of Information Commissioner, Alice Linacre, and the Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind. Our engagement with the community has surged in 2025-26. This escalation is underpinned by growing concerns to preserve and assert privacy and information access rights in an increasingly complex and dynamic digital environment. Complaints about social media have more than doubled over the last two years. At this time of immediate and irreversible transformation, our authority is actively and increasingly urgently sought by the community, industry and government. We're called upon to advise and adjudicate novel and complex legal and technical issues that impact privacy and information access rights across all demographic segments and economic sectors. Like other national regulators, we derive practical and profound regulatory insights because of the cohesion we apply to regulating both of these important rights.

Our 2026 to 2029 strategic plan confirms our commitment to our crucial mandate by highlighting the key strategic impacts we strive to achieve through applying a proactive, proportionate, purpose driven and people focused approach. We aim to address power and information asymmetries, promote information integrity and embed fairness, accountability and transparency in new technology. Responsive to the increase in community lodgements, we implemented a targeted program of case management improvements to ensure that we can deliver timely resolutions. Some key highlights for 2025-26 include the following. Privacy complaints increased by 60 per cent to 5,268 that year compared to the same period in 2024-25. Despite this increase, 7 per cent more complaints were finalised than in the previous year. Eighty-three per cent of privacy complaints were closed within 12 months, an increase from 76 per cent in the previous year. The average time to resolve a privacy complaint is now six months, a reduction from 7.6 months in the prior year. Applications for review by the Information Commissioner increased by 42 per cent to 3,025 compared with the previous year. Six per cent fewer IC reviews were finalised than in 2024-25, although we exceeded our KPI and finalised 83 per cent of IC reviews within 12 months. That's an increase on what was 67 per cent in 2024-25. The average time taken to finalise an IC review reduced to seven months—down from 13.5 months in the previous year. The number of FOI complaints received increased by 35 per cent, and our closure rate increased by 19 per cent.

We also engaged our broader regulatory tools to achieve impactful outcomes during the year. For example, our FOI webinars have reached over 1,000 practitioners for each webinar. Our compliance activities were targeted to risk and maximising impact. For example, we delivered a report regarding government agencies' use of automated decision-making and ongoing compliance obligations with the FOI Act. This work complements the forthcoming obligations under the Privacy Act.

We conducted our first privacy compliance sweep across a range of high-risk businesses that collect personal information. Our enforcement actions continued, including our thematic investigation into four agencies' compliance with timeliness requirements under the FOI Act. We secured the first ever civil penalty under the Privacy Act, requiring Australian Clinical Labs to pay $5.8 million in penalties.

We've consulted extensively to ensure the successful operationalisation of the new requirements relevant to the Privacy Act. We proactively engaged with key stakeholders, developing guidance and dedicated resources, including for industry, parents and carers, and for children and young people, to support social media minimum age reforms. We worked closely with industry and stakeholders to provide practical guidance to support new privacy requirements under the anti-money laundering counterterrorism financing reforms that commenced in July 2026 and brought more than 120,000 new entities within the jurisdiction of the Privacy Act.

We consulted extensively with parents, children and industry to support the development of the Children's Online Privacy Code, to be registered on 10 December 2026. Our endeavours are directed to achieving conduct by industry that reflects the best interests of the child and support industry to adopt best practice approach to handling children's personal information. We're striving to ensure that AI is supported by information integrity and trust by developing a statement of rights preservations in government's use of AI for agency heads and also to provide practical guidance to the APS. The OAIC is at the epicentre of digital transformation with our jurisdiction and approach assuring the preservation of rights that are highly valued by the Australian community. The three-commissioner model, and our committed staff, are the lynchpins to achievement of these positive outcomes, notwithstanding the increase in demand and complexity. As an independent commission, it is our honour and privilege to strive to accomplish our mandate. Thank you, Chair.
