agency: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
text: Thank you. I'm looking around for questions. Actually, it doesn't look like any senators have questions for you. Thank you very much for that opening statement. It means that we are now in a position to dismiss you. Thank you so much for hanging around while the committee ran a bit behind today. I really appreciate it.
Mr Reed, would you like to make an opening statement?
No, I would not, but I think the commissioner would.
Yes.

I acknowledge the traditional owners of the lands on which this hearing is being conducted today, and I pay my respects to elders past and present and to any First Nations people here today. As I stated in another Senate inquiry last week, the commission was deeply appalled by the attack on Dr Helen Haines last week. As some of you have already noted this morning, she was instrumental in the establishment of this commission and she's currently the deputy chair of the PJCNACC. The commission continues to keep her and her support network front of mind at this sad time. We trust she will receive all of the care and treatment she needs to make a strong recovery.

Turning now to a brief update on the commission's performance. Our 2025 annual report was tabled on 23 October. The report details the commission's significant effort in 2025-26 to address a backlog of cases from the previous two years and the impact that had on achieving the key performance indicator for referrals. We finalised 2,603 referrals, up almost a third on the 1,994 finalised the year before. For the first time, we closed more referrals than we had received. Of the 715 referrals we carried over into 2025-26, we finalised 618 of those while also closing almost 2,000 of the 2,428 referrals that arrived during 2025-26. Across three years, 7,878 referrals have been received and 93 per cent of those have been dealt with.

Close to 90 per cent of these referrals were finalised at what we call the triage stage. The major reasons for this is that are they are not about Commonwealth public officials or, if they are, the matters being referred are not conduct as defined in the NACC Act. As of last Friday, the commission had 498 referrals awaiting assessment. We acknowledge that, of these, 228 have been with us for over the 90 days we aim for, but are not required to finalise assessments within, and that's mainly because we're receiving or waiting on additional information from referrers and others before we can finalise those assessments.

Our investigators have also been busy. In our first three years of operation, we commenced 56 corruption investigations and 23 of those were finalised by 30 June 2026. Of these, three established serious or systemic corrupt conduct and investigation reports were published. The other 20 were discontinued at a point when we determined we could not substantiate serious or systemic corrupt conduct. Of the 22 corruption investigations we inherited from the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity, three remain ongoing, one where we're undertaking the final steps in preparing an investigation report ,and two matters are before the courts.

Overall, we've slightly exceeded the KPI for investigations being finalised within two years. We currently have 11 preliminary investigations and 30 corruption investigations underway, and we're overseeing 31 investigations we've referred to other agencies to undertake. In 2025, we significantly exceeded the KPI for our corruption prevention and education function. We delivered 130 corruption prevention sessions to a range of Commonwealth agencies and other stakeholders, as well as publishing a range of corruption prevention guides and resources, all of which are also available on our website.

A significant highlight of our prevention and education activity was planning to host the 10th Australian Public Sector Anti-Corruption Conference that took place in September here in Canberra. This is an event that's been held biannually since 2007. It's hosted by different anticorruption commission each time, and this year it was our turn. ASPSAC 2026 was attended by more than 650 delegates from across Australia and the Pacific, who heard from 65 integrity experts including Dr Helen Haines. I thank the Attorney-General for opening that conference.

Finally, last Monday, the government announced it intends to recommend to the Governor-General the appointments of the Hon. Deputy Chief Justice Robert McLellan AO as the National Anti-Corruption Commissioner and Mr Christopher Savundra as one of the three deputy commissioners. We're very much looking forward to them joining us on 11 January 2027. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Ms Kilgour. Senator Hodgins-May.

Ms Kilgour, you told senators last week that aspects of the Community Development Grants Program piqued your interest. Has the NACC received any referrals about that program, how many are there, and what is their status?

I'm a bit limited in what I can say about receipt of referrals. We have received some referrals. A lot of them are telling us about the Centre for Public Integrity's report. Beyond that, I can't really say much more than we are looking at those and, when we're in a position to decide on those, we will make decisions.

You said you would defer to a possible ANAO investigation. Under what provision of the NACC Act does the commission defer a corruption issue to an auditor that has no power to make corruption findings?

It's not so much that we defer. It's more about—until I get to a point where I can be satisfied that I've got an actual corruption issue that's before the commission, either through a referral or through own motion, we are waiting to see the results of what's coming out of your Senate inquiry process, the referrals that we've received and any other information that comes before us. If the ANAO, for example, make a decision that they're not going to audit this program, and we do get a viable referral about corrupt conduct, it may be that we do get into jurisdiction. But what I was explaining last week was that, at this point in time, we're not in jurisdiction. The ANAO's submission was saying that they were considering undertaking an audit, and I was waiting to hear whether they've made a decision one way or the other about that. So it's not so much a deferral; we're not there yet.
I know that I was also on that committee last week—
Yes.

but officials confirmed that Labor headquarters guided a $560 million grant scheme. If party headquarters directing public money to electorates isn't within the NACC's jurisdiction, I suppose I'm trying to unpack further what is.

That's new information to me that was reported in the media. That information—I hadn't heard that until the media reports came out with, I think, Minister King giving some clarifying comments about how the process ran. So that's new information that I received through media reporting. Sorry, what was the second part of your question?
If that doesn't fall within the NACC's jurisdiction, what does, or do you think it does? It could still fall within the NACC's jurisdiction.
I'd have to have a further look at the details about what exactly that information is that has come forward.
Yes, and you're also examining the potential unconstitutionality ahead of the adjustment.

I think that was the other thing I mentioned, which was that that was new information to us as well. There seems to be this version of the guidelines that came out that didn't use section 96 of the Constitution, and then a further version came out. Again, that was new information that came out last week. But the thing I've been conscious of is you are conducting a Senate inquiry, and I don't want to run roughshod over your process.
So what will be the next steps that you'll take with the information that you've received?

We listened to all the evidence, and, for the bits where I wasn't in the room, I've now caught up on all of that evidence. We've read all the submissions. I think you indicated that you are going to bring the ANAO in, and there was an indication that there might be some further hearings on 12 November. So I'd be waiting to hear those, and then I'd be starting to think about what is the appropriate action for the commission to be taking in this matter. But I'd probably want to be engaging with your inquiry a bit further as well because you might have other information that you haven't been talking about in your hearings that you might also want to refer to us.

And perhaps the minister will take us up on our invitation. We'll see. The NACC has previously declined to investigate the Morrison-era grant rorts. Has the commission ever opened a corruption investigation into a grants program?
I can't talk about ongoing investigations.
Sorry. Historically, has the NACC ever opened an investigation into a grants program?

If you're talking about that particular referral that was declined, no, we didn't start an investigation into that particular referral for the reasons that the former commissioner gave to that referral, which I understand there's been some media reporting about. It is difficult for me to comment about whether or not we have ever opened an investigation into the Commonwealth grants program, without talking about ongoing investigations.
There are potentially open investigations, but there's not been a finding handed down in relation—
But I'm not in a position to talk publicly about them.
You said the NACC isn't in jurisdiction yet. Does jurisdiction, under the NACC Act, turn on whether there's a corruption issue and doesn't have anything to do with whether the ANAO decides to audit?
No, I've said that. It's not that.
Why wouldn't an ANAO decision change whether you have jurisdiction? Is that what you're suggesting?

You're doing your Senate inquiry, so I've been pausing to let that process take place. If the ANAO then says it's going to do an audit, usually what would happen is that the NACC would consider whether it's appropriate for us to start an investigation as well. Because we've got a very complex ecosystem in the integrity space, we need to also be mindful about our obligations under the PGPA Act about efficient, effective use of Commonwealth public resources. If you've got another integrity agency conducting a process, it's not necessarily appropriate for us to come in. Does that make sense?
But you can start an investigation on your own initiative.

We could, if we got information that gets us to that threshold. It might be that we'd be having a conversation with the ANAO to say we need to investigate. It might be a very specific issue, for example, as opposed to the entire program. I think one of the other things I said to the committee last week was that our jurisdiction is investigating individuals not the entire program, if that makes sense—although it may be that every single thing in that program is a problem. But, at the minute, what I've been hearing is it's more about that there's a regulatory framework that allows for election commitments to be made and for them to be managed in accordance with particular procedures under the Commonwealth grant rules.
For this particular case that we're discussing, you don't need an ANAO decision; you can start an investigation of your own volition—
If I get to the requisite standard.
if you get to the requisite standard. Okay. And we don't really have much more prescriptive guidance on what that standard might—

It would need to raise a corruption issue, as defined under section 8 of the NACC Act. That would be that there's evidence that suggests—again, when we start corruption investigations, it's always an open question about whether or not something has happened; whether or not there's been an adverse impact on a public official's performance of their duties, functions or powers; whether there's been a breach of public trust; whether there's been an abuse of office; or whether there's been a misuse of official information. That's corrupt conduct. Then we also have to be satisfied it's serious or systemic for our investigative powers to be able to be used.
That could happen without the Senate inquiry finishing, theoretically. It doesn't depend on the Senate inquiry playing out.

Possibly. No, it doesn't depend on that. But I have been mindful. For example, if I started a corruption investigation, I would usually go to another agency and say, 'I need you to stop what you're doing, right now.' The decision that I've taken at the moment is to let the Senate inquiry do its work, listen to that carefully—
I suppose I'm just thinking about the situation. We almost didn't get that Senate inquiry up. What would have happened if that Senate inquiry didn't get up? Could we have had confidence that—

Then the information may have come to us through a different mechanism, and we might be doing it through an assessment of a referral that had been received by us and making a decision based on that referral.
Are you able to share with me how many referrals you've received about the community—
Can I take that on notice because I haven't got that number in front of me?

Yes—and when the first one you received was supplied. If the ANAO does decide to audit, will the NACC stand back entirely until that audit's done, which could take a year or more? Could you intervene, or will you intervene, sooner?

I'd need to have a conversation with the ANAO about how they would go about doing what they're going to do and whether there's particular information that we already think might be serious or systemic corrupt conduct that the NACC might say that we need to take that part. For example, ANAO sometimes will do a sample of 50 out of all the grants made, and that might be the focus of their ANAO audit. There might be a particular case that comes to us, through various mechanisms, where it might be that that's the serious or systemic corrupt conduct corruption investigation angle, so then maybe we'd be taking that particular issue.
Thank you.
Senator Shoebridge.

Thank you all for being here. There was correspondence that I understand the NACC sent to the Attorney-General, saying that there were no findings made or proposed in the draft report from the NACC inspector. Are you aware of that correspondence?
I am aware of that correspondence, but I'm going to turn to the CEO to answer it because it was his correspondence.
That's right, and, as you'll be aware, Senator Shoebridge, that was released under FOI recently.
Yes. Sorry, I think I might have misspoken. I said 'no findings'; I think your correspondence said 'no recommendations'. Is that right?
That's right.
What has been provided is a highly redacted copy of the draft report, through the FOI. Were there any findings made? Were there any findings proposed?
I'd have to take that question on notice.

Well, with all due respect, Mr Reed, this would be an incredibly important matter in your work with the NACC. It's a matter of incredible importance in relation to the former commissioner. If there were proposed findings included in that, I would imagine that they would stick in your mind. So I'm going to ask you, again, the question: were there any proposed findings in the draft report?

As you're aware, the inspector put out a statement on 8 July as to why she had discontinued the investigations. As a result of that, the reports have never been finalised, and therefore, as a result of that, I'm not in a position to discuss what was in that letter, which related to the draft report, without further consideration about the matter. In the first instance, that would need to be in a discussion with, or seeking consultation with, the Attorney-General as the minister responsible for consideration of whether it would actually be in the public interest to disclose this correspondence, beyond what's already been made public.
Did you have that discussion before you wrote that there were no recommendations made?
No, I was advising—
Did you go through that process?

As you'd be aware, there's a requirement for me, as the accountable authority under the PGPA Act, to identify and alert—those aren't quite the words—the minister, which, in this case, is the Attorney-General, to any significant issues that are occurring within the agency. As a result of that, on a needs basis, I write letters to the Attorney about significant issues. This happened to be a significant issue at the time because I had received, or the commission had received, a draft report, and, as a result of that, having already advised the Attorney about the existence of the investigation, I then felt that it was important that I advise the Attorney about the receipt of the draft report, which is what I did.
I note that you said there were no proposed recommendations—
Yes.
but it was an important matter, wasn't it?

Well, any investigation, as you're aware, having previously gone through the process of an investigation by the inspector into the decision of the commission not to investigate the robodebt referrals—the outcome of that was a report, and you're fully aware of that. It was publicly released on 30 October 2024. That led to significant issues for the commission, including having to change the way that conflicts of interest were managed and how the NACC Senior Assessment Panel operated. So, of course, anything of substance coming from the inspector is going to be a significant issue that warrants me alerting the Attorney-General to, but that doesn't mean that at this point in time I'm going to do anything but take this question on notice—the release of the unredacted letter.

Yes, by all means, consider me asking you to provide to this committee the unredacted letter. Consider me also asking you to provide to this committee the unredacted draft report as two separate requests. I assume you're taking both of those on notice, Mr Reed.
Yes.
But I was asking you a far simpler question. You've released—
The two things are interwoven.

Perhaps if you'd just let me finish. You released details that said there were no proposed recommendations in the draft report. I've asked you whether there were any proposed findings, and that is the question I'm asking you to address, not the one that you have reframed it as. I ask you to address that.

The redactions in the redacted letter were made under sections 47E(d) and 47F(1), which relate to operations of the agency and personal privacy. That was the basis of the redactions, and at this point I'm not going to talk about those redactions, but I'll take that on notice to consider.
I want to be clear that at this stage I'm not asking you to detail the findings. I'm asking whether or not there were proposed findings.
I think that's the same thing, and at this point I'm not—

But you've been able to tell the public there were no proposed recommendations. If there were no proposed findings, tell us that. If there were proposed findings, tell us that. I'm not asking for details.
I think I've answered the question. I'm taking it on notice.

On 8 July, Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare's conflict declaration covered some health department matters. It is my understanding that two days later Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare was recused from all such matters involving the health department. Can we get some clarity about what led to this? Were there any matters before the acting deputy commissioner? Take us through what happened.

Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare is here. They weren't matters where she was the decision-maker on. When both the acting deputy commissioners were appointed, on the first day that they were with me, we went through all of the ongoing investigations that were underway, and we conflicted out both Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare and Deputy Commissioner Lowe on matters where it was obvious they had a perceived or real conflict of interest.

I think the particular media reporting that you're referring to was about material that we released under FOI, where it was an assessment panel decision-making process. I was the decision-maker at that. Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare was not the decision-maker, but, because it's a deliberative process where a group of us meet and assess or talk about assessments, in that particular moment, that particular declaration that she made was that she knew of somebody but never had worked closely with them. The ruling in that particular moment was that I didn't consider there was a perceived or actual conflict of interest because it wasn't a close working relationship. Subsequently, I think Deputy Commissioner Lowe, Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare and Deputy Commissioner Gauntlett had a conversation about how it might just be better, out of an abundance of caution, whether or not individuals have real or perceived conflicts of interest—a bit like what we'd done with the commissioner's recusals around all defence matters—that Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare wouldn't be involved in any decision-making on any matters involving that department because of her current role as a deputy secretary.

Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare, thank you for your attendance today. I don't mean to address criticism in relation to you. You take advice from the organisation you're in, and you declared the potential conflict of interest in the course of that. Is that right?
Could you please repeat the question?

You, as I understand it, in the course of that assessment panel meeting, declared the nature of your interests and did what was right in identifying the connection and the previous connection in the course of that meeting. Is that what you did?
Yes.
Then, did it happen with Ms Kilgour, who was, I assume, chairing the meeting?
Yes.
Did she make a determination on the conflict of interest?
That's correct.
And did you continue to participate in the process?
I remained at the meeting. At other items, I left the meeting. As Ms Kilgour said, I was not a decision-maker.
Was a decision made in that meeting, Ms Kilgour?

I would have to go back to the records and check. I haven't got that referral in front of me. Can I take that on notice? We don't always make decisions right in that moment. Sometimes, we'll send things back for further information or defer decisions to get additional material.
Mr Reed, were you present in that meeting? Are you normally present in those meetings?
It was on 8 July.
Yes, I would have been present at the time.
Did you provide any advice about how to address a conflict-of-interest matter when it arose in the circumstances we've just heard, given the history of conflicts of interest in the NACC?

You'll be aware of the protocol that I put in place—which has also been released publicly—on 18 June, which commenced on 7 July about declarations of interest by all the statutory office holders. We had that process already underway, and that ultimately led to each of the statutory office holders writing to the Attorney-General about their declarations of interest. But, of course, we were already operating under the terms of reference of the NSAP, which had been changed after the inspector's report of 30 October 2024. They were changed in November. It made it quite clear how conflicts of interest or potential conflicts of interest should be handled. That is still in place, and that is exactly how things operated on that day.

You see, Mr Reed, this is the difficulty, isn't it? You had, just the previous day, on 7 July, the new process come into effect for declarations and the like. It had come into effect just the previous day, and, then, the next day, you're sitting in a meeting chaired by the acting commissioners, and one of your acting deputy commissioners raises a valid point in relation to prior knowledge of a matter of a person who—and I don't need to know the full detail—was in some way involved in a referral that had happened to you. As the acting commissioner then made a ruling that the acting deputy commissioner could continue notwithstanding, did you say anything? Did you say: 'Well, hang on a sec. We've had this experience with former commissioner Brereton; conflicts of interest have caused this organisation so many problems.' Did you say anything at all?

I've already explained that the National Anti-Corruption Commission's Senior Assessment Panel terms of reference, which everybody in that meeting was aware of and which changed in November 2024 and which had been released publicly on multiple occasions, are in place, and we are operating under those terms of reference. There is no issue. There's no difference here between the document that commenced on 7 July, which happened to be the day after—
The day before.

No, it was the day after the commencement of the acting commissioner arrangement, the day after the commencement of the two acting deputy commissioners. They had had discussions with a number of people, including the acting commissioner, about how we managed conflicts in the context of the NSAP, and nobody has challenged that since it was put in place, in terms of the fact that we are following a process which is different to what was in place prior to that date, prior to November 2024, and which has in my mind largely overcome the problems that were identified leading into that initial investigation by the inspector of robodebt.

My question was very simple. When Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare made her declaration and prior to Acting Commissioner Kilgour making the ruling that, notwithstanding the declaration, she could remain in the assessment panel, did you say anything? Did you say, for example, 'Hang on; these new rules have come into place yesterday' or, 'Hang on; we've got into trouble in situations like this with Commissioner Brereton before' or 'Hang on; I think the appropriate thing in this situation is for Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare to step outside.' Did you do any of that?

It wasn't my place to do that. I was not chairing the meeting. Acting Commissioner Kilgour was chairing the meeting. We were following the terms of reference of the meeting. The appropriate action was taken in the meeting and what I was referring to here in the instruction that I issued is in terms of declarations of interest under rule 16 of the PGPA Act, which is where previously there has been criticism of the commission in terms of what's been declared to the Attorney and what process we went through in relation to that. The two things there have an interrelationship, but they're not contingent on each other, if that makes sense.

Your CEO, Mr Reed, said the appropriate action was taken in the course of that meeting, Acting Commissioner Kilgour, and yet, as I understood the evidence earlier, following discussions amongst deputy commissioners that followed that decision, a different decision was then made two days later. Can you talk me through what happened?

There's a distinguishment between that particular case and the decision that we made at NSAP, and then a subsequent conversation about, rather than me every single time Penny says, 'I know this person because I worked with them in the department,' I was going to make a ruling on each individual case because the facts do matter about whether a conflict of interest arises or not. A proposal was put to me that, for all Department of Health matters, Penny would just not participate in those matters. Dr Gauntlett has a similar arrangement because he's a participant in the NDIS, so he doesn't have anything to do with NDIS matters. There are some arrangements around Deputy Commissioner Lowe as well because of agencies that she's worked in before. We've just had an abundance of caution. Whether or not a conflict in a particular matter arises, they're not being involved in those matters.
Did the decision you made two days later change the position you had adopted in relation to the decision you made on 8 July regarding that referral?
I can't recall in this moment what the decision was that I made on the sixth on 8 July, so I'd need to go back and check, but my memory is no.

Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare, my understanding of your evidence earlier was that on 8 July you declared your conflict or your potential conflict or your perceived conflict—however you want to describe it. You did that, correct?
What would you like me to explain what happened from my perspective?
That would be terrific.

We were at the point of the meeting where people were asked to declare any potential conflicts relating to the subject matter of the meeting. I did that for this particular matter. The declaration was considered against the arrangements for managing conflicts of interest for that particular meeting, and the decision was that in this matter the prior association with one of the people involved was not sufficient to raise an actual or perceived conflict of interest.
And this was in relation to a Department of Health matter, was it?
It was in relation to a matter that involved the Health portfolio.
And then there were discussions with other deputy commissioners that followed that. Can you take me through that?

Yes. There are quite a lot of people that work in the Health portfolio, many of whom I do not know. But we decided that, in the dividing up of cases that would be considered by different deputy commissioners, health matters, aged-care matters and other things in that portfolio would go to other deputies to avoid any issues with conflict of interest and, as Ms Kilgour has explained, to make sure that we weren't having to make constant decisions and having a lot of process around individual matters.
And was any of that discussion in light of what had happened on 8 July?
No, it was a subsequent discussion between deputy commissioners, and we also discussed with the acting commissioner how we would be dividing up work.

Given what happened with Commissioner Brereton and how it took such a long time for the NACC to say, 'Well, if one of our commissioners has had significant involvement in a department'—in that case, the Department of Defence—'when the matter involving the department comes before them, they have no part to play in it.' It took months and months and months to get there with Commissioner Brereton. Do you remember that?
Yes.

How did you not apply that learning straight off with Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare, who had—and it's no criticism of Acting Deputy Commissioner Shakespeare—made the declaration and set out the history? Why didn't you apply that straight off the bat?

It is because I was applying the process under our NSAP terms of reference, which are that I'm meant to look at each case on a case-by-case basis. We then had further conversations about how best to manage the all of our conflicts and potential conflicts and the work between us all, and we agreed that a better process, rather than always doing it on a case-by-case basis, was we would just say that, for certain portfolios or agencies, particular deputy commissioners would not be involved in those matters if they'd had long working relationships in them and/or they'd received services from those agencies.

My final questions are about the question of public hearings. The parliamentary joint committee recommended in May that the commission publish guidance on what counts as 'exceptional circumstances' for a public hearing. Has that been brought to your attention?

I don't recall that as a recommendation, but, if it is, I'll go back and find out why we haven't done it, because I don't have a problem with publishing such guidance. It would outline what the case law says, similar to what I said at the PJCNACC hearing on 18 September when Dr Haines asked me a question about public hearings, exceptional circumstances and the public interest test.
Alright.
I'm sorry if we've missed implementing that.

Parliamentary recommendations are responded to by ministers and departments normally, so normally you would be engaged in that and have a process to be engaged in that and you wouldn't be off your own bat responding. My understanding is that it would normally happen through the Attorney-General's Department, so I don't want to put any misinterpretation about what your role is here. You'd normally feed into a process. The question of public hearings is a matter of continuing public concern. When will the new commissioner start?
He starts on 11 January 2027.

I can understand the difficulties you may find yourself in between now and January, when a new commissioner starts, to be making determinations on a matter which may be so important to the role of the new commissioner. Are you having any communications with the new commissioner?

I called him on the day of his appointment to congratulate him on his appointment. He is making arrangements to come and meet with some of the staff in November and to start some conversations about what he's thinking about the role and for me to provide him with any information he needs before he starts. But obviously he can't make decisions until he's in the post.
That goes without saying. Have you done the same in relation to the incoming deputy commissioner?
I've had conversations with Mr Savundra, yes.
And is there a process where he can come and you can start doing some of that familiarity with Mr Savundra as well, as the proposed new deputy commissioner?

Yes. We haven't put anything in place yet, because obviously the commissioner is probably the first off the rank in terms of meeting with him, but the offer's there to Mr Savundra. If there are issues that come up between now and January that I think he needs to be involved in, we'll talk to him.
Acting Commissioner Kilgour, in no way let this be a restraint on you in having a public hearing between now and January. I wish you all strength to hold the public hearing between now and January.
Thank you. I would love to do one.
I'd urge you to do that for the benefit of the—
If I get the right matter, I will do one.
Thank you.

Thank you for bearing with us as we're running a little bit behind on time. That concludes the questions that we have for you this afternoon, so thank you very much thank you for appearing before the committee.

text: Please proceed.

I would like to provide the committee with a brief update on matters relating to the provision of transcript and recording services that support the Federal Court of Australia and the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia. These matters have previously been raised before this committee, and there have been a number of developments since the last hearing. The entity determined not to exercise its two-year option to extend its contract with VIQ and has now formally terminated the contract once the transition-out arrangements under the contract were completed. Following the decision not to extend the VIQ contract, the entity successfully transitioned to an in-house controlled and administered operating model, which has been operational from 1 July 2026.

This was a significant operational transition, both for the entity and the courts. Entity controlled and owned recording equipment has been installed in more than 190 courtrooms across Australia, and the entity has control and oversight over all of the court's data, including all historical data. The entity has contracted with a panel of five transcription providers to deliver formal transcription services, materially reducing reliance on a single external provider. The contracts with these providers expressly prohibit offshore processing and set requirements for data sovereignty and security. The providers are meeting workload demands for the courts in a timely manner. An in-house recording and transcription team has also been established to triage and allocate all transcript orders and to closely monitor the operation of these panel providers to ensure compliance with the requirements under their respective contracts. Critically, this transition has been achieved without disruption to court operations or to the courts' users.

At the previous hearing, I advised that the entity had engaged CyberCX, as independent cybersecurity experts, to undertake an independent assurance assessment of the unauthorised access incident involving VIQ, identifying control gaps and making any recommendations to reduce any security risks going forward. That assessment has now been completed. CyberCX determined that the incident arose from a limited and specific access control process failure that resulted in the assignment of court recordings to unauthorised VIQ resources. CyberCX concluded further that the incident resulted from a highly specific, internal VIQ process failure and would have been difficult for the entity to detect beforehand.

CyberCX was also engaged to perform a data exposure assessment, and, as part of that assessment, CyberCX undertook a very detailed search for VIQ-sourced court data, which involved gathering information from the surface, deep and dark web, third-party global intelligence providers, close sources and internally generated data. That assessment did not locate any information consistent with exposure of data related to VIQ's transcription services.

CyberCX found that the contractual, privacy and security requirements applying to VIQ were appropriate, while also identifying areas in which the entity's third-party security assurance arrangements could be strengthened. The entity has accepted those findings and is strengthening its approach to third-party risk and supplier assurance. These measures include greater controls over supplier data handling practices, strengthening audit rights and explicit data sovereignty and residency requirements.

Although the entity was not required to notify the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner under the Notifiable Data Breaches Scheme, as the circumstances fall within an exception under the Privacy Act, the entity has assisted the commissioner in its consideration of the matter and has provided information to the commissioner in relation to their preliminary inquiries into VIQ. The entity, on behalf of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, also notified the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, who subsequently advised that the matter was more appropriately to be dealt with by the Australian regulator.

The focus now is shifting from stabilisation and continuity of these services to the implementation of a sustainable future in-house recording and transcription operating model that enhances resilience, control, security, affordability and access to justice while positioning each of the courts to take advantage of emerging technologies and evolving user needs. The entity, on behalf of the court, is progressing planning and consultation on this future operating model, supported by the design review work undertaken by Nous. Data security and confidentiality remain core principles underpinning the design of the future model, as is a system that makes transcription services more accessible and affordable to the court's users. Thank you, Chair. I would be happy to assist the committee with any questions.

agency: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
text:
Yes, that would be helpful. Thank you. Today I wish to address you about the topic of family and sexual violence and the courts, on behalf of the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 1) and the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2). Before I do begin, however, I would like to acknowledge the Independent member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines MP, who was very seriously injured outside her electorate office on 19 October. On behalf of the Chief Justice, the judges of the courts and all our staff, I extend our deepest sympathies to Dr Haines, her family, her staff and her community, and we wish her a speedy recovery. This shocking attack, which has no doubt been deeply felt by everyone in this House, is a confronting reminder of the risks faced by those who serve the public. The courts are deeply concerned by aggression and violence towards all public officials, including judges, registrars, court child experts and court staff, who work every day with people who are experiencing some of the most difficult periods in their lives. Last financial year, the courts across our agency experienced 611 reported incidents, 224 of which can be classified as violent or aggressive and hundreds of others as being of a serious nature. As such, we strongly endorse the current increased focus on protecting all public officials.

I now turn to the issue of recent public commentary about the family law courts. The courts take seriously the experiences of families and victim-survivors who rely on the family court system. The Chief Justice has made clear that the courts are always open to feedback and are always keen to improve how they operate. However, some recent commentary has presented an inaccurate and sometimes misleading picture of how the family courts operate today, providing at times incomplete versions of cases and seemingly drawing on criticisms of a bygone system that has since been substantially reformed.

The courts engage openly with the media to support accurate and informed reporting. This includes offering journalists the opportunity to speak with the courts' specialists in family and sexual violence and family law and, where possible, sharing relevant anonymised judgements so that individual cases can be understood in their full context. Despite these offers, some media outlets have declined these opportunities in favour of making broad assertions without all the relevant facts. As such, it is important for the committee and the public that I provide a brief and accurate account of how the courts now identify and respond to risk and how they keep children and at-risk parents at the centre of their decisions. Again, I've tabled the statement, but I think there are a few things I should briefly summarise.

Our courts in family law receive over 100,000 family law applications each year. The notice-of-risk data indicates that 84 per cent of parenting matters involve allegations of family violence, and 70 per cent of matters involve four or more major risk factors, including mental health factors and substance abuse. That's the context. There have been a lot of changes in recent times, and that includes the legal framework. The Family Law Act amendments in recent times have changed the definition of 'family violence' and have ensured that the interests of the child are at the centre of everything the court has to consider. In addition to that, led by the Chief Justice, the courts have in recent years fundamentally changed the way we address risk. Consulting with specialist family and sexual violence legal services, sector stakeholders and others, we have implemented many reforms. That includes the Lighthouse program, the high-risk Evatt List and many other reforms that ensure that we address family violence properly.

More than half of the court's judges are women, and 79 per cent of family law registrars are women. They come from backgrounds of specialty, including legal aid commissions, and have been specialist practitioners, including independent children's lawyers. We also have social scientists, highly qualified social workers and psychologists, who work hard to make sure that the voice of the child is heard in proceedings. Thousands of child impact reports are prepared by them every year which bring the children's experience, views and safety needs before the court in those matters. We've also recently brought on a children's charter and Kids' Corner, which has principles which align with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, ensuring that the safety of the child is at the centre of the court's considerations.

In recent years, we've also had significantly enhanced training, and that includes training about coercive control, the Safe and Together model, First Nations cultural capability training, trauma informed practice training and, recently, a program on sexual violence against adults and children. These changes that we are making extend to practical factors as well, including upgrading safe rooms and court facilities ensuring that escorting arrangements for affected individuals are changed, duress alarms and CCTV footage, and we're piloting privacy screens as well. We've also had recent innovations including a proactive safety-at-court pilot. These are important innovations. By looking at safety flagged matters, we are able to initiate contact with people who may need support. What that has led to is a fourfold increase in safety court plans in that pilot, which ran across Parramatta and Canberra registries, and a ninefold increase in the high-risk Evatt List matters getting safety plans.

The efficiencies that we have undertaken are also very important. The longer the matters are in the court, the higher the risks can get. The backlog has been significantly reduced, as have judicial dockets, and now the median time to a matter finalising is eight months. We have a number of specialist lists, including those for child abuse cases, critical incidents, international cases and various other lists, such as the specialist Indigenous lists. Conscious of time, I won't mention the rest of the reforms. It is important to note that the whole leadership of the court is focused on safety. We have dedicated roles and directorships that are focused on that, including family violence directorships, access equity and inclusion, Indigenous policy operations and support, and cultural language and diversity.

The courts operate now fundamentally differently to the way they did even five years ago. There are also rights of appeal and rights of review and a robust complaints system for people to use if they need to. That doesn't mean that there isn't room for improvement; we're open minded about that. However, commentary about our courts needs to be accurate. And confidence in the family law judicial system is important, as inaccurate or misleading commentary can run the risk that some parents will be dissuaded from bringing their cases to the courts, thereby resulting in at-risk children and parties being left without the protective orders and support referrals that the courts can provide. So all that we ask is that, when the media and other commentators critique the courts—which we welcome—they do so based on evidence and facts and that they avail themselves of the anonymised judgements and information that we offer to them so that their commentary can be fair, informed and accurate.

In terms of improvements, my tabled statement outlines a number of areas that the courts can improve in, including ensuring that lighthouse funding is ongoing and extending it to property cases and regional Australia, growing our Indigenous Family Liaison Officer team and a number of other important reforms, including our education and training. I welcome any further questions from the committee, but I thought those were important things to list first. Thank you.

text: Previously, I asked about situations where one parent might breach a court order by making an excuse for why the other parent can't see a child. agency: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
text: In essence, we call those contravention applications when somebody's saying the other party has failed to comply with a court order. In the past, before the reforms implemented by the Chief Justice in 2021, it used to be about eight to nine months before those matters could be listed, which obviously—you could imagine—made it very difficult for one parent or the other and dissuaded a lot of people from bringing those matters to the court. We now have a system where those matters are listed within a number of weeks, usually around four to six weeks, in front of a registrar and sometimes a senior judicial registrar, and that means the matter can be triaged and quickly assessed by that registrar. Where possible, it's resolved by discussions with the parties there, or it could be referred to a judge, particularly if it's a more serious matter of contravention.

An indicator that the allegations are not far off the mark is, for example, in our Lighthouse Program, when confidential risk screens are undertaken. If a party raises that they have safety issues, there is a triage process through a very highly qualified counsellor who then grades it as high, medium or low risk, and then a highly trained registrar will look at it as well. In Lighthouse Program, no less than about 61 per cent of matters are screening as high risk, so we know that the figure is very, very high. That's after careful analysis by highly qualified people. text: President de Kretser, do you have an opening statement you would like to make?

A very brief one. I acknowledge the Ngunnawal and Ngambri elders and ancestors, their culture and their unbroken connection to the beautiful country we're on.

I want to acknowledge the devastating attack on Dr Helen Haines outside her electorate office in Victoria. Our thoughts are with her and her family. This attack happened against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians. Parliamentarians must be able to carry out their duties safely. We must address intimidation, hatred, threats and violence that undermine our democracy and democratic institutions.

I want to recognise that this is the last estimates appearance of my colleague the Human Rights Commissioner, Lorraine Finlay. Commissioner Finlay's term ends on 21 November this year and, over the course of her term, she has made important contributions on a wide range of human rights issues, including ensuring human rights are considered and protected in responses to emergencies and disasters; implementing Australia's obligations under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture to prevent mistreatment of people in detention; protecting the human rights of people in immigration detention; and addressing antisemitism. I particularly recognise and thank her for her leadership highlighting the impact of new technology on human rights and recommending responses to it. This work has happened at a time of immense technological change. The work of Commissioner Finlay and her team has been cutting edge. It has meant that the commission is seen as one of the leading national human rights institutions in the world on these issues. We wish Commissioner Finlay all the best for her move to Europe with her family and sincerely thank her for her contribution to our work.
Chair, can I just make a few comments from the government before we start—
Absolutely, Minister.

just to concur with the comments from the president. The government also thanks Commissioner Finlay for her contributions across her five-year term. In particular, I want to acknowledge some very important work considering the impact of emerging technologies and artificial intelligence on human rights; the inquiry into human rights impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and advocating for the prioritisation of human rights in future emergencies; and participating in the National Roundtable on Human Trafficking and Slavery. The government wishes Commissioner Finlay well for her next chapter—and no more estimates!
Thank you, Minister. Senator Cash.

Thank you very much. I also acknowledge that this is Commissioner Finlay's last estimates appearance. On behalf of the coalition, I sincerely thank you, Commissioner Finlay, for your service. You've just had an admirable list read out for the Hansard record, but, on behalf of the coalition in particular, we would like to thank you for being a lone voice in the commission in relation to the recognition of the biological rights of women and, in particular, the only commissioner who voted for the exemption to be granted to the Lesbian Action Group. I know that they were very grateful that they had a voice in the commission that was prepared to stand up for their biological rights. So, again, thank you for all you have done. You have championed fundamental freedoms with courage, principle and common sense, especially during times when it was unpopular to do so. On behalf of the coalition, we wish you all the very best in whatever the next role is.

I now turn to questions to the Sex Discrimination Commissioner. Dr Cody, you would be aware that the High Court refused the special leave application in the Giggle v Tickle case on 10 September, with the result that the full court's decision is now final. I was, sadly, unable to get a response from the department this morning on this: in plain English, what does the law now mean for, for example, a women's refuge, a women-only organisation, that wants to exclude a biological male who identifies as a woman if it doesn't apply for an exemption?
Senator, can I clarify that, when you use the phrase 'biological man identifying as a woman', you're referring to a trans woman?
Well, what else would I be referring to? It's a biological man identifying as a woman.
The Sex Discrimination Act includes within women trans women, and it's very important to recognise the dignity of all women in the Sex Discrimination Act.

I'm assuming this is not your personal opinion, but that this is the law we're talking about, because, obviously, you've now got a full Federal Court decision which has determined the law. You are saying that, at law, under the Sex Discrimination Act, 'woman' does not just mean 'biological woman'; it also means a man who identifies as a woman.
I'd refer you to the explainer on our website, which gives clear indication of the meaning that is now understood within Giggle v Tickle.

That's very kind of you to refer me to something, but I would like to have the discussion with you at estimates tonight for the Hansard record. So, again, what does the Sex Discrimination Act, at law, now reflect in relation to the recognition of a woman? Is it merely biological?
I refer you to that explainer and also to my previous answers in Senate estimates.
Your previous answers were that men who identify as women are recognised, at law, as women. Is that correct?
I refer you to my previous answers.
Do you have an issue with answering these questions, Dr Cody?
I've already answered them.

I'm asking you again. It's a separate estimates hearing. The last time we discussed the full Federal Court case I am now discussing, that was then on appeal to the High Court. It is now the stated law in Australia. There's no dispute about that now. I am trying to explore this with you, given the department this morning was unable to provide me with any further clarification on what the law says. Are you able to define, under the Sex Discrimination Act, what 'a woman' actually entails?
As I have said, I have answered that question previously and, because the High Court has refused special leave, that answer from the full Federal Court is the same answer.

That means a man who identifies as a woman is a woman for the purposes of the Sex Discrimination Act. As the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, is the only way that you could therefore recognise biological women as biological women—and give them the ability without an exemption to turn away a biological man who identifies as a woman—would be to change the law?

There are measures within the Sex Discrimination Act. The Sex Discrimination Act protects people from discrimination on the basis of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, breastfeeding, marital status and intersex status. There are special measures within that, which an organisation or a business can take if they are for the purpose of achieving substantive equality, which enable different treatment that is lawful. There are also exemptions within the Sex Discrimination Act which enable different treatment, and there is also a process for seeking temporary exemptions under section 44 of the act.

Is that what the Lesbian Action Group did three years ago when it tried to seek an exemption, which I said Commissioner Finlay was kind enough to vote in favour of? The Lesbian Action Group merely wanted to meet as biological lesbians. They sought an exemption and, three years later, they're still going through the court process. Is that correct?
The matter has been referred to the Administrative Review Tribunal for a decision.
Yes. Can you just remind me, what was the status of the commission in relation to any of those cases? Did you intervene at all?
We were a party at the Federal Court.
Arguing for the exemption for the Lesbian Action Group or against it?
No, the case was around appealing the first decision of the Administrative Review Tribunal, and we were a party to that case.
What were you arguing in that case?
It was around the exemption process.

Yes. Did the commission grant the exemption? Did you, as the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, grant an exemption to the Lesbian Action Group so that they could meet as biological women and exclude biological males?
The exemption decision is a decision of the whole commission.
Yes, but I'm asking you, as the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, what did you vote?
I refer to my previous answer on this.

You voted against it. The only commissioner who voted for the exemption—and I think we must have worked through this at the last estimates—was Commissioner Finlay. In terms of small business post the High Court not accepting the special leave application, there is now a lot of concern amongst small businesses in relation to what the status of the law actually is. And again, sadly, I put these questions to the department this morning, and they were unable to assist these small businesses in any way and in fact advised them that they should get a lawyer, which I was very disappointed with, because they're battling to keep their heads above water, let alone having to go and get a lawyer to answer the questions. One of the questions I've been sent from a small business in Australia. They've advertised a biological women's only event. It's sold out. It's going to be held on 7 November. They have tried to get guidance. They genuinely want to do the right thing here. They have tried to get guidance from lawyers, from the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission commissioners, a human rights lawyer at Monash Centre and several small businesses. All they want to know is this, and I'm hoping that you, the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, who are responsible for this law, are able to tell them. Have they not got an exemption? It is a sold-out event. They will have people on the door. All they want to know is, if a man turns up and says he identifies as a woman, do they have to allow that person in? That's all they want to know.
I cannot give advice or answers to hypothetical scenarios.

That is not a hypothetical. It's a question that I have in front of me from a small business who is literally now at its wits end in trying to get advice as to what is a simple question. Are they entitled to say no at the door to men who identify as women?

I cannot answer that question. Firstly, I don't have all the facts. Secondly, we may receive a complaint about it, and so I cannot prejudge and the commission cannot respond to something about which we may receive a complaint.
Is it set out in your guidance on your website for small businesses?

We have guidance—the exemption guidelines—which provides information to businesses and organisations. I am also aware that, if a business or an organisation rings the commission, generally that person will be spoken to about whether there is a need for an exemption to be sought, and they will be talked through the process for seeking an exemption.

I said to them I'd put these questions to you in the hope that they might be able to get some guidance. So, in good faith, I will put those questions to you. As I said, this is a sold-out women's only event that will be occurring on 7 November; 250 biological women are expected. These are very simple questions. The first one: can our privately operated ticket event legally be women only, without an exemption?
As I've said, I refer to my previous answer. I cannot answer that question.

Okay. For this purpose, how does the law define who is eligible to attend? Surely, as the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, who administers the Sex Discrimination Act, you're able to answer that question.
I'm unable to answer that question.
Okay. If someone identifies as a woman, is that sufficient for admission to this event?
As I've said, in a hypothetical situation, I cannot answer those questions.

It's not a hypothetical situation. Again, it's a real situation that more and more businesses are facing on a daily basis, but the human rights commissioners aren't able to give them guidance. What can their staff legally ask someone if there is uncertainty at law?
I cannot answer that question.
When, if ever, can they legally refuse entry?
I cannot give legal advice to them or to you—
Can you at least outline to them what the law says, or is that also impossible?
and I refer that business to the Giggle and Tickle explainer on our website and also to our exemption guidelines.
When is this small business that's battling to keep its head above water going to go on your website to read a Tickle and Giggle explainer?
I think that's a rhetorical question.

No, it's a genuine question. That's what you've referred them to. You're the Sex Discrimination Commissioner. You administer this act. I'm merely asking you for clarification for this business as to what the law now says, and you have told them that they can go on to your website to look at a Tickle and Giggle explainer. Is that your evidence?
I refer to my previous answer.
Senator Cash, I'm going to need to rotate the call.
That's fine. We'll come back to this.
Senator Faruqi.

Good evening, everyone. Thank you for being here. I have some questions, as well, for the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, Dr Cody, on pregnancy discrimination. In 2017, when I was in the New South Wales parliament, I was quite shocked when a woman called my office and said that she had been legally discriminated against and fired because she hadn't disclosed to the employer at the time of hiring that she was pregnant. Indeed, when we looked at the antidiscrimination laws, there were exemptions where employers could not hire, or fire, people who had not disclosed at the time of hiring that they were pregnant. I did get going to get that law changed, and that was changed. So I really want to thank you from the bottom of my heart for the work that you've done, especially in your latest report on pregnancy discrimination, which was also highlighted recently in the Four Corners episode. The report found that, despite legal protections, pregnancy and caring related discrimination is still really commonplace. What needs to be done to make a cultural shift—that we clearly need—to ensure that pregnancy, breastfeeding and caring responsibility aren't a barrier to workers' rights?

Unfortunately, as you say, pregnancy discrimination, family responsibilities discrimination and breastfeeding discrimination are all still far too common. From the people that we consulted with, we heard that this is commonplace across all industries—in some male dominated industries it's more frequent, more common—and that, despite many changes in our law to enable better paid parental leave, there are still barriers in place for the sharing of care within families. We have 18 recommendations in our report. I'd be very happy to meet with you and brief you on the findings of our project.

Okay. Your report makes clear that this discrimination is compounded for First Nations people, people of colour and temporary visa holders. We know that the intersection of racism and misogyny is something that women of colour often come against in a workplace. How did you see this manifest in your research in particular?

One of the requirements to get unpaid parental leave is 12 months continuous service, and we know that migrant women, First Nations women and women with disabilities are more likely to be in casual or temporary work. Therefore it's harder for them to demonstrate that they have that 12 months continuous service. We also know that many of those women, particularly on visas, don't have that entitlement to any of those benefits either.

The other part of it is definition of 'family'. For First Nations families, many of those families have a more extended and broader understanding of kinship and family, and that's not recognised within the law. Similarly, caring responsibilities in migrant refugee families will often go across different countries, and that's not recognised within the law.
Commissioner, have you briefed any ministers or agencies on the findings of the report?
We have sent the report to, and offered to brief, a range of ministers and members of parliament. We are in the process of arranging some of those meetings.
So you haven't yet heard back from the government on what it intends to do with the findings of your report?
No, we haven't.
Does the existing positive duty on employers create obligations to avoid pregnancy discrimination?

Pregnancy discrimination and discrimination on the basis of breastfeeding would definitely be covered within the positive duty. So, yes, there is a positive responsibility on employers to eliminate, as far as possible, that form of sex discrimination.
But that still hasn't manifested, because we're seeing it happening.
Unfortunately, it is still frequent.
Is more funding needed to support working women's centres to represent women affected by pregnancy discrimination?

There is now a network of working women's centres funded from the government around each state and territory who are being very effective in representing women who are experiencing pregnancy discrimination or other forms of discrimination.
Do you think it's sufficient at the moment, from what your research suggests?
It is, although the concern would be that it would be an ongoing, permanent funding arrangement.
And it isn't at the moment; it's grant based.
My understanding is it's five-year funding.

Yes. It was really devastating to see the women on Four Corners who lost their jobs because of pregnancy discrimination or were forced out or demoted after having kids. I was particularly concerned that one of the women who spoke to the program is employed in the Public Service, because, for me, how can we expect business or private organisations to do better if our own Public Service is failing acceptable standards? What would you like to see change in the APS to address this?

There are a range of recommendations in the report—certainly, a broader understanding of notions of care as well as removing the requirement for 12 months of continuous service, strengthening the access to parental leave and also the right to request flexible working arrangements. One of the recommendations is that, rather than it being a right to request, the onus should be on the employer to demonstrate that it's unreasonable not to have flexible working arrangements. There's also the use of redundancy. We know that that's one of the mechanisms that employers use around pregnancy and around caring responsibilities. Again, the recommendation is to put the onus on the employer to demonstrate that it's a genuine redundancy if that occurs.
Dr Cody, do you intend on having a meeting with the APS commissioner as well to talk through the report and its recommendations?
We are intending that.

Going through the report really made me reflect on where we're at right now. It certainly feels like women are copping it from all sides at the moment. Recently, the University of Melbourne released what I think is pretty scary research about young people's attitudes towards women. One of the most horrifying statistics for me was that almost a quarter of boys aged 13 to 17 believe feminism is damaging to our society and should be resisted with violence if necessary. At the same time, we've seen 60 women killed by violence this year. Given you do so much work in sex discrimination, do you have a sense that things have shifted, in particular with the rise of the manosphere and its extremely misogynistic content, which is so readily available online these days?

I think we're seeing a relationship between an online and social media environment and then violence in reality and that that certainly is a part of young men's experience. We know that those concerning attitudes that you detailed of 14- to 17-year-olds—that research is very strong and powerful. We have a lot of work to do, and, certainly, the second action plan on violence will be a very important plan to focus on those younger men and younger communities and ensure that respectful relationships are embedded within our community.

Commissioner, obviously, the intersection of violence, of hate, of racism, of discrimination and of misogyny is very overwhelming. How do you view these intersecting discriminations, and what role do you feel they play in policymaking?

It's vital in my area, sex discrimination and LGBTQI+ discrimination, to recognise that there is that diversity within the group of women—'women' includes First Nations women, women's experience, women with disability, migrant and refugee women—and make sure that policy is shaped by the communities that it is attempting to assist or to influence. It is very important. Some of the recommendations out of the reports that I have done are to ensure that there is input from those communities in the shaping of policy.

Minister, I have a couple of questions for you. You've heard the commissioner talk a few times about removing the requirement that an employee work in a role for 12 months before they're eligible for paid parental leave. This came up quite a few times. It is one of the problems where pregnant people are discriminated against as well. It is very clear that it is necessary to make this change. Is closing this loophole something your government will commit to changing?

Thank you for the question. I do want to acknowledge those reports on Four Corners and the experience of those women. Of course, as you know, our laws prohibit discrimination of that kind. What they highlight and what the report from the commission highlights is the discrimination occurring despite the laws that we have. We are considering the report now. So I don't have any further information for you this evening. But we will go through those findings and have more to say if there's a response from government.
And nothing about the specific removal of the 12 months—
Not tonight. We've just received the report, as I understand. So we will do what we should and consider it in the full context of those findings.
And, Commissioner, I really want to thank you for the excellent work that you and your team do. Thanks, Chair.
Senator Blyth.

I might stay on that report if I may. Dr Cody, at the last estimates hearing, you argued that a biological male who identifies as a woman could potentially experience discrimination on the grounds of pregnancy or potential pregnancy. Do you still stand by that position?
I refer to my previous answer.

I'll take that as a yes. You can answer the questions that we ask. You are required to answer questions if you have that information available to you. That was a different question to last time. I'm just asking if you stand by that position. It's a yes or no.
From my hearing of that question, it was the same question that I had already been asked at the last Senate estimates hearing.
It is, and I'm asking if you still stand by that. So, yes—
I refer to my previous answer—correct.

Your previous answer—it's easier if you say yes or no. Do you believe that protections specifically intended for pregnancy and breastfeeding should apply to biological males who have never been pregnant and cannot become pregnant?
Can you clarify who you're referring to when you're referring to 'biological males'?
I'm referring to biological males.
Men cannot be subject to or cannot be protected by the pregnancy discrimination provisions.
What about men who identify as women? They're still biologically men.
So can I clarify that you're referring to trans women in that situation?
If that's the terminology you use.
I would refer to my previous answer.
What was the previous answer?
So do you believe that the protections specifically intended for pregnancy and breastfeeding should apply to biological males? That's the question. I don't believe you've been asked that before.
It's a matter of opinion—
It's not a matter of opinion.
My role is not to provide a matter of opinion; my role is to give you an answer in relation to what the law says under the Sex Discrimination Act.
No, it's not. You've refused to answer any of my questions, with all due respect, Commissioner.

Senator Cash, Senator Blyth has the call. We've been pretty good all day at not interjecting over the top of one another. We have a short amount of time with each other left, and I would ask that we proceed in the same way we have for most of the day. I might even invite a small intake of breath before we respond and ask questions.
I'm just going to reclarify this, because it's not asking for opinion, and that might be a really easy way for you to try and dodge questions.
That's not fair to say.

This is asking for the application of the Sex Discrimination Act, of which you are in charge. Do you as commissioner believe that the protections specifically intended for pregnancy and breastfeeding should apply to biological males? Is that how the act works?
The act refers to pregnancy and potential pregnancy.
Okay—'and potential pregnancy'.
Because men can potentially get pregnant!

If we go to page 21 of your new Balancing act report, you include evidence about people inducing lactation and specifically refer to men who identify as women. Can I ask why the commission included the experiences of biological males inducing lactation in a report examining pregnancy and breastfeeding discrimination?

The report covers the experience of pregnancy discrimination, breastfeeding discrimination and discrimination on the basis of family responsibilities. The process for developing that report was hearing from a range of stakeholders, including migrant women, First Nations women and LGBQTI+ communities, so it includes the experiences of those communities in relation to those three issues.
Are you suggesting that induced lactation in a biological male should be treated in the same way as breastfeeding following pregnancy and childbirth?
It would depend on the circumstances.
In what circumstances would you say yes or no?
Sorry; I'm not going to speculate on a hypothetical.

It's not a hypothetical. I'll ask you the question again. By including this in your report, are you suggesting that induced lactation in a biological male should be treated in the same way as breastfeeding following pregnancy and childbirth?
Breastfeeding is widely defined within the Sex Discrimination Act, and it includes expressing milk as well as breastfeeding as well as induced lactation.

Inducing lactation in a biological male can involve hormone treatments and medications that stimulate milk production. Published studies involving men who identify as women who do this remain limited and largely consist of individual case reports. Before including this evidence in your report, did you, as commissioner, obtain independent medical advice about the safety and effectiveness of induced lactation in biological males?
I refer you to the report. It does not refer to biological men, as you term them, who have induced lactation. The case study is about a woman who induced lactation.

A biological man—that woman you're describing is a biological man who induced lactation. You might want to try to be cute with words, but I will say—and the question in this is—did you obtain any independent medical advice before including that in your report?
And I would refer you to those pages 20 to 22 in which one of the case studies is about a woman—

Did you obtain independent medical advice? You're trying to answer things that I'm not asking you. I'm asking you if, before including this in your report, you obtained independent medical advice? It's a yes or no question.
Except that I don't accept the characterisation in what you're saying the report includes, so that's why I'm referring to the report.
Did you get independent medical advice about the safety and effectiveness of induced lactation? Yes or no?
It's not included in the report.

No; I'm asking you if you got independent medical advice. You've included induced lactation in your report. You say that it's part of the Sex Discrimination Act. I'm asking you if you got independent medical advice.
Our process—
I will say that you cannot mislead the Senate. This is a yes or no.

Thank you, Senator. The process that I outlined is that we went through a review of research, both domestic and international, around the experience of those three forms of discrimination, as well as having five stakeholder consultations. We did not seek medical advice.
Thank you. That's all I was asking. The research that you've spoken about and that you've relied on in your report: is that easily available, or is that something you are able to table?
There is a bibliography at the back of the report, and I'm very happy to provide you with both a copy of the report as well as a briefing on the recommendations, as I offered to Senator Faruqi—

I don't need a briefing. I'm just asking. You've just mentioned, in the evidence you've just given, that you relied on different case studies. Are they readily available or is that something that you can table?
The case studies on which we relied are in the report.
And the other research that you said you've looked at?
Academic research.

If you could table that which you've relied on for that induced lactation, that would be very helpful. Section 7A(a) of the Sex Discrimination Act specifically refers to discrimination against a woman on the grounds of breastfeeding. The explanatory memorandum introducing those protections stated they were intended to apply to women who breastfeed. Does the commission interpret section 7A(a) as providing breastfeeding discrimination protections to a biological male who identifies as a woman and induces lactation?
Yes.

Your report also includes a stakeholder's concern that workplaces do not adequately understand or accommodate induced lactation. Does the commission believe an employer should be legally required, or are they legally required, to provide lactation breaks and breastfeeding facilities to a biological male who has medically induced lactation?
They are subject to the same protections as anyone who is breastfeeding.

Last week, the New South Wales parliament reversed changes to an internal breastfeeding policy. The policy sought to include gender neutral language. The decision was reversed and now makes it clear that only women breastfeed babies. Does this policy noting women breastfeed babies comply with all of your guidelines, recommendations and practices?
I would have to take that on notice.
I might go back to the Tickle v Giggle, unless you are—
I was just going to indicate that you're at your first 10-minute block.
No problem. We can share the call.
Chair, I have questions for the Race Discrimination Commissioner.
We will share the call. We will no doubt resume. I'll go to Senator Faruqi.

Good evening, Commissioner. As you know, at every estimates since the National Anti-Racism Framework was completed and delivered to the government, I've asked you what the government has actually done with it.
