Almost two years on I will repeat some of those questions, so please excuse me. Has the government now, after two years, formally responded to the National Anti-Racism Framework and its 63 recommendations, or is it still sitting in some government shelf gathering dust?

The government itself hasn't yet responded. There have been responses from government departments. So, when you say government, if it's government departments, I can tell you about some of those responses.
Please go ahead.

In the interest of progressing the really important work under the National Anti-Racism Framework and having not had a response from government, we are going to convene a national antiracism taskforce ourselves and we've written to key stakeholders who would form part of that taskforce. Amongst those, we wrote to the Attorney-General's Department, and we did receive a response from the Attorney-General's Department supporting the formation of the taskforce and providing some feedback on the terms of reference and the parameters of the taskforce. So, in that sense, that's supportive. We've written to some other government departments and gotten positive feedback as well—the department of infrastructure, in particular. So I would say in that sense there is some response within departments but certainly not from the minister or the three ministers, really, that are involved with the work as of yet.

So that is one of the recommendations out of the 63 recommendations that you have decided to go ahead with yourself. Is that being funded by government? Do you have the funds for that? Will you use current funding or just nothing?

No, we're redirecting our own funds that—well, it is government funded in the sense that all of the money comes from the government, but it's not a specific allocation. We're redirecting money that we've already been given. I should just make clear, you're right that it is only one recommendation, but it was always the critical one because we knew that the framework was broad in its scope and bold in its ambition, and the purpose of the taskforce was to identify which recommendations to move with as a matter of priority; for example, ones that align with the two envoys against antisemitism and Islamophobia, ones that may align with findings that will come out of the parliamentary inquiry into racism towards First Peoples or the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. So in that sense, it's one but it's a critical one and that's why we're moving on it.
Yes. But despite all of those things that have happened in the last two years, the 63 recommendations still stand as recommendations that are needed to tackle systemic racism in this country, right?
Yes, absolutely.
None of them at the moment have received a response from the government?
No.
Since last estimates hearing in May, have you met with the Prime Minister, the Attorney-General or any other minister specifically on implementing the National Anti-Racism Framework?
I've never met with the Prime Minister, but I have met with ministers Rowland, McCarthy and Aly about progressing the National Anti-Racism Framework.
Do you know why it's not being progressed?
What I've been told is that it's still under consideration.
Have you received any indication about when there will be a response?
Not a clear indication in terms of timing.

Commissioner, what are the consequences of two years having gone by without implementing any of the really important recommendations of the National Anti-Racism Framework? What do you see as the consequences of that?

We think that implementing the framework would go some way towards creating a society where we can all live with equity, dignity and respect. We've seen horrific racist violence in the last two years, incredibly horrific. When I think about, for example, the massacre at Bondi and what happened there, we don't know if any one thing might have stopped that from happening. But we know that, of the two alleged perpetrators, at least one went to school here, they both had jobs, and those are two touch points at which that person who went on a pathway to that hateful outcome may have been diverted from that pathway of hate. So there is opportunity to build racial literacy, to improve understanding, and to build that equity, dignity and respect we want in our society. Our framework provides the opportunity to do that.
Minister, you've heard the commissioner talk about the consequences of two years of this framework sitting there. Why hasn't the government responded to the framework?

Well, there are a couple of things. I don't think it's accurate to say that it's just been sitting there. There's no requirement for the government to respond to the report but nevertheless it has been guiding policy decisions and policy development, and there have been a number of things that the government has progressed. We're taking a multifaceted approach over several portfolios. Some of the things that we've progressed is further funding to the commission for a number of projects, a review of the Australian curriculum to embed antiracism principles. I can take you through the rest of the list, but I think the key point that you are seeking to understand is that we are still considering the recommendations.

When will you actually respond to the recommendations? You heard the commissioner say racism has been rising in the last two years. The commissioner gave a horrific example. But there's racism like Muslim women's hijabs being torn off. There are antimigrant rallies. There was a huge one just last weekend. There was someone on the public transport who called a 13-year old girl an 'immigrant mutt'. These are just the tip of the iceberg. Why would you not tackle racism systematically as the framework recommends? There are zero recommendations of the framework that you have implemented. Why not? What are you waiting for?

I really can't add to my previous answer other than to reiterate to you what I've said to you before, which is that we are considering the recommendations of the National Anti-Racism Framework and we are progressing work to address racism in a number of ways. The department can take you through some of that work that we're doing, but to say that we're not taking any action is not true.

No action from the framework. I come back to you, Commissioner. The commission's 'Change the system. Change the story.' campaign makes clear that tackling workplace racism requires leadership and institutional responsibility, not simply expecting individuals experiencing racism to deal with it themselves. Do you think parliament, as a workplace, should be setting the standard on antiracism?

It is very important for leaders, whether they be in politics, business or civil society, to engage in behaviours that they want people to follow and the behaviours that should be reflected in the rest of society. That is something I've said previously. People look to leaders for guidance. In that sense, it's very important for parliamentarians and others to model antiracist behaviours. That's why one of the recommendations in the National Anti-Racism Framework is, specifically, antiracism training for parliamentarians and standards to be set in parliament.
Do you think that antiracism training should be mandatory for parliamentarians and senior staff?
It is one of the recommendations in the framework.

I have a couple more questions for the minister on this topic, but I want to clarify with you first, Commissioner. There was reporting in August this year that highlighted that you had said that someone very senior in government had told you to stop talking about racism because you're disrupting the social cohesion. Was that accurate reporting?
Yes.
Minister, are you aware of who—which very senior person in government—asked the commissioner to do that?
No.
Do you think it is responsible for that very senior person to say to a race discrimination commissioner, 'Stop talking about racism because you're disrupting social cohesion'?

Again, I'm here representing the Attorney-General, and I seek to speak on her behalf. I think the Attorney-General's view is that there's no place for racism in Australian society and any form of hatred or discrimination is fully condemned. I don't know the context of that commentary or the conversation. I have nothing in front of me about it, and I will be very cautious in how I respond. The Attorney-General's view is that, no matter anyone's race or religion, they should be able to enjoy life in Australia without prejudice or discrimination.

Minister, you don't need a context for that. The commissioner has just said the reporting was accurate. Someone very senior in government told the commissioner, 'Stop talking about racism because you're disrupting the social cohesion.. Do you agree that the commissioner should stop talking about racism?
I'm not going to—
Minister, you're here to answer our questions. It's a very straightforward question.

Excuse me, Senator. If you would like to hear my answer, you can give me the call. I'm not going to add to my previous answer. I've reiterated the position of the Attorney-General in relation to racism and to the work of the commission, and I'm not going to add to any of that other commentary.
Minister, does your government believe that we should stop talking about racism?

That is not the position of the government. I have talked about racism this evening. Also, it's not borne out in the facts, with what the government has done not only to fund the commission but to develop work in this space. The new antiracism campaign funded by the government is a very clear example of the government seeking to talk about this issue to Australians.

Could you make a commitment today to talk to this very senior person who asked the commissioner to stop talking about racism and maybe, probably, give them some antiracism training. I have a few more questions for you, Minister—and then I'll finish, Chair.
Thank you.

Minister, in a recent New South Wales Supreme Court case, Justice Fagan found that the IHRA formulation of antisemitism does not reflect the established usage and understanding of antisemitism in Australia and said that it is so verbose and imprecise that it could not realistically be attributed to an ordinary, reasonably informed Australian. Has the government reviewed its adoption of the IHRA definition in light of that judgement?

Senator, you have to bear with me. The context of that I don't think is relevant to the Australian Human Rights Commission. I've got information in front of me about the government's funding of the commission. I can get some more information for you. Otherwise I can take that on notice.

It is a question about racism and the definition of a certain type of racism, which a judge has said 'does not reflect the established usage and understanding of the term "antisemitic".' You can't answer that question?
Senator, what I'm saying to you is I will seek to get information for you. If I can do that before the end of this session, I'll come back to you.

I guess my question is: has the government reviewed its adoption of the IHRA definition? Also, Justice Fagan warned that using the label 'antisemitic' for criticism of Israel or Zionism can unfairly harm people and risks undermining the seriousness of genuine antisemitism. I want an answer from your government whether the government accepts that concern, and, if it does, why does the government still think it is appropriate to continue using and promoting that definition?
I will ask officials to respond, because I think there's a more formal response to that, and, if there's anything I can get for you from the minister, I will come back to you, Senator.
What I would say is that I understand that particular statement by the judge was made in a specific criminal case, which isn't necessarily a commentary on the definition in all the contexts.

I have one quick question for you, Commissioner. Since the minister didn't want to comment on the very senior person in government who asked you to stop talking about racism, are you willing to tell us who that was?
It's important for me to maintain relationships with the government and everyone that I work with so—

I don't want to force you. I do understand that. Coming back to the commentary on the IHRA definition, what the judge said was entirely the commentary on the IHRA definition, so I'm not sure how it's not relevant.
It was in a criminal matter, as I understand it. We can't comment or give an opinion on a statement by a judge, but it was specific to a criminal case.
Yes, but it was very specific to the IHRA definition more broadly. I don't know if you've read the judgement of Justice Fagan or not.
I have seen reporting and aspects of that judgement.
Yes, that's fine.
Senator Blyth.

We'll go back to the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, if I may. I have a quick question that stands alone. In the Lesbian Action Group Inc. v the Australian Human Rights Commission there was found to be deficiencies in their temporary exemption guidelines, which the court mentioned in its findings as it set aside the decision and sent it back to the ART. Have those guidelines been updated?
They're in the process of being updated.
When do you expect them to be updated?
We anticipate that in the next two months they will be updated.
So anyone who's wanting to apply for an exemption, are they using the old guidelines?

They would be using the old guidelines, but they can also seek information, as I said previously, from members of the commission to take them through the guidelines but also the specific issue around section 10A and indivisibility and universality of human rights.

Given some of the questions that we've posed today to the Attorney-General's Department, do you think that, given the recent outcome of Giggle v Tickle, perhaps those temporary exemption guidelines should be updated a little faster? We've got a lot of businesses where people aren't quite sure whether they need to apply for exemptions and how to do it.
We are working on it as speedily as we can.

Okay. Senator Cash went into the decision of the High Court which has now refused special leave. Do you now accept Professor Gerber's assessment that this makes it 'crystal clear that employers cannot lawfully exclude men who identify as women from female-only recruitment drives designed to address the underrepresentation of women' in those particular industries?
Sorry, could you repeat the question, Senator?

Professor Gerber's assessment is that it makes it 'crystal clear employers cannot lawfully exclude men who identify as women from female-only recruitment drives designed to address underrepresentation of women' in those particular fields.
I'd have to take that on notice, but that appears to be correct.

I would appreciate that. In light of the full Federal Court's finding that special measures under section 7D cannot come at the expense of transgender women or men who identify as women, what practical advice is the commission now giving to employers or government agencies running targeted female recruitment or promotion programs in male dominated industries?

As I said previously, there are measures through the Sex Discrimination Act where men and women can be treated differently if the aim is to achieve substantive equality. Any individual situation will rely on an assessment of those circumstances.
Would those processes require that an exemption be applied for?
Under the Sex Discrimination Act, there are special measures as well as exemptions, as I outlined previously.
How will someone know whether it's a special measure or an exemption?
As I said in my previous answer, they can contact the commission and we can explain the exemption process, and one of the first steps of that is assessing whether or not an exemption is necessary.
Okay. So an engineering firm that is looking to hire more females would need to get in touch with you first to figure out if it's able to do that?

Not necessarily. There are also provisions within the act itself, for example, which allow single-sex spaces, such as in schooling or in accommodation, so they don't necessarily need to seek advice on that if they read the act.

When you say that in terms of accommodation or schooling, are you saying that in the case of schooling, where there is an exemption that is being applied so you can have a girls school and a boys school—and there are lots of cases of that across the country. So you could have a school that, if it's an all-girls school, can't enrol boys who identify as girls?
I've just been refreshed that on our website there is detailed guidance about the application of special measures, so anyone could seek assistance from reading through that.
On the website?
Correct.

But in terms of where you're wanting—I'm using your words here—single-sex accommodation or single-sex schools, are they single sex—if it's, say, accommodation for females, could a man who identifies as a woman be included in that, or would a workplace have to apply for an exemption?
If they are seeking to exclude someone on the basis of gender identity, then they would need to seek an exemption.
And that would be the same, I'm assuming, for—

Sorry, I will clarify that. In relation to religious schools, there is an exemption provided to religious schools that they can treat people differently, or discriminate lawfully, on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, sex, marital status—

So religious schools can. In the case of Giggle v Tickle, you appeared as a friend of the court in the matter. Can you confirm whether the commission's submissions aligned with the full court's ultimate conclusion that measures to promote equality for women cannot justify differential treatment on the ground of gender identity? And would you be willing to table those submissions?

The submissions that we made in the full Federal Court related to the understanding of section 7D and the understanding of special measures and how they functioned, which includes the—there are a range of special grounds within section 7D.
Are you willing to table those submissions?
I'd have to take that on notice.
Certainly. If you could, I would appreciate those being tabled.
Sorry, Senator—those submissions are already public. They're on the Federal Court website.
The submissions that you made are available?
Correct.

Given the outcome of Giggle v Tickle, can employers still lawfully maintain single-sex facilities, change rooms and recruitment processes restricted to biological females for reasons of privacy, safety or competitive fairness?
I refer to my previous answer. There are a range of—
I know there are a range, but I'm asking specifically on these. It's privacy, safety or competitive fairness. So I'm not—
There is a different answer to each of those questions. There are about five questions within that one question. So I would have to take it on notice and refer to that.

If you could, that would be very helpful. Senator Cash has previously questioned you on pregnancy protections applying to men who identify as women. Does the commission now interpret the act as requiring employers to treat men who identify as women identically to biological females in recruitment and pregnancy related decisions, even where biological differences are material?
That's speculating on a hypothetical scenario. I can't respond to that.

It's not speculating. I'm happy for you to take it on notice, if you're not able, but I'm not asking you to speculate on a hypothetical. I know you've probably been coached to say that to things you don't want to answer.
Senator Blyth, is that necessary?
Was there coaching involved? Were there any meetings in relation to how you should be answering questions prior to estimates, President?
Of course we prepare for Senate estimates every time.
Did you have any meetings in relation to how any of the commissioners would respond to questions?
Every Senate estimates we have a meeting of all commissioners to prepare how we answer questions relating to Senate estimates—
Did you meet with anyone else other than the commissioners?
We engaged a communications consultant to assist with this round of Senate estimates, and I think we have previously as well.
You engaged a communications consultant?
Correct.
Did the taxpayer pay for that?
Yes.
What was the cost to the taxpayer of a communications consultant being engaged by the commission to help—are you paid $550,000 a year or thereabouts?
You're talking about my own remuneration?
Yes, your own salary.
That's set by the Remuneration Tribunal. It's a salary of just under $500,000.
You're telling me you needed—what did you say—a communications consultant?
Correct—for one short session. And I can take it on notice and provide the cost of that to the committee.
Were there any other meetings with anyone in this room in relation to how the commission might answer questions at estimates?
I'm confused by the question, but no.
So no one—
Sorry, I don't know who's sitting behind me, so it's hard to answer.
No—in front of you.
In front of me?
The committee.
Sorry. We had a meeting last Monday with Senator Blyth and Senator Stewart.
In relation to—
The conduct of Senate estimates.
Thank you.
I'm handing the call back to Senator Blyth.

I just have one last question for this. The High Court refused leave primarily on the construction of section 7D of the act. Has the commission sought or received any legal advice on whether the meaning of 'sex' itself remains open to further litigation, and does the commission consider that the current state of the law adequately protects the biological rights of women to single-sex spaces and opportunities?
There are two questions within that question. If you could separate them out, then I will answer each question.
You want me to ask you one at a time?
Correct.
Certainly. Has the commission sought or received any legal advice on whether the meaning of 'sex' itself remains open to further litigation?
Not that I'm aware of.
Does the commission consider that the current state of the law adequately protects biological women's rights to single-sex spaces and opportunities?

As I said previously, the Sex Discrimination Act provides protection from discrimination on the basis of sex, on the basis of sexual orientation and all the other grounds and that the understanding of 'woman' is an inclusive definition.
This is quite specific, though. I'm asking whether the commission considers that the current state of the law adequately protects biological women's rights to single-sex spaces and opportunities.
That it protects all women, including—

No. I haven't asked you that, because you use a different definition of 'women' that is really quite offensive. I'm asking you whether the commission feels as though the law is adequately protecting the rights of biological women to single-sex spaces and opportunities. It's a yes or no.

My understanding of the Sex Discrimination Act is that it has the means within it to provide protections and balance the interests and rights of all women. That includes your framing. Can I add one clarification to a previous question that Senator Cash asked, which was about our role in the Lesbian Action Group—
I was about to ask about that, so that was exactly the topic I was about to go to.
Yes, you can answer that question.
That was exactly where I was about to go to.
I'm also going to hand the call to Senator Cash, so, if you want to respond, I'll give her the call.
In relation to that, we became a party because there was no other contradictor, and that's why we were in the Federal Court.
That was my question. Could you confirm that the commission was the only contradictor. Was that in the Federal Court?
I think, perhaps, we take this question on notice to provide an absolutely correct answer.
Are you a contradictor before the ART currently?
No. We're not involved in the case.
You're not involved in the ART case?
No.
No—that's correct.
You refused it at first instance, and it then went to the ART?
Yes. My understanding is that we weren't involved at the ART, we weren't involved in the Federal Court and we're now not involved in the remittal back to the ART, but we will clarify that further.
But when did you become a contradictor?

That's what I'm saying—that we weren't a contradictor and that the government normally stands in the shoes of the commission. That's the usual practice. But, again, I want to provide a completely accurate answer for the committee, so can I take that on notice and we'll clarify for the committee.
Did you provide any submissions to either the ART or the Federal Court in relation to the Lesbian Action Group application?
My understanding is we didn't. But, again, I caveat that with—

Commissioner Cody, do you know, as the Sex Discrimination Commissioner? Did you provide any submissions to either the ART or the Federal Court in relation to the Lesbian Action Group's application for the exemption?
Senator, I would prefer to take this question on notice to be one hundred per cent accurate.

How do you not know that? This case has been going on for three years. It's been discussed publicly across Australia. You don't know if the commission provided submissions. Is that your evidence to this committee?
My evidence to the committee is that it's a question I've taken on notice.
You don't know, here, today, if you provided a submission to either the ART or the Federal Court?
Sorry, Senator, I don't want to—
Is that your evidence? You don't know.
It's a question I've taken on notice, Senator.

Good grief! You know you don't take something on notice when you have the information in your possession. So is your evidence to the committee that it is not within your knowledge as to whether or not the Australian Human Rights Commission or the Sex Discrimination Commissioner provided a submission to either the ART process or the Federal Court process in relation to the Lesbian Action Group's application for an exemption.
Senator, can I clarify because the team is listening to this, and they're advising me that we were a contradictor in the tribunal and the court, so I retract what I said before.
Yes, that's what I thought.
My apologies.
Thank you. You were a contradictor.
This was because there was no other contradictor, and we provided submissions in both forums. So my apologies, and I'm happy to be able to clarify that.
And I do appreciate you being up front about that. Do you have to accept the role as a contradictor?
Can we take that on notice and get back to you about the usual course?
That's fine.
When our decisions are appealed, there's a process with the government where we talk to the government and sometimes the government appears as a contradictor.
Just quickly, in relation to the Cost Protection Act, did the commission campaign for the Cost Protection Act on the basis that adverse costs deter vulnerable litigants?

We had a more complex position than campaigning for it. We had had a range of different positions over a period of time, and ultimately our submission was that there should be less of a disadvantage on an applicant bringing a case to the Federal Court, but I wouldn't frame it as campaigning for it.
Okay, but can I confirm you then sought costs against the Lesbian Action Group in their case.

In the Lesbian Action Group case, the parties or the commission and the Lesbian Action Group agreed that they would follow the normal rule that the costs would follow whoever was successful, and in that situation, the costs were awarded against the commission.
Did the commission ever consider simply not seeking costs against the Lesbian Action Group, given that they are a volunteer organisation?
It was an agreement between the Lesbian Action Group and the commission that they would follow the normal rule in costs.

External counsel, I understand, costs $38,000 before GST plus in-house staff time. What was the total cost to the commission of opposing the Lesbian Action Group across the tribunal, the Federal Court and the appeal?
In the tribunal, it was $10,700. In the Federal Court—I can give you the individual amounts, but I can't add them up in my head.
That's okay. Individual amounts are fine.
Counsel fees and disbursements are $16,832. Flights and accommodation are $1,966. Transcripts are $2,134. And then the costs that we paid to the Lesbian Action Group was $125,000.
The costs you paid.
Because we lost, so we paid the Lesbian Action Group's costs.
Yes, but then you sought costs against the Lesbian Action Group.
But they weren't awarded in our favour because we lost.
So you ended up having to pay the Lesbian Action Group?
Correct.
That was $125,000 that you paid to the Lesbian Action Group. Is that correct?
That's correct.
And that was on top of all of the other—
Our own costs.
Your own costs, okay, but the exemption still has not been granted.
No.
Senator Blyth.
Dr Cody, how many exemptions or special measures exemptions have you granted during your tenure as commissioner?

I don't grant special measures decisions. That is something that is accepted that no exemption is needed and therefore a special measure applies. In terms of exemptions, they are published on our website. From memory, the commission has granted four exemptions.
Senator Shoebridge.

Thanks, all, for your attendance. It always ends up being late; I'm sorry about that. I appreciate all the work you do and the work of the commission. It's one of those critical institutions that sometimes pushes back against other narratives in society, and I just want to thank you all for continuing to do that work. It's really appreciated. Dr Cody, recent research from Dr Sara Meger from the University of Melbourne suggests that misogyny and antifeminism are often linked with broader extremist attitudes and forms of prejudice. She published a recent paper in this with detailed research. First of all, are you aware of that work?
I am aware of that research.

How does the commission's work address those interconnected things—misogyny, often homophobia, transphobia and other forms of discrimination—and, when you look at that research, what implications does it have for us if we're trying to make decisions to stop hate and keep people safe?

We do identify the interlinking between rigid ideas around gender and increasing misogyny within the community. That was brought out partly through our Equal identities report as well as in the most recent report on pregnancy discrimination and family responsibilities discrimination. We would see that sharing of care and the breaking down of some of those rigid gender roles as being one means to try and tackle the rigidity between caring and working and therefore ideas around gender. So that would be one way, and the education around sexual harassment and the positive duty would be another means to try and address some of the understandings of relationships and what is appropriate behaviour within the workplace.

In your work, if you look at the impact of misogyny in particular, how do you see it in terms of the age demographics of people who are perhaps falling down the path of being misogynist? Where do you see the age—

The research shows that it is in fact increasing in younger age groups and that the higher age groups are in fact tending more towards gender equality or gender-friendly attitudes and understandings. It demonstrates the need for education across primary education and secondary education and right through into the workplace around the appropriate levels of respectful relationships and consent.

Often the work you do as a commission is focused on governments as employers and employment relationships—those very formal relationships that are often largely operating at an adult level. Have you considered undertaking work to focus upon dealing with young men and boys in particular, and have you considered how you would do some work to address the data that you're seeing?

One of the recommendations coming out of the Speaking from Experience project was about the need for education around respectful relationships. My colleague the commissioner for children and young people, Commissioner Deb Tsorbaris, is looking at some of that work with young people and some of those attitudes.
Do you see that as combined work between the two commissioners—working together on that?
It is combined work. We work very effectively together.

There's been a lot of discussion tonight, as we've seen every time you've come here in my recent memory, about the Giggle v Tickle case. Given the large amount of public commentary about it and the large amount of parliamentary time that's been devoted to discussion of it, have you seen any change, during this time, in the number of complaints, inquiries or reports of harassment involving trans and gender diverse people? Have you seen any trends in that regard?

I'm not aware of, within our complaint data, those having increased. But, certainly, from our engagements with stakeholders in the LGBQTI+ community, we know there is rising harassment and abuse of trans and gender diverse people, as we know that social media also does translate into real-life harassment.
Is that what the community's telling you?
Yes.
That their experience is increasing harassment? What does that mean for the daily life of our trans community or our gender diverse community?

I think that the experience of harassment and denial of identity is very painful for that very small but significant part of our community and makes it very difficult for people to be able to participate fully and to be treated with full dignity and respect.
What about personal safety? Are they speaking to you about concerns about personal safety or impacts on their personal safety?
The most recent report in which I spoke was the Equal Identities report, and, certainly, in those consultations, people were concerned about those issues.
Thanks, Commissioner. Commissioner Fitzgerald, we didn't want your visit to be in vain, so it's nice to see you.
Indeed, I think I've just lost a bet.

Well, I'd ask you then to give double to a charity to make up for that. Commissioner, you participated in the Ageing in Difference conference. One part of the conference communique highlighted that LGBTI older people are continuing to experience barriers to inclusive and culturally safe aged care. Do you have any observations about that communique? What is your understanding of it?

Yes. Older people that are LGBTIQA+ have always experienced discrimination, particularly in relation to residential aged care. In an inquiry that I headed for the Productivity Commission in 2010, we highlighted the need for the special needs and considerations of LGBTIQ older people to be taken into account. Immediately following that report, one of the providers, the Uniting Church, issued a new protocol in relation to that community within their own aged care. But the evidence to date from the community itself is that they feel they are still discriminated against, that they're not able to be with their partners and that some institutions treat their visitors differently. So we've got a lot more work to do on that. The new Aged Care Act, of course, requires providers to take into account a whole range of issues, including the lived experience of people, issues of sex and gender and issues in relation to their cultural and spiritual background.
Is that now a legislative requirement, and are you responsible in any way for its oversight?

The new aged care legislation that came into being in November of last year has about two to three pages of both consumer and human rights in that particular area. They deal with the lived experience of individuals, including trauma and, as I indicated, cultural and spiritual rights. They are not enforceable directly at law, however. Similar to that which is in the NDIA act, they are incorporated in practices such as standards, complaint handling and accreditation, and they can be subject to complaints through the complaint commissioner with the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission. That's the body that deals with those particular matters. They are able to be complained about, but they're not able to be actioned directly at law.

Given they're such critical rights based provisions—particularly for the LGBTIQ community, but I would imagine there'd be other vulnerable communities who need that inclusive wraparound for aged care as well—have you considered whether or not it might be appropriate for you to undertake an inquiry or some kind of formal body of work to review how aged-care residential facilities are providing that inclusive environment?

The answer is no. Just bear in mind that there is the Inspector-General of Aged Care, and that particular role oversights the entire aged-care system, including that which is provided directly by the government and through the community at large. But it is a matter that I think, over time, is very important. The question for everybody in relation to aged care is: how will we ensure that the rights that are embedded into this new legislation are actually given presence in the actual lives of older people? So I think the notion of an inquiry on an ongoing basis, around specific issues or generally, is very prudent. The question would be who would be best placed to do that.
Are you having discussions, or is there any formal engagement with that other office?

We've had engagement with the inspector-general's office as we've had engagement with the aged-care quality and safety issues around how in fact these rights become enforceable in the way that I've described. We haven't had discussions in relation to the need for an inquiry.

One other matter that's been raised with my office is that people in faith based aged-care facilities who are seeking to take advantage of state and territory laws in relation to end of life are finding themselves often in conflict with aged-care facilities. Their decisions are not being respected and not being permitted, in some instances. Have any complaints to that effect been raised with your office?

Not that I'm aware of—certainly not with me. And I'm not aware that it would have come through the complaints area of the commission. The legislation is complex because it's legislation that's been passed in each state and territory, and each state and territory has slightly different versions as to the exemptions that are provided to faith based residential aged-care facilities. The vast majority of legislation does not require a faith based organisation to actually facilitate voluntary assisted dying, but it does require them to be able to aid and assist the person to access those services outside of the aged-care facility. But I just want to indicate that it does vary from state to state. The provisions generally, in relation to these issues at a national level, would go through the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission.
Thank you very much, Commissioner; I'm sorry about the bet. I have some questions for Commissioner Kayess, but I understand she's unwell. Is that right?
She's unwell.
Those questions in relation to the NDIS reforms and their implementation and what, if any, work that has given to the commission—President, are you aware of anything in that regard?
Commissioner Kayess has been closely involved in providing submissions on behalf of the commission to—

It's probably best I put those questions on notice for Commissioner Kayess. Queensland, as you know, has passed laws banning a certain slogan in relation to Palestine, and I understand more than 20 people have been charged under those Queensland laws. Has the commission, President, assessed whether or not those laws are compatible with human rights and freedom of political communication and considered whether or not it would participate in any way in the High Court challenge?

I'll answer part of the question. I know there are parliamentary inquiries that are looking at whether or not those phrases should be banned. We have made a submission to at least one of those parliamentary inquiries, which said that, in general, we don't think it's a good idea to ban specific phrases. Obviously, those cases are before the High Court. We haven't had a discussion as a commission about whether or not the commission should intervene in that particular case. For interventions relating to constitutional issues, as I understand it, we need the permission of the government to be able to intervene. We have not sought that permission.

One of the basic human rights, of course, is freedom of speech. That freedom is not unlimited in our country. It's recognised that, if you are threatening violence against another person, there are reasonable limitations. But the basic concept of freedom of speech is something I assume the commission supports.
Absolutely. It's fundamental to human rights.
Thanks very much.

That concludes the questions that we have for you this evening. I want to conclude by saying thank you to Commissioner Finlay. I don't know if we should apologise, or maybe you consider it an estimates blessing that you haven't had to come to the table! But thank you very much for all the time you've given to us in Senate estimates. You go with our thanks. We'll also apologise in advance for the estimates speed dating we're about to do to get through the remaining three agencies by 9.30.
Senator Cash, you have the call.

Thank you, Mr Hawkins. I will put a lot on notice for you in relation to statistics. Can I go to protection visa reviews, just to clarify the position in relation to payment. Is it correct that a person refused a protection visa by Home Affairs can apply to the ART for merits review without paying a single dollar up front?
I understand that to be the case at present.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Yes, that's correct.
If the ART sets aside the decision and sends it back to Home Affairs, is it correct that the applicant generally would not pay a fee for that review?
They will be entitled to a refund.
To a refund?
I'm sorry. I shouldn't have used that term. They don't have to pay the fee.
If the ART upholds the original refusal, the applicant is ordinarily charged, I understand, $2,293?
I'm not sure of the amount.
I'll get you to take that on notice. How many unsuccessful protection visa applicants actually pay that fee?

We'd have to take that on notice, but I would venture that there aren't many because they go home and don't pay the fee. The penalty, of course, is that they can't return to the country with an outstanding debt to the Commonwealth.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: The 2024-25 financial statements recorded $17.494 million in expected credit losses associated with protection visa review fees. What does that actually mean? What is the credit loss associated with them? How is that incurred?
I might check with our CFO on that.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: In regard to your question, that would be an impairment loss, and that's sort of like a bad debt.
It's just a bad debt.
Yes.
They were charged the fee but didn't pay the fee.
Correct.
How much of the protection visa review fees invoiced in 2025-26 has actually been collected, and how much remains unpaid?
I'll have to take that on notice in terms of the specifics, but the percentage is around 20 per cent.
Collected. In terms of the ART's time in a dollar figure, what is the average cost of conducting a protection visa merits review?
I'll take that on notice.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Okay. Can I also then ask, after deducting fees recovered, what the net cost is to the Australian taxpayer.
We'll take that on notice for you.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Thank you very much. As at 31 July 2026, you had 133,745 outstanding matters. Is there an updated figure on that, Mr Hawkins, as at 26 October?
I could give you to 30 September.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Fantastic.

witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Sadly, there are more and more applying and you're obviously just not able to keep up, hence the ART bill coming is something that does, obviously, need support. That might, hopefully, assist you in some small way. Chair, these are all statistical. I'm happy to go to Senator Shoebridge if he has questions here as well.
Thank you, Senator Cash. Senator Shoebridge.
Good to see you, Mr Hawkins.
Congratulations to you, Senator, on your ascension to the leadership of your party.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Thank you very much. I appreciate it. Despite having more finalisations than ever, I think a quote from you is, 'Demand for our services grew faster than our capacity to finalise matters, reaching the highest level to date.' I think that might be a quote from the annual report.
Yes.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: The tribunal's cases on hand have increased from, per the last numbers I had, 112,591 at the start of the reporting period for the last financial year to 133,749. Is that at the end of the financial year?
That's at the end of financial year, correct.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Where are they now?
As I said to Senator Cash, it's 136,236.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: What has driven that case load?
Lodgements.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: I understand that.
Our finalisations are 109 per cent of our target.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: What is your target?
It's 74,000 and some.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: How many lodgements did you have last year?
There were 87,000 lodgements last year.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Those numbers aren't matching.

No, they're not. As we explained before, we do have a funding model by which we are appropriated. The funding model has a cap on it of our business-as-usual funding of 345 FTE of members. When our lodgements for the previous 12 months—which is not necessarily a calendar year or a financial year; it is the 12 months of most recent data—are provided, a calculation is then made of the number of finalisations we should be able to achieve given the spread of cases and case types against that cap of 345.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Can I just focus on two case flows that that you have—or case loads as the case might be. The first is in relation to the NDIS. It appears that lodgements with the tribunal contesting an NDIS decision have grown by about 130 per cent from 2023-24.
Over the past two years, yes.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: And about 70 per cent of applications lodged for review ended up having the decision changed in some way. Is that right?
Yes.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: What's going wrong that we are seeing so many NDIS matters coming before you? What's the explanation for so many successful applications?
Ninety per cent or more of the NDIS case load are resolved by registrars doing alternate dispute resolution. There is a very high proportion of consent decisions that are reached with the NDIA.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Have you spoken with the NDIA about their ability to do that before it comes to you, with all the costs and delay in bringing a separate agency in?
It's obviously a matter for them, but I would expect that in any matter of a litigious nature where a settlement is reached, consideration is given to the greater cost of prosecuting.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: But you're having no ongoing discussion with the NDIS?
Not at all. I'm having a lot of ongoing discussions with them about their future case load, so yes.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Indeed. Do you have any expectations about what those changes will mean to your future case load?
No, we just don't have the detail.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Minister, could you take on notice whether or not there's been any communication between the Attorney and the minister responsible for the NDIS about this—I think it's appropriate to call it a surge, the 130 per cent increase in lodgements in relation to the NDIS over the last two years—and whether or not any efforts have been made at the NDIS end to stop feeding these matters into the ART—
Yes, I'll take that on notice for you.
and, if so, what are the outcomes? The other case load is the student visa case load. Legislation's been passed or is in the process of being passed.
Which parts? We've got the decisions on the papers legislation—
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: decisions on the papers, which has passed.
which came into effect on 1 June.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Yes. Tell me what's happened in relation to that. What's happened in terms of directions given to registrars and/or others?

Let me just get some statistics for you. We're scaling up our capacity for members to be able to do these matters on the papers, which requires, as you're probably aware, a service of a notice, a 367F notice on applicants, to basically put their best case forward. Approximately 7,000 of those invitations have been sent to applicants since 1 June, and I must stress that it's taken us that month of June to gear up. From 1 July, we've really hit our straps with a great number of those notices being issued. A life of a notice could be 11 weeks. By the time you go from a notice, allowing 28 days for a response, then looking at the response—indeed, if there is a response—in which case it will go straight to a registrar for dismissal. If there is a response, there might be a further direction or order issued and then a response to that, and then that'll go to a member. That could take 11 weeks, so we're right in that sweet spot at the moment of allocating those types of matters to registrars and members.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: So some 7,000 367F notices, did you say, have been issued?
Yes.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Can you provide to this committee the standard 367F notice.
What it looks like?
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Yes.
I can do that for you, sure.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Given the time and I know there are other agencies wafting, can you provide as much granular detail as you can about the number of notices that have been issued, the number of matters that have been determined on the papers, the number of matters that have been dismissed, and the number of matters where there's been a contest and it's been determined not to deal with a lot of papers.
Sure. I can tell you that 866 matters have been finalised on the papers to date. Members have disposed of 533 of those matters, registrars 333.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: How many of those were dismissed?
I'm expecting that the 333 by the registrars would have been dismissed but I will give you specific details.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: And of the other 533?
In relation to the members, no. I'd have to give you more granulated detail.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Can you provide to the committee whatever directions and/or guidelines and/or training has been given to registrars for the purpose of that work?
Sure.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: I assume that there has been some—
Training? Much training.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Are there guidelines?
I'd have to take that on notice.
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar

text: Alright. Thank you, Mr Hawkins.

Thank you very much to the ART.

text: Recognising that some matters that we prosecute are of significant public interest, the CDPP maintain webpages about a number of cases, and we are conscious that prosecutions are rightly the subject of public discussion. However, public commentary around ongoing proceedings must be approached carefully. It is not only direct interference that undermines trust in our system, but we all have to guard against conduct that might create a perception that the independence of my office has been impacted or compromised, or conduct that may impact ongoing proceedings. To that end, we have now also provided some general guidance on our website about publications and statements that may pose a risk to the administration of justice in the form of ongoing proceedings. Thank you, Chair.

text: The government told the Senate on 13 August that 'the director has considered her position and sees no conflict' in relation to the Ben Roberts-Smith prosecution. Is that an accurate statement of your position, Ms Sharp?

text: Does that conclusion cover an actual conflict, a potential conflict and a perceived conflict of interest?

text: When did you first formally consider whether you had an actual, potential or perceived conflict of interest in relation to the prosecution of Mr Roberts-Smith?

agency: Office of the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions
text: I was appointed in December 2023. In March 2024, before I made any decisions in any war crimes matters, my former role as counsel assisting the Office of the Special Investigator was the subject of formal consideration within the CDPP, and consideration of the conflict was undertaken at that time.

text: You wrote to the department seeking consent on 30 March. My understanding is that the consent to prosecute Oliver Schulz took six days; and the Syrian returnees, 25 days. This was not you, but the Collaery and Witness K cases actually took two years and eight months. Again in relation to the Ben Roberts-Smith prosecution, why was this one turned around so quickly?
